title: Incidence
in30Seconds: Incidence is the number of new cases of a disease that appear in a population over a set time period — the working definition used by MedlinePlus and the CDC. An incidence rate puts the count in perspective: new cases per population per time, like 5 new cases per 1,000 people per year. Incidence shows how fast disease spreads. It is not prevalence, which counts existing cases — that is a sibling topic. Incidence is a speedometer; prevalence is a snapshot.
whyItMatters: Incidence answers the question public health most needs answered: is a disease gaining ground or losing it? When new cases climb, the disease is spreading faster; when they fall, it is slowing. That movement is the earliest signal of a problem — an outbreak taking off, a prevention program working, a vaccine campaign paying off. A count of all existing cases cannot show that movement, because it mixes old and new illness together. Incidence isolates the new cases, and new cases are where action happens. Every outbreak alert, and every success story, starts with new-case counts.
learningObjectives: State the working definition of incidence — the number of new cases of a disease in a population over a time period — and attribute it to MedlinePlus and the CDC.
Explain what an incidence rate adds: new cases per population per time, and compute one with an original worked example.
Distinguish incidence from prevalence: new cases versus existing cases; prevalence is a sibling topic.
Explain why incidence matters: it shows how fast a disease is spreading in a population.
Explain why the time period is part of the measurement, with an original example.
Describe the general practice of measuring incidence — case counts over population denominators — and the honest framing that incidence is a speedometer while prevalence is a snapshot.

collegeVersion.heading: What incidence is
collegeVersion.body: Incidence is the number of new cases of a condition that develop in a population during a specific time period. MedlinePlus, the consumer health reference from the U.S. National Library of Medicine, defines incidence as the number of new cases of a condition, symptom, death, or injury that develop during a specific time period, such as a year. The CDC's Principles of Epidemiology course uses the same core idea: incidence refers to the occurrence of new cases of disease or injury in a population over a specified period of time. Two words in that definition do the work — new and period. New separates a case that began inside the window from one that already existed when the window opened. Period fixes how long the window is: a week, a season, a year. Change either word and the number changes. Incidence is never a free-floating count; it is a count tied to a population and a time period.

collegeVersion.heading: The incidence rate: new cases per population per time
collegeVersion.body: The raw incidence count answers 'how many new cases?' but not 'how fast, relative to how many people?' That second question is what an incidence rate answers. The CDC describes a rate as a measure of how quickly disease occurs in a population, and the incidence rate expresses new cases per population per time. Original example: two towns each report 20 new cases of a skin infection over one year. The counts are identical, but Town A has 2,000 residents and Town B has 20,000. Town A's incidence rate is 20 per 2,000 per year — 10 new cases per 1,000 people per year. Town B's is 20 per 20,000 per year — 1 new case per 1,000 people per year. Same count, ten times the speed. The rate is the fair comparison because it puts new cases on a per-person scale and pins them to a period. Epidemiologists often build the period directly into the denominator as person-time, but for everyday reporting, new cases per population per time carries the same idea in simpler arithmetic.

collegeVersion.heading: Incidence versus prevalence: new versus existing
collegeVersion.body: Incidence and prevalence are the two classic frequency measures of illness, and the CDC's course introduces them side by side: measures of morbidity frequency characterize the number of persons who become ill (incidence) or are ill at a given time (prevalence). Prevalence counts existing cases — everyone with the condition at a point in time, new and preexisting together. Incidence counts only cases that began during the period. Original example: a neighborhood clinic tracks a chronic condition. On January 1, 120 residents have it — a point-in-time count of existing cases. During the year, 30 more residents develop it for the first time — that is the year's incidence. The 120 and the 30 answer different questions: how many people carry the condition now, versus how fast new people are joining them. Prevalence is a full sibling topic of its own in this course; this lesson claims only the distinction.

collegeVersion.heading: Why it matters — and why the period matters
collegeVersion.body: Incidence matters because new cases are the earliest signal of change. When incidence rises, a disease is spreading faster; when it falls, spread is slowing. That is why outbreak detection and the evaluation of prevention programs lean on new-case counts. The period is not a detail; it is part of the measurement. Original example: a college clinic counts new cases of a respiratory illness. In the first two weeks of September, 30 students develop it — 30 new cases in 14 days. Over the whole 15-week semester, 120 new cases appear. Both numbers are incidence, but they describe different windows. Reading them as directly comparable would say the semester was 'four times worse,' when the pace was actually 15 new cases per week in September versus 8 per week across the semester. Same campus, same illness, two different speeds — the period is what makes the speed visible.

collegeVersion.heading: Measuring it — and the honest framing
collegeVersion.body: Measuring incidence follows a general practice: count the new cases, set them against the population, and attach the period to both. The CDC adds an important refinement: the denominator should be the population at risk — the people who could actually develop the disease. A count of new ovarian cancer cases, for example, belongs against a denominator of women, not the whole town. The counts themselves come from case reports, clinics, laboratories, and disease surveillance systems — the machinery that feeds the numerator. Then the honest framing: incidence is a speedometer, and prevalence is a snapshot. A speedometer shows how fast new cases are appearing; a snapshot shows how many cases exist at a moment. A speedometer cannot tell you how full the road is, and a snapshot cannot tell you how fast traffic is moving. Public health needs both, and the honest note is that each answers one question well and the other not at all.

vocabulary.definition: The number of new cases of a disease that develop in a population during a specific time period; the working definition used by MedlinePlus and the CDC.
A person who develops the disease for the first time within the counting period; a case that already existed when the period began is not new.
New cases divided by population and by time, expressed like 5 new cases per 1,000 people per year; the fair way to compare spread across different-sized populations.
The window the count covers — a week, a season, or a year; changing the period changes the incidence number, so it is always stated with the count.
The people who could actually develop the disease and therefore belong in the denominator, such as women for ovarian cancer counts; the CDC's term for the correct denominator.
The raw number of new cases recorded during the period, before it is set against the population and the time to build a rate.
The population, and often the period, that the new cases are divided by when an incidence rate is calculated.
The number of existing cases — new and preexisting together — at a point in time; the sibling measure that incidence is contrasted with in this lesson.

eli10.simplifiedExplanation: Incidence is a simple idea: it counts NEW cases of a disease. If a town has 40 new cases of flu this week, the incidence for the week is 40. It only counts people who got sick for the first time inside the window — not people who were already sick before it started. The time period is part of the definition: new cases in a week, a month, or a year are three different incidence numbers. To compare towns fairly, public health turns the count into a rate — new cases per 1,000 people per year — so a small town and a big city can be compared on the same scale.
eli10.analogy: Think of a bathtub filling with water. Incidence is the flow from the faucet — how much NEW water pours in each minute. Prevalence is the water already in the tub — everything that has accumulated. You cannot tell how fast the tub is filling by staring at the water level alone, because the level also depends on the drain. If you want to know whether the tub is filling faster, you watch the faucet, not the level. That is what incidence does for public health: it watches the new flow, and the rate tells you how fast the flow is per minute — per person, per year.
eli10.analogyLimits: The bathtub is not a perfect picture of disease. Water does not change people's lives, while illness does, and a person who recovers is not 'drained away' in a way that erases the event — the new case still counted. Incidence also counts episodes, not just people: one person can catch the same illness twice, and each episode is a new case. And 'new' depends on where you draw the line — a case is new only relative to the period you chose. Still, faucet-versus-level captures the core difference: flow versus accumulation.

workedExample: Meadowbrook is a town of 10,000 people. At the start of the year, no one in town has a certain foodborne illness. Over the next 12 months, 25 residents develop it for the first time. The incidence for the year is 25 new cases. Now build the incidence rate: divide the new cases by the population and by the time — 25 new cases ÷ 10,000 people ÷ 1 year. That equals 2.5 new cases per 1,000 people per year. The count (25) tells you how much illness appeared; the rate (2.5 per 1,000 per year) tells you how fast it appeared on a scale that any town, of any size, can compare against. Same number of new cases — the rate makes Meadowbrook comparable to everywhere else.

commonMistakes.mistake: Counting old cases as new.
commonMistakes.correction: Incidence counts only cases that began during the period. Someone diagnosed last year is not a new case this year, even if they still have the illness.

commonMistakes.mistake: Reporting a raw count as if it were a rate.
commonMistakes.correction: A count without the population denominator cannot be compared across towns — 40 new cases means something different in a town of 800 than in a town of 80,000.

commonMistakes.mistake: Ignoring the time period.
commonMistakes.correction: New cases over one week and new cases over one year are different numbers. Comparing them directly misreads how fast a disease is spreading.

commonMistakes.mistake: Dropping the period from the rate.
commonMistakes.correction: 5 new cases per 1,000 people per year is not the same as 5 per 1,000 per month. The period is part of the rate and must be stated with it.

compareContrast.distinction: Incidence counts new cases that begin during a period; prevalence counts existing cases — new and preexisting together — at a point in time. New flow versus current level.
A case count is the raw number of new cases; a rate divides new cases by population and time so different-sized populations can be compared fairly.
Incidence is a speedometer — it shows how fast new cases are appearing; prevalence is a snapshot — it shows how many cases exist at a moment. Each answers one question well and the other not at all.

keyTakeaway: Incidence is the count of new cases of a disease in a population over a time period — new cases, per population, per time. It is the speedometer of disease spread; prevalence, the count of existing cases, is the snapshot.

questionBank.prompt: A county health department announces that the incidence of a respiratory illness this season is 120. Which statement correctly describes that number?
options: 120 people in the county developed the illness for the first time during this season
120 people in the county currently have the illness, including people who had it before the season
120 out of every 1,000 residents developed the illness this season
120 people in the county died from the illness this season
questionBank.explanation: Incidence counts new cases — people who developed the illness for the first time during the period. Counting everyone who currently has it (including preexisting cases) describes prevalence; the per-1,000 version is a rate; and deaths are a mortality measure, not incidence.

questionBank.prompt: Lakeview has 8,000 residents and recorded 40 new cases of a stomach illness over one year. Which of the following states the incidence rate correctly?

40 new cases per 1,000 people per year
5 new cases per 1,000 people per year
5 new cases per 8,000 people per year
questionBank.explanation: The incidence rate divides new cases by population and by time: 40 new cases ÷ 8,000 people ÷ 1 year = 5 new cases per 1,000 people per year. Option A drops the population, option B misdivides (40 per 1,000 would need 40 cases in a population of 1,000), and option D keeps the wrong scale.

questionBank.prompt: In January, a clinic counts 60 people with an ongoing skin condition, including 10 who were newly diagnosed that month. Which statement is correct?

The incidence for January is 50, because the 10 new cases should be subtracted

questionBank.prompt: A public health officer says, 'Incidence is a speedometer; prevalence is a snapshot.' Which statement best matches that idea?

title: Prevalence
in30Seconds: Prevalence is the total number of existing cases of a disease in a population at a given time — the people living with the condition, not the people newly getting it. Point prevalence counts one moment; period prevalence counts a window of time. Prevalence shows the total burden of disease. New cases, recoveries, deaths, and migration all change it. Measuring it means counting current cases and dividing by the population. Prevalence is a snapshot; incidence, its sibling topic, is the movie.
whyItMatters: Prevalence matters because it answers the question behind most health planning: how many people need help right now? A hospital system deciding how many diabetes clinics to staff, a school district budgeting for asthma care, a country weighing a vaccination campaign — all of them start with the count of people living with the condition today. Prevalence also changes how you read health news. When a report says one in ten adults has a condition, it is describing a snapshot, not a flow. Knowing that lets you ask the next question, whether new cases are rising or falling, without confusing the two. The count of existing cases is where public health begins its work.
learningObjectives: Define prevalence as the total number of existing cases of a disease in a population at a given time, using the working definition attributed to the CDC's Principles of Epidemiology.
Distinguish point prevalence, measured at one moment, from period prevalence, measured over a window of time.
Distinguish prevalence from incidence: existing cases versus new cases, with incidence named as a sibling topic.
Explain what prevalence shows — the total burden of disease — and name what changes it: new cases, recoveries, deaths, and migration.
Describe how prevalence is measured, counting current cases over the population, and apply the honest framing that prevalence is a snapshot while incidence is the movie.

collegeVersion.heading: What prevalence is
collegeVersion.body: The working definition used in this lesson comes from the CDC's Principles of Epidemiology, the agency's standard training manual. Prevalence, sometimes called prevalence rate, is the proportion of persons in a population who have a particular disease or attribute at a specified point in time or over a specified period of time. In plainer words: prevalence is the total number of existing cases of a disease in a population at a given time. Three parts of that definition carry the meaning. The count is of existing cases, so a person diagnosed last week and a person diagnosed five years ago count exactly the same, as long as both still have the condition when the count happens. The count is tied to a population, so it only means something when the group being counted is named, whether it is the residents of a town, the students of a school, or the adults of a country. And the count is tied to a time, because existing cases are not a fixed fact; they are true of one moment or one window and can change by the next. Prevalence is usually stated as a share of the population, such as 4 percent, which is what makes it useful for comparing one place, group, or year to another.

collegeVersion.heading: Point prevalence and period prevalence
collegeVersion.body: The phrase 'a given time' can mean two things, and the CDC keeps them separate. Point prevalence is prevalence measured at a particular point in time: the proportion of persons with the disease or attribute on a particular date. Imagine a health team that visits every clinic in a town on the first of June and counts everyone living with asthma that day. That single-day count is a point prevalence. Period prevalence is prevalence measured over an interval of time: the proportion of persons with the disease or attribute at any time during the interval. Imagine a school nurse who records every student who had the flu at any point during the school year, whether in October or in May. That year-long window is a period prevalence. The difference is the width of the lens: one moment versus a window. Both count existing cases, new and preexisting alike, which is what separates both from incidence, the sibling topic that counts only cases that begin during the window.

collegeVersion.heading: Prevalence versus incidence, and what prevalence shows
collegeVersion.body: Prevalence and incidence are frequently confused, and the CDC says the key difference is in their numerators. The numerator of incidence is new cases that occurred during a given time period. The numerator of prevalence is all cases present during a given time period, which includes new cases and preexisting cases together. Incidence is a sibling topic with its own lesson; this lesson only needs the distinction: incidence is the number of new cases, prevalence is the total number of existing cases. What prevalence shows is the total burden of disease — how much of the population is living with the condition right now, and therefore how much care, support, and cost the condition carries. That is why the CDC notes that prevalence rather than incidence is often measured for chronic diseases such as diabetes or osteoarthritis, which last a long time and have onset dates that are hard to pinpoint. An original example: a fictional county health department counts everyone living with type 2 diabetes in the county, finds 400 people out of 10,000 residents, and reports a prevalence of 4 percent. That number tells the county how many residents need diabetes care at this moment, which is exactly the question a clinic planner, a budget office, or a community program starts with.

collegeVersion.heading: What changes it, how it is measured, and the honest framing
collegeVersion.body: Because prevalence is a count of existing cases, four forces move it, each named here with one line. New cases raise the count: each new diagnosis adds a person to the existing cases. Recoveries lower the count: a person who no longer has the condition stops being a current case. Deaths lower the count: a person who dies with the condition is no longer counted among the living with it. And migration moves the count: people with the condition moving into the population raise it, while people with the condition moving out lower it. Measuring prevalence is the general practice of counting current cases over the population. The WHO's Global Health Observatory states the operational version plainly for its indicators: the number of people with the condition divided by the total number of people counted, usually gathered through population-based surveys. The arithmetic never gets harder than that. If 250 of 5,000 residents have the condition, the prevalence is 250 divided by 5,000, which is 5 percent. The honest framing keeps the whole topic in proportion. Prevalence is a snapshot; incidence is the movie. A photograph of a crowd tells you how many people are there at one moment, not how fast the crowd is growing. CDC's teaching makes the same point: prevalence is based on both incidence and duration of illness, so a high prevalence might reflect many new cases or long survival, and a flat prevalence can hide rising new cases that are balanced by people living longer with the disease. When the snapshot does not move, the movie still can.

vocabulary.definition: The total number of existing cases of a disease or condition in a population at a given time, usually stated as a proportion or percentage of the population.
Prevalence measured at a single moment, such as the proportion of people with the condition on one particular date.
Prevalence measured over a window of time, counting everyone with the condition at any point during the window.

The number of new cases of a condition that appear in a population during a period of time; it is a sibling topic of this lesson, and prevalence counts new and preexisting cases while incidence counts only new ones.
A person currently living with the condition being counted, whether the condition began last week or years ago.
The group of people being counted, such as the residents of a town, the students of a school, or the adults of a country.
The total impact of a health condition on a population; prevalence describes it by showing how many people are living with the condition at a given time.
A common way of measuring prevalence, in which a population is asked or tested to count who has the condition, with the count divided by the total number of people.

eli10.simplifiedExplanation: Prevalence is a count of who already has a disease in a population at a given time. It does not care when the disease started. A person diagnosed last year and a person diagnosed last week both count, as long as both still have the condition when the count happens. Health officials usually state it as a share of the population: if 400 of 10,000 residents have the condition, the prevalence is 4 percent. The count goes up when new people get the disease, and it goes down when people recover or die. It also moves when people with the condition move in or out of the area. Because it is a single count at a single time, it is a snapshot, not a story of how the disease is moving through the population.
eli10.analogy: Think of a busy highway. Prevalence is a photograph of the road at this moment: how many cars are on it right now. Incidence is the flow — how many cars merge onto the highway during an hour. Cars leave when their trips end, which stands for recovery, or when they break down, which stands for death. If trips get longer, more cars sit on the road at any moment even when the same number enters each hour, just as longer survival keeps more people living with a disease.
eli10.analogyLimits: The highway analogy has limits. A car trip lasts minutes, but a chronic condition can last decades, and some diseases end in recovery while others never do. Traffic also treats every car alike, while diseases differ in severity and duration. The comparison is a way to see the difference between a count and a flow, not a model of any single disease.

workedExample: The fictional town of Glenhaven has 8,000 residents. On the first of March, its health department runs a survey and finds that 320 residents are currently living with type 2 diabetes. The prevalence of diabetes in Glenhaven that day is 320 divided by 8,000, which is 0.04, or 4 percent. Because the count was taken on a single date, this is a point prevalence, and it means about one in every 25 residents has diabetes that day — the burden the town's clinics must serve. One year later, the survey counts 360 residents with diabetes out of a population that has grown to 9,000. The prevalence is again 4 percent (360 divided by 9,000). The snapshot looks unchanged, but the town cannot conclude that nothing happened: new diagnoses may have risen while some residents with diabetes moved away or died. The snapshot stays level; only the flow, which is incidence, the sibling topic, shows the motion.

commonMistakes.mistake: Confusing prevalence with incidence.
commonMistakes.correction: The CDC warns that prevalence and incidence are frequently confused and that the key difference is in their numerators. Prevalence counts all existing cases, new and preexisting; incidence counts only new cases that began during the time period. One way to keep them apart: prevalence is who has it now, incidence is who just got it.

commonMistakes.mistake: Reading a high prevalence as proof that a disease spreads fast.
commonMistakes.correction: CDC notes that high prevalence might reflect high incidence or prolonged survival without cure, or both. A long-lasting disease can show a high prevalence even when few new cases appear, because people keep living with it for years. A high count of existing cases is about burden, not necessarily about speed.

commonMistakes.mistake: Treating a point prevalence as if it covered a whole year.
commonMistakes.correction: A point prevalence is a count on a single date, and a period prevalence is a count over a window. When NIMH reports 'past year prevalence,' it is reporting a period measure, not a single-day count. Mixing the two changes the question the number can answer.

commonMistakes.mistake: Assuming a stable prevalence means nothing is changing.
commonMistakes.correction: Prevalence is a snapshot, and a snapshot can stay level while the movie moves: new cases may be rising while people live longer with the disease, leaving the total count unchanged. A flat prevalence is a reason to look at incidence, the sibling topic, not a reason to stop looking.

compareContrast.distinction: One counts who has it now, the other counts who just got it. Prevalence is the total number of existing cases, new and preexisting; incidence is the number of new cases during a time period. The CDC places the difference in the numerators. Incidence is a sibling topic with its own lesson.

One is a snapshot at a single moment, the other is a count over a window. Point prevalence is the proportion of people with the condition on a particular date; period prevalence is the proportion with it at any time during an interval. Same numerator idea, different width of lens.

Prevalence shows the total burden at a given time and can stay level while the situation underneath changes; incidence shows the flow of new cases. Reading a snapshot as if it were a movie is the most common mistake in using these measures.

keyTakeaway: Prevalence is the total number of existing cases of a disease in a population at a given time. It shows the total burden of disease and changes with new cases, recoveries, deaths, and migration. It is a snapshot; incidence, its sibling topic, is the movie.

questionBank.prompt: The fictional county of Lakeport reports that the prevalence of asthma among its residents is 6 percent. Which meaning is closest to what the report is saying?
options: Six percent of residents are living with asthma at the time the count was made, whether diagnosed last week or years ago
Six percent of residents were newly diagnosed with asthma this year
Six percent of residents died from asthma this year
Six percent of hospital beds are occupied by asthma patients
questionBank.explanation: The CDC's Principles of Epidemiology defines prevalence as the proportion of persons in a population who have a particular disease or attribute at a specified point in time or over a specified period of time. Prevalence counts all existing cases, new and preexisting, so someone diagnosed years ago counts the same as someone diagnosed last week. New diagnoses are incidence, a sibling topic; deaths and bed occupancy are different measures entirely.
questionBank.skill: Apply the working definition of prevalence to a reported figure

questionBank.prompt: On June 1, a health team in the fictional town of Millfield visits every school and counts every student currently living with the condition being studied, on that single day. What did the team measure?
options: Period prevalence, because the count covered a window of time
Point prevalence, because the count was made at one moment in time
Incidence, because it counted new cases only
A death rate, because it tracked outcomes over the year
questionBank.explanation: CDC defines point prevalence as prevalence measured at a particular point in time: the proportion of persons with the disease or attribute on a particular date. A single-day count is the textbook example. Period prevalence covers an interval and includes anyone with the condition at any time during it; incidence counts only new cases.
questionBank.skill: Distinguish point prevalence from period prevalence

questionBank.prompt: In the fictional town of Ashgrove, a survey finds 50 of 1,000 residents living with a condition. A year later, after some residents without the condition moved away, a new survey finds 50 of 800 residents with the same condition. What happened to the prevalence?
options: It stayed the same, at 5 percent
It fell, from 5 percent to 4 percent
It rose, from 5 percent to 6.25 percent
It cannot be determined from the information given
questionBank.explanation: Prevalence is current cases divided by the population. The first survey gives 50 divided by 1,000, or 5 percent. The second gives 50 divided by 800, or 6.25 percent. The same number of cases over a smaller population is a higher proportion, so prevalence rose even though no new cases appeared. This is the arithmetic behind the lesson's measuring practice: count the existing cases, divide by the population.
questionBank.skill: Compute and compare prevalence across two surveys

questionBank.prompt: A reporter notes that the prevalence of diabetes in a fictional county has been flat for three straight years and writes that 'nothing is changing.' A public health officer reads the claim. Following the honest framing of this lesson, which response is correct?
options: A flat prevalence proves that no one is getting diabetes anymore
A flat prevalence proves that diabetes has been eliminated from the county
A flat prevalence proves that new cases must be falling
The snapshot can stay level while new cases rise and people live longer with diabetes, so the claim goes beyond what prevalence shows
questionBank.explanation: CDC notes that prevalence is based on both incidence and duration of illness: high prevalence might reflect high incidence or prolonged survival, and a level count can hide motion in both. Prevalence is a snapshot, and a snapshot does not show the flow; new cases rising while people live longer with the disease can leave the count unchanged. Incidence, the sibling topic, is the measure that shows the motion.
questionBank.skill: Apply the snapshot framing to interpret an unchanging prevalence

questionBank.prompt: The clinic at a fictional nursing home records every resident who had arthritis at any time during the past year, including residents who were diagnosed many years earlier and are still living with the condition. Which measure did the clinic produce?
options: Period prevalence, the proportion of residents with the condition at any time during the interval
Point prevalence, a count taken on a single date
Incidence, the number of new cases during the year
A survival rate, the share of patients alive after diagnosis
questionBank.explanation: CDC defines period prevalence as prevalence measured over an interval of time: the proportion of persons with the disease or attribute at any time during the interval. Because the clinic counted everyone with the condition across the whole year, including long-standing cases, it is a period measure. A single-date count would be point prevalence, and new cases alone would be incidence.
questionBank.skill: Classify a count as period prevalence versus related measures

title: Risk
in30Seconds: In public health, risk is the chance that a health problem will occur in a person or a group. It is a number, not a verdict: a 2 in 100 risk means that out of every 100 similar people, about 2 will develop the problem and 98 will not. Risk factors raise the chance, but higher risk is still not certainty. Public health compares risks, follows groups over time to find them, and says the numbers plainly — because a chance you understand is a chance you can act on.
whyItMatters: Every health decision, big or small, rests on a risk. A family deciding whether to treat their well water, a city choosing where to build a new walking trail, a nurse explaining a screening test — all of them are working with chances. When risks are understood correctly, people and communities can act on the numbers instead of on fear or reassurance. When they are misunderstood, the same numbers become a source of panic or false comfort. Learning what risk is — and what it is not — is the difference between making a health choice with your eyes open and making one in the dark.
learningObjectives: Define risk in public health as the chance that a health problem will occur in a person or a group, following the CDC's framing of risk as a probability.
Explain what a risk factor is, and give an original example of a modifiable and a non-modifiable risk factor.
Explain why a link between a factor and a disease does not by itself prove that the factor causes the disease.
Distinguish a higher risk from a certainty, and compare risks stated in plain numbers.
Describe how public health studies risk by following groups of people over time.

collegeVersion.heading: Risk: the chance of harm
collegeVersion.body: Public health defines risk as a probability: the chance that an event will occur, such as a person being affected by, or dying from, an illness, injury, or other health condition within a specified time or age span. The CDC's epidemiology self-study course puts it that way, and that is the working definition used here: risk is the chance that a health problem will occur in a person or a group. A probability runs from zero to one — impossible to certain — but in everyday public health it is usually a small number. A risk of 2 in 100 does not mean two people are doomed; it means that out of 100 similar people, about 2 are expected to develop the problem while about 98 are not. Risk is about groups and patterns, not about predicting any single person's future.

collegeVersion.heading: Risk factors: what raises the chance
collegeVersion.body: A risk factor is a characteristic, behavior, or exposure that is associated with a higher chance of a particular health problem. The CDC's epidemiology glossary describes risk factors as aspects of personal behavior or lifestyle, environmental exposures, or hereditary characteristics linked to an increase in illness, injury, or other health conditions. The World Health Organization names the big modifiable risk factors for chronic disease: tobacco use, physical inactivity, unhealthy diet, and harmful use of alcohol. Some risk factors cannot be changed — age and genetic susceptibility are built into a person. Two original examples: a delivery driver who sits for most of a shift and eats fast food every day carries risk factors that raise the chance of heart problems, while a family living with a cracked foundation and standing water near the walls carries a risk factor for mold-related breathing trouble. And here is the honest note: a factor can be linked to a disease without causing it. Studies show associations — statistical links — and a link can look causal when a third factor explains both, a problem epidemiologists call confounding. Correlation is not causation.

collegeVersion.heading: Higher risk is not a guarantee
collegeVersion.body: Risk compares chances; it does not deliver verdicts. If one group's risk is 2 in 100 and another's is 6 in 100, the second group has three times the chance — but even there, 94 out of 100 people are not expected to develop the problem. Higher risk means a bigger chance, nothing more and nothing less. This is why a headline that says 'twice the risk' can frighten people: doubling a small chance still leaves a small chance.

collegeVersion.heading: Comparing risk
collegeVersion.body: Most of public health's work with risk is comparison: is the chance higher, lower, or about the same in one group than in another? The CDC's epidemiology course describes the tools — a risk ratio compares the chance in one group with the chance in another, and the excess risk is the difference between the two. For a plain example from the CDC, children younger than 5 are three times more likely to be hospitalized if they get a Salmonella infection, and adults 65 and older, pregnant people, and people with weakened immune systems face higher risk of severe foodborne illness. Comparing risks is how a community decides where to aim its prevention. How often new cases actually occur — incidence — is its own lesson; here the focus is the chance itself.

collegeVersion.heading: How risk is studied: following groups over time
collegeVersion.body: To learn which factors really raise risk, public health follows groups of people over time. The CDC's epidemiology course calls such a group a cohort: a well-defined set of people who share a common experience or exposure and are then followed to see who develops new health problems. Researchers record who has the factor and who does not, then wait and count. An original example: a university enrolls 1,000 office workers, notes who walks to work each day, and checks everyone's health every year for a decade. If walkers develop fewer cases of high blood pressure, the study has evidence that the behavior is associated with lower risk. Watching real people over real time is slow, but it is how public health learns which chances are real. The full toolkit of study designs belongs to the epidemiology lesson.

collegeVersion.heading: Communicating risk: saying numbers plainly
collegeVersion.body: A risk that nobody understands protects nobody. The CDC, following the U.S. government's Healthy People 2030 definition, describes health literacy as the ability to find, understand, and use health information for health decisions. That means translating numbers into pictures people can hold. Instead of 'the probability is 0.02,' say 'about 2 out of every 100 people.' Instead of 'the risk is 25.7 percent,' say 'about 1 in 4.' An original example: a health department poster warns that of 100 people in a town who get a certain foodborne illness each year, about 15 need a doctor's visit — a sentence that works because the listener can picture the 15 and the 100.

collegeVersion.heading: The honest framing: a forecast, not a prophecy
collegeVersion.body: Here is the reality check. Risk is a weather forecast, not a prophecy. A 30 percent chance of rain does not tell you whether it will rain; it tells you that on similar days, it rained about 3 times out of 10, and you still choose whether to carry an umbrella. A health risk is the same: it describes what tends to happen across many people, it can change as circumstances change, and it never dictates what will happen to you. Understanding that difference is the point of this lesson — a chance you understand is a chance you can act on.

vocabulary.definition: The chance that a health problem will occur in a person or a group within a given time, expressed as a probability.
A number from zero to one, or a percentage, that describes how likely an event is; zero means impossible and one means certain.
A characteristic, behavior, or exposure that is associated with a higher chance of a particular health problem.
A risk factor that a person or community can change, such as physical inactivity or an unhealthy diet.
A risk factor that cannot be changed, such as age or genetic susceptibility.
A statistical link between two things, such as a factor and a disease.
A situation in which a third factor distorts the apparent link between a factor and a health outcome, so the link can look causal when it is not.
A study that follows a defined group of people over time to see who develops a health problem.
The ability to find, understand, and use health information to make health decisions.
A comparison of the chance of a health problem in one group with the chance in another group.

eli10.simplifiedExplanation: Risk is a way of talking about luck with numbers. It does not say what will happen to you; it says what tends to happen across a crowd of people like you. If a health department says the risk of a certain illness is 3 in 100, it means that in a crowd of 100 similar people, about 3 will get it and about 97 will not — and nobody knows which 3. Risk factors are things that tilt the odds: a habit, a place, a body trait that makes the chance bigger. Public health's whole job is to find the tilts, tell people about them in plain words, and give people a way to tilt the odds back.
eli10.analogy: Think of risk like tomorrow's weather forecast. A 30 percent chance of rain does not mean it is raining, and it does not mean it is dry. It means that on days that looked like this one, it rained about 3 times out of 10. You still decide whether to carry an umbrella — the forecast just makes the decision smarter. Health risk works the same way: the number describes the pattern, and you still get to choose.
eli10.analogyLimits: The analogy breaks down in one important way: you cannot change the weather, but you can often change your risk. Some risk factors are fixed — your age, your genes. Many are not: smoking, activity, diet, and parts of the neighborhood you live in can be changed by people and communities. Also, a forecast is the same for everyone, while a health risk can differ sharply between groups — which is why public health keeps comparing one group with another.

workedExample: Two neighboring towns, Maple Creek and Birch Falls, each have about 10,000 residents. The county health department wants to know whether adults in Maple Creek face a higher chance of asthma than adults in Birch Falls. It enrolls 500 adults in each town, records who has a damp basement or bedroom, and follows everyone for five years. In Maple Creek, 30 of the 500 (6 in 100) develop new asthma; in Birch Falls, 10 of the 500 (2 in 100) do. The chance is three times higher in Maple Creek, where damp homes are far more common. The department reports: 'For every 100 adults like these, about 6 in Maple Creek and 2 in Birch Falls developed asthma over five years.' Nobody can say which individuals will be affected — the numbers describe the group, not the person. That is risk: a chance, measured, compared, and said plainly.

commonMistakes.mistake: A high risk means I am definitely going to get sick.
commonMistakes.correction: Higher risk is a bigger chance, not a promise. Even a 50 in 100 risk means half the group is not expected to develop the problem.

commonMistakes.mistake: A risk factor causes the disease.
commonMistakes.correction: A risk factor raises the chance of a health problem. A link found in a study is an association; it does not by itself prove causation, because a third factor may explain both.

commonMistakes.mistake: If I know my personal risk, I know what will happen to me.
commonMistakes.correction: Risk is measured on groups. It describes patterns across many similar people; it cannot name which individuals will be affected.

commonMistakes.mistake: A 1 in 100 risk and a 10 in 1,000 risk are different.
commonMistakes.correction: They are the same chance written two ways. Communicating risk means choosing a format people can picture, not changing the number.

compareContrast.distinction: Risk is a chance somewhere between impossible and certain; certainty is a guarantee. A 6 in 100 risk is three times a 2 in 100 risk, but neither one promises what happens to any individual.

A risk factor raises the chance of a health problem; a cause produces the problem. A factor can be linked to a disease without causing it — the link may be distorted by a third variable (confounding).
Risk is the chance that a health problem will occur in a person or group; incidence counts the new cases that actually occur over a period. Incidence is the sibling topic's measure.

keyTakeaway: Risk is a chance, not a verdict: it describes what tends to happen across a group so people can compare, understand, and act — and it never promises what will happen to any one person.

questionBank.prompt: A community health worker is explaining the word 'risk' to a new volunteer. Which answer gives the public health definition of risk?
options: The chance that a health problem will occur in a person or a group within a given time.
A promise that a person will develop a specific illness.
A list of every disease a community has seen in the past year.
The number of new cases of a disease counted during one month.
questionBank.explanation: Public health, following the CDC's epidemiology course, defines risk as a probability — the chance that an event such as an illness, injury, or other health condition will occur within a specified time. A promise is the opposite of a chance; a list of past diseases is a record, not a risk; and counting new cases in a month is a measure of incidence, which belongs to its own lesson.

questionBank.prompt: A city notices that residents of the Northside neighborhood visit the emergency room for asthma more often than residents of other neighborhoods. Investigators find that Northside has more older buildings with damp basements. Which statement is the most accurate public health claim?
options: The damp basements prove that mold causes asthma in Northside.
Damp basements are a risk factor: they are associated with a higher chance of asthma, but they do not guarantee it.
Because not every person with a damp basement has asthma, the damp basements are irrelevant.
Asthma risk cannot be compared between neighborhoods until every resident has been tested.
questionBank.explanation: A risk factor is a characteristic or exposure associated with a higher chance of a health problem, not a guarantee, so the damp basements raise the chance without causing every case. Claiming proof of causation, dismissing the factor because it is not a guarantee, and refusing to compare risks are all mistakes this lesson corrects.
questionBank.skill: Applying the risk-factor idea to a community scenario

questionBank.prompt: A screening program tells 1,000 people that their risk of a certain condition is 5 in 100 over the next ten years. Which conclusion is correct?
options: Exactly 50 of the 1,000 people will develop the condition.
About 950 of the 1,000 people will certainly stay free of the condition.
The number describes a pattern across the group: about 5 in every 100 similar people are expected to develop the condition, but no one can say which individuals.
Each person's risk is 5 percent higher than everyone else's.
questionBank.explanation: A risk of 5 in 100 is a group pattern, not a fixed count and not a guarantee: about 5 in every 100 similar people are expected to develop the condition, without naming who. 'Exactly 50' turns a chance into a count, 'certainly stay free' turns a chance into a certainty, and comparing a person to 'everyone else' misreads what a single risk number means.
questionBank.skill: Distinguishing a group-level risk from an individual guarantee

questionBank.prompt: A study follows 5,000 adults for ten years and finds that people who drink more coffee are also more likely to develop a certain condition. Which analysis of the finding is the most scientifically honest?
options: The study proves that coffee causes the condition.
Because the study followed people over time, the link must be causal.
The condition must make people drink more coffee.
The study shows an association, but the link could be distorted by a third factor that coffee drinkers share, so it does not by itself prove causation.
questionBank.explanation: An association is a statistical link, and correlation is not causation: the link between coffee and the condition could be distorted by another factor shared by coffee drinkers — a problem called confounding. Following people over time makes the study strong, but it does not turn an association into proof, and claiming the condition causes the behavior is a guess with no support.
questionBank.skill: Analyzing why an association does not prove causation

questionBank.prompt: A health department wants to tell residents that a health risk is 10 percent, in the plainest way possible. Which message says the same number most clearly?
options: The probability is 0.1 on a scale from zero to one.
Out of every 100 people, about 10 will be affected.
The risk is ten times higher than the risk of winning a raffle.
Most people will not be affected, so the risk is low.
questionBank.explanation: Communicating risk means putting numbers in a form people can picture, and 'about 10 out of every 100' translates 10 percent into a concrete image. A decimal on a zero-to-one scale is precise but hard to picture, a raffle comparison is irrelevant, and 'most people will not be affected' quietly changes the number into a judgment.
questionBank.skill: Translating a risk into plain numbers

title: Disease Surveillance
in30Seconds: Disease surveillance is the public health radar: the ongoing, systematic collection and analysis of health data to detect and track problems. Health agencies pull together reported cases, laboratory results, emergency visits, and death records, then watch for new outbreaks, trends, and unusual patterns. That early warning enables fast response, better planning, and honest evaluation. The catch: surveillance depends on clinics and labs reporting, so not every case gets counted.
whyItMatters: Outbreaks almost never start with a headline — they start with a report nobody has filed yet. Surveillance is what lets a health department notice two similar cases before they become twenty, and it is the quiet machinery behind flu forecasts, vaccine planning, and the phrase 'cases are rising.' It matters because it turns scattered, ordinary records — a lab result here, an emergency visit there, a death certificate somewhere else — into an early warning system for the whole community. And its blind spots matter too: because surveillance depends on reporting, the cases that never get reported are exactly where surprise outbreaks hide.
learningObjectives: Define disease surveillance as the ongoing, systematic collection and analysis of health data to detect and track problems, per the CDC's working definition.
Name the four main data sources — reported cases, laboratory results, emergency visits, and death records — and state what each contributes.
Explain what surveillance watches for: new outbreaks, trends, and unusual patterns.
Describe the reporting chain from clinics and laboratories to local, state, and national health agencies, using an original example.
Explain what surveillance enables — early response, planning, and evaluation — and state its honest limits.

collegeVersion.heading: The working definition
collegeVersion.body: Public health surveillance is the ongoing, systematic collection and analysis of health data used to detect and track problems so that public health agencies can act. The CDC's working definition, from its surveillance guidelines, is more complete: the ongoing, systematic collection, analysis, interpretation, and dissemination of data regarding a health-related event, for use in public health action to reduce illness and death and to improve health. The word surveillance itself comes from the French sur (over) and veiller (to watch) — watching over. Two words in the definition carry the weight. Ongoing: the watching never stops; it is a standing system, not a one-time study. Systematic: the data are gathered the same way, on a regular schedule, so that a number from one week can be compared with a number from the week before. The CDC's epidemiology manual puts the essence simply: surveillance is the use of data to monitor health problems so that they can be prevented or controlled.

collegeVersion.heading: Where the data come from
collegeVersion.body: Surveillance runs on ordinary records that already exist. Reported cases: when a doctor diagnoses a disease on the state's reportable list, the clinic files a report, and these notifications are the backbone of case surveillance. Laboratory results: tests that confirm a diagnosis add precision, because a suspected case and a confirmed case are different things. Emergency visits: emergency departments see the sharp end of illness fast, so a spike in ER visits often shows a problem before diagnoses pile up. Death records: death certificates note the cause of death, which is how agencies track diseases that kill and measure severity over time. The CDC's manual groups these under health-care providers, facilities, and records — physician offices, hospitals, outpatient clinics, emergency departments, and laboratories — plus death certificates. One catch governs all of them: someone must recognize the illness and create a record of it before it can be counted. A disease that produces mild symptoms in most people will always be counted less completely than one that sends people to the hospital.

collegeVersion.heading: What the radar watches for
collegeVersion.body: The point of gathering all this data is to spot trouble early. Surveillance watches for three things. New outbreaks: more cases of a disease than expected in a place and time — the CDC's guidelines call this the detection of epidemics. Trends: the direction the numbers move over weeks, months, and years — rising, falling, or flat — which tells agencies whether a problem is getting better or worse. Unusual patterns: clusters or spikes that stand out from the usual background, like a handful of similar cases in one neighborhood or a season that shows more illness than the same season usually does. Often an unusual pattern is the first sign of an outbreak that has not been named yet. Surveillance does not explain why a pattern exists; it raises the flag. Figuring out the cause is the work of outbreak investigation, a separate step that gets its own lesson.

collegeVersion.heading: How reports travel
collegeVersion.body: Surveillance depends on a reporting chain, and it starts with a legal requirement. Each state keeps a list of notifiable diseases — conditions that clinics, laboratories, and other providers must report when they diagnose them. A report moves up the chain: the clinic or lab files it with the local health department; the local agency reviews and forwards it to the state health department; and states send de-identified summaries of notifiable diseases to the CDC, which compiles them into the Morbidity and Mortality Weekly Report, the MMWR. Here is an original example. A walk-in clinic in a small city diagnoses three cases of a rare bacterial infection in a single week — more than the county has seen in a decade. The clinic's nurse manager files three reports with the county health department. The county epidemiologist checks the state system, finds a neighboring county with two similar reports, and calls the state. Within days, the state has alerted regional clinics. The chain worked: three clinic reports became a statewide heads-up.

collegeVersion.heading: What surveillance makes possible — and its honest limits
collegeVersion.body: Surveillance is not an end in itself; it earns its keep through what it enables. Early response: when a problem is spotted while it is small, agencies can act before it grows — alerting clinics, warning the public, targeting vaccines or treatment. Planning: long runs of data show where disease is concentrated and where resources are needed, so programs can be aimed at the right places and populations. Evaluation: by comparing data from before and after a program, agencies can tell whether the program worked — whether new cases actually fell. The limits are honest ones. Surveillance depends entirely on reporting, and reporting is incomplete: the CDC's manual notes that for many notifiable diseases only a fraction of cases are ever reported, and that surveillance need not be perfect to be useful. Cases that are never diagnosed or never reported simply do not appear in the data. That is why a quiet surveillance screen is not proof that a community is healthy — it may just mean the radar is pointed elsewhere or a report was missed.

vocabulary.definition: The ongoing, systematic collection and analysis of health data used to detect and track health problems so that public health agencies can act on them.
A disease that health-care providers and laboratories are required by law to report to public health authorities when they diagnose it.
A record of one diagnosed illness that a clinic, hospital, or laboratory sends to a health agency as part of the reporting system.
The general direction a disease's numbers move over time — rising, falling, or holding steady across weeks, months, or years.
More cases of a disease than expected in a particular place and time, compared with the usual background level.
The failure of some cases to be diagnosed or reported, so that official counts are lower than the true number of illnesses.
The outcome of a test that confirms or rules out a diagnosis, giving surveillance systems a precise check on suspected cases.
Information from a death certificate about who died and the cause of death, used to track fatal diseases over time.

eli10.simplifiedExplanation: Disease surveillance is the public health radar: a standing system that collects health data — reported cases, lab results, emergency visits, death records — week after week, and watches for anything unusual. It is not one big investigation; it is the everyday watching that happens before investigations are ever needed. A doctor reports a case, a lab confirms one, an emergency room logs visits, a clerk records a death — and someone in a health department puts the pieces together and asks: is this normal? If the answer is no, the agency can act while the problem is still small. Surveillance itself does not fix anything; it notices things, so that fixing can start early.
eli10.analogy: Think of a coast guard radar on harbor watch. The radar sweeps constantly, and the watch officer compares each sweep with the ones before it. A single blip is usually nothing; three blips in the same corner, moving together, is something worth a closer look. Surveillance is that sweep: the same scan, over and over, so that what is normal becomes familiar and anything different stands out immediately.
eli10.analogyLimits: A radar only sees what its beam covers, and disease surveillance only sees what gets reported. A ship too small or too low to reflect the beam never appears — just as mild or unreported cases stay invisible. And the radar only warns; it does not launch the rescue boat. Acting on the warning is the work of response and investigation.

workedExample: Here is one week at the Meridian County health department. On Monday, the surveillance system flags three reports of a bacterial illness that the county usually sees about twice a year. By Wednesday, the state laboratory confirms all three, and the county's emergency departments log a small rise in related visits. The county epidemiologist calls the region's clinics, asks them to watch for more cases, and posts a reminder about handwashing and careful food handling for the public. Over the next month the count holds at three — no new reports — and the episode stays small. That winter, the county uses the episode in its food-safety outreach to churches and community kitchens. Surveillance spotted the blip while it was small, the response contained it, and the follow-up review turned it into a lesson.

commonMistakes.mistake: Surveillance and outbreak investigation are the same job.
commonMistakes.correction: They are different stages. Surveillance is the ongoing watching for problems across a population; investigation is what happens after a problem is spotted, to find its source and stop it. Surveillance feeds investigations; it does not replace them.

commonMistakes.mistake: If the surveillance data look quiet, the community must be healthy.
commonMistakes.correction: Quiet data can mean underreporting — cases that were never diagnosed or never reported. Surveillance is only as complete as the reporting behind it, so silence is not proof of health.

commonMistakes.mistake: Surveillance counts every case exactly.
commonMistakes.correction: It depends on reporting by clinics and labs, and for many diseases only a fraction of cases are ever reported. The data are excellent for spotting trends and changes, but they are not a perfect census.

commonMistakes.mistake: Surveillance only matters during emergencies.
commonMistakes.correction: The same systems run every day, and their steady data are what make planning, budgeting, and evaluation possible between emergencies — not just during them.

compareContrast.distinction: Surveillance watches continuously for problems across a population; investigation responds to a specific problem that has been spotted, tracing its source and spread. One is the radar; the other is the response team.

Reported cases are the ones clinics and labs actually filed; actual cases include unreported ones. For many diseases the gap is large, which is why surveillance numbers are treated as indicators of trends rather than exact counts.

Passive reporting waits for providers and labs to file reports as required; active surveillance has the health agency go looking, for example by calling clinics or testing at sentinel sites. Passive systems are cheaper but more incomplete.

keyTakeaway: Disease surveillance is the public health radar — ongoing, systematic watching that turns routine reports into early warning, early action, and honest planning. It is only as good as the reporting behind it.

questionBank.prompt: A county health department's surveillance coordinator is explaining the job to a new hire. Which description matches the CDC's working definition of disease surveillance?
options: The ongoing, systematic collection and analysis of health data used to detect and track problems and guide action.
A one-time survey of a community's opinions about its health services.
The treatment plan a doctor writes for a patient with an infection.
A hospital's billing record for a single patient's stay.
questionBank.explanation: The CDC's guidelines define public health surveillance as the ongoing, systematic collection, analysis, and interpretation of health data for use in public health action. A one-time opinion survey, a treatment plan, and a billing record are not surveillance — they are a snapshot, clinical care, and administration.
questionBank.skill: Recognizing the CDC's working definition of disease surveillance

questionBank.prompt: A clinic's laboratory confirms two cases of a disease on the state's reportable list within one week. What happens next under routine disease surveillance?
options: The clinic keeps the information private and handles the cases quietly.
The clinic files reports with the local health department, which passes them up to the state and then to national systems.
The state waits for a national alert before taking any notice of the cases.
The laboratory discards the results because two cases are too few to matter.
questionBank.explanation: Notifiable diseases are reported by clinics and laboratories to local health departments, which forward them to state agencies, which report summaries to CDC's national system. Keeping cases private, waiting for a national alert, or discarding results would all break the reporting chain.
questionBank.skill: Applying the reporting chain to a new scenario

questionBank.prompt: An emergency department records more flu-like visits than usual for late summer, when flu is normally quiet. A surveillance analyst sees the same bump in the city's data. Why does this pattern matter?
options: It proves the flu vaccine has failed this year.
It means the emergency department's records are inaccurate.
It is an unusual pattern that can signal an early outbreak, giving health agencies a head start on response.
It is normal, because emergency visits always rise in late summer.
questionBank.explanation: Surveillance watches for unusual patterns — clusters or spikes that stand out from the usual background — because they can be the first sign of an outbreak, and the CDC's guidelines note that surveillance data are used to detect epidemics. A vaccine failure, record errors, and a normal seasonal rise are not what the pattern indicates.
questionBank.skill: Interpreting an unusual surveillance pattern

questionBank.prompt: A student argues that disease surveillance gives public health agencies a perfect count of every case in a community. Which response states the honest limit of surveillance?
options: Surveillance can count every single case, because reporting is mandatory.
Surveillance works without any input from clinics or laboratories.
Surveillance tells agencies exactly what caused each outbreak it detects.
Surveillance depends on reporting, so cases that are never diagnosed or reported are not counted.
questionBank.explanation: The CDC's manual is explicit: for many notifiable diseases only a fraction of cases are ever reported, and surveillance need not be perfect to be useful. Surveillance depends on clinics and labs reporting; unreported cases simply do not appear in the data, and finding causes is the separate work of investigation.
questionBank.skill: Recognizing the honest limits of surveillance

questionBank.prompt: A state health department uses five years of surveillance data to decide which counties most need a new tuberculosis screening program, then checks later whether new cases fell in those counties. Which pair of uses does this show?
options: Writing news releases and posting on social media.
Planning where to focus the program and evaluating whether it reduced new cases.
Treating individual patients and billing insurance.
Licensing restaurants and enforcing parking rules.
questionBank.explanation: The CDC's surveillance guidelines describe surveillance data as serving program planning and evaluation: long runs of data reveal where disease is concentrated so programs can be aimed there, and comparing data before and after shows whether the program worked. Writing releases, treating patients, and licensing are not the planning-and-evaluation uses of surveillance data.
questionBank.skill: Applying surveillance's planning and evaluation uses
