title: Vital Signs
in30Seconds: Vital signs are the basic measurements that reflect the body's essential functions — the body's way of reporting how it is running. The five measured in routine care are temperature, pulse, respirations, blood pressure, and oxygen saturation. Adult reference ranges exist for each one, but 'normal' depends on age, health, and the individual. A single reading means little by itself; the baseline and the trend over time carry the message. Sudden changes are signals worth taking seriously.
whyItMatters: Every healthcare visit starts with vital signs because they are the fastest honest snapshot of how the body is running. A sudden change — a fever that appears, a pulse that climbs, an oxygen level that dips — is often the first clue that something is wrong, sometimes before the person feels any different. For students entering nursing and allied health, taking and interpreting vital signs is a daily skill and an early professional responsibility. For everyone else, understanding the basics makes you a better observer of your own body and a more informed partner in your own care.
learningObjectives: Define vital signs as the basic measurements that reflect the body's essential functions, following the OpenStax nursing-textbook description.
Name the five vital signs — temperature, pulse, respirations, blood pressure, and oxygen saturation — and state what each one measures.
Explain why adult reference ranges are only a guide and why 'normal' varies with age, health, and the individual.
Apply the baseline-and-trend idea to decide whether a single reading is concerning.
Analyze a change in a patient's vital signs and explain why it prompts checking and reporting.

collegeVersion.heading: A working definition
collegeVersion.body: Vital signs are the basic measurements that reflect the body's essential functions. The OpenStax nursing textbooks describe them as markers of physiological homeostasis — the body's balanced, steady internal state — and as measurements essential for monitoring a patient's progress. MedlinePlus, the consumer health service of the U.S. National Library of Medicine, says vital signs reflect essential body functions, including heartbeat, breathing, temperature, and blood pressure. Two parts of that definition carry the weight. First, 'basic': these are quick, mostly painless measurements taken at the bedside or in the home, not laboratory tests that need blood or urine. Second, 'essential functions': each one reports on a system the body cannot do without — heat regulation, the heart's pumping, breathing, the pressure inside the arteries, and the oxygen reaching the blood.

collegeVersion.heading: The five measurements and what each one tells you
collegeVersion.body: Routine care measures five vital signs, and each one answers a single question about the body. Temperature measures how hot the body is — how well heat production and heat loss stay balanced; a climbing temperature often means the body is fighting something, such as an infection. Pulse, also called heart rate, counts the heartbeats per minute — how fast the heart is pumping. Respirations count the breaths per minute — how fast and how well the person is breathing. Blood pressure measures the force of blood against the artery walls — how hard the heart works to push blood and how much resistance the vessels offer. Oxygen saturation, or SpO2, estimates the percentage of hemoglobin that is carrying oxygen — how well oxygen is reaching the blood. Each of these five has its own full lesson in this course; here the point is the set. In practice the five are read together, because they are connected: a fast respiratory rate often pairs with a fast pulse, and falling oxygen saturation can show up alongside a falling blood pressure.

collegeVersion.heading: Reference ranges: real, but flexible
collegeVersion.body: Adults have reference ranges for each vital sign, and they are genuinely useful. For a resting adult, common textbook references are roughly: temperature 97–99°F (about 36–37°C) by mouth, pulse 60–100 beats per minute, respirations 12–20 per minute, blood pressure below 120/80 mm Hg, and oxygen saturation 95–100 percent on room air. The honest note: these are guides for a healthy resting adult, not universal truths. MedlinePlus warns that normal vital signs change with age, sex, weight, exercise capability, and overall health. What is normal for a newborn — a resting heart rate around 130 — would be alarming in an adult. The same adult's numbers move with activity, anxiety, illness, and medication. A reference range tells you where most healthy adults sit; it does not tell you where this particular person sits.

collegeVersion.heading: Why they matter: changes are the message
collegeVersion.body: Vital signs matter most when they change. The OpenStax nursing text puts it plainly: changes such as a fever, a climbing heart rate, or a falling blood pressure are signs that the body is no longer in balance, and understanding these signs can help prevent a life-threatening emergency. Original example: Mei, age 62, is recovering at home after knee surgery. Her temperature has run about 98°F all week, and her resting pulse has stayed in the high 70s. On Thursday morning she feels warm; the thermometer reads 101.2°F and her pulse is 104. Either number alone sits near the edge of the adult ranges, but the change from her own baseline is the message — so she calls her care team, who ask her to come in. A urine test finds an infection and treatment starts the same day. The vital signs did not diagnose anything; they sounded the alarm early.

collegeVersion.heading: The practice: baseline, trends, and who measures them
collegeVersion.body: Vital signs are gathered on the first encounter with a patient to establish a baseline, then routinely afterward according to the person's condition and the facility's orders. What matters is the trend: a series of readings over time that maps what is normal for that particular patient. One reading is a snapshot; the trend is the story. Nurses are the professionals who obtain, validate, interpret, and document vital signs, and they use nursing judgment to recheck them whenever a patient's condition changes, even if the scheduled time has not arrived. Nursing assistants measure vital signs such as blood pressure and temperature as part of routine care and report changes to the nurse. Patient care technicians and medical assistants take them too, in hospitals and clinics. And with training, patients monitor vital signs at home — blood pressure cuffs and pulse oximeters are common household tools — which is why understanding the basics serves everyone, not just clinicians.

vocabulary.definition: The basic measurements that reflect the body's essential functions — temperature, pulse, respirations, blood pressure, and oxygen saturation.
A person's usual set of vital sign values, established at the first encounter and used as the comparison point later.
The pattern formed by a series of vital sign readings taken over time, showing what is normal for that individual.
A measurement of how hot the body is, reflecting the balance between heat production and heat loss.
The pressure wave felt in the arteries each time the heart beats; reported as the heart rate in beats per minute.
The breaths a person takes per minute, counted as part of the vital sign assessment.
The force of blood against the artery walls as the heart pumps, reported as two numbers such as 120/80.
An estimate, usually from a pulse oximeter, of the percentage of hemoglobin in the blood that is carrying oxygen.
The typical span of values seen in healthy adults, used as a guide rather than a hard rule for any one person.
The body's balanced, steady internal state, which vital signs help monitor and which illness can disturb.

eli10.simplifiedExplanation: Vital signs are the body's basic signals — quick measurements that tell you how the engine is running. There are five main ones: temperature (how hot), pulse (how fast the heart beats), respirations (how fast you breathe), blood pressure (how hard the blood pushes on the artery walls), and oxygen saturation (how much oxygen the blood is carrying). They get checked at almost every healthcare visit, partly to catch problems early and partly to build a record of what is normal for you. The numbers have typical adult ranges, but the range is a guide, not a verdict: what is normal for a newborn is not normal for an adult, and what is normal for you can differ from what is normal for your neighbor. A single reading tells you little; the change from your own usual numbers is what speaks.
eli10.analogy: Think of the check-engine light. The light does not tell you which part failed — it just says something under the hood is off, and you would not drive cross-country ignoring it. Vital signs work the same way. A temperature that climbs, a pulse that quickens, an oxygen level that drops: none of them names the problem, but each one says 'look under the hood now.' The person who knows their usual numbers — their baseline — is the one who notices when the light comes on.
eli10.analogyLimits: The comparison has limits. A check-engine light is a single warning, while vital signs are five gauges that are also useful when nothing is wrong: they build the baseline that makes the warning meaningful. And unlike a car, a person's numbers move for ordinary reasons — exercise, nerves, a hot day, a cold. A change is a prompt to check and ask, not an automatic emergency. The gauges also need a skilled reader: the same reading that is routine for one person can be a red flag for another, which is why trends, context, and a clinician's judgment complete the picture.

workedExample: Priya is a first-year nursing student on a medical-surgical unit. At 0700 she takes Mr. Delgado's vital signs: temperature 98.4°F, pulse 74, respirations 16, blood pressure 118/76, and oxygen saturation 98 percent. She checks his chart and sees that his numbers have run close to these all week — his baseline is stable. At 1300, after lunch, his nurse asks her to recheck him because he feels warm. Priya measures: temperature 100.1°F, pulse 92, respirations 20, blood pressure 124/80, and oxygen saturation 96 percent. Every number has moved away from the morning baseline. Priya does not diagnose anything — she documents the readings, reports the change to the nurse, and the nurse notifies the provider, who orders a urine sample that comes back positive for a urinary tract infection. The vital signs did not name the infection. They noticed it first.

commonMistakes.mistake: A single reading tells you everything you need to know.
commonMistakes.correction: One number means little on its own. Readings are gathered at the first encounter to build a baseline, and the trend over time is what shows whether this patient is stable or changing. A pulse of 96 is unremarkable for the general population but a clear change for a patient whose usual resting pulse is in the mid-60s.

commonMistakes.mistake: 'Normal' is the same for everyone.
commonMistakes.correction: Adult reference ranges are guides for a healthy resting adult. Normal varies across the life span — a newborn's resting heart rate of about 130 is expected, while the same number in an adult would be fast — and it also varies with health, fitness, medication, and the individual's own baseline.

commonMistakes.mistake: Vital signs are only checked when someone is sick.
commonMistakes.correction: Vital signs are taken routinely, including for healthy people, precisely so there is a baseline to compare against later. A baseline taken when someone is well is what makes a later change visible.

commonMistakes.mistake: Only nurses take vital signs.
commonMistakes.correction: Nursing assistants, patient care technicians, and medical assistants measure vital signs as part of routine care in hospitals, clinics, and long-term care facilities. Nurses obtain, validate, interpret, and act on them, and people at home can be taught to measure their own.

commonMistakes.mistake: Any change in a vital sign is an emergency.
commonMistakes.correction: A change is a prompt to check, document, and report — not an automatic crisis. Ordinary factors such as activity, anxiety, a hot day, or a recent meal move the numbers, so the reader considers context and the trend before deciding how urgent the change is.

compareContrast.distinction: A baseline is this person's own usual values, built from their past readings. A reference range is the typical span for healthy adults in general. The baseline tells you what is normal for this patient; the range tells you where most adults sit. When the two disagree, the change from baseline usually carries more weight.

A single reading is a snapshot of one moment — useful, but easily affected by activity, anxiety, or equipment. A trend is the pattern of readings over time, which smooths out those bumps and reveals whether the body is stable, improving, or moving in a concerning direction.

Vital signs are quick bedside measurements that reflect the body's essential functions in real time — no needles, no waiting for a lab. Laboratory tests analyze samples of blood, urine, or other fluids and give deeper detail about specific substances or cells. Vitals raise the alarm; labs help explain what is behind it.

keyTakeaway: Vital signs are the body's basic signals: five quick measurements — temperature, pulse, respirations, blood pressure, and oxygen saturation — that reflect how the essential systems are running. Adult reference ranges are a guide, but your own baseline and the trend over time carry the real message: sudden changes are the body's check-engine light.

questionBank.prompt: A nursing student is explaining vital signs to a family member visiting the unit. Which description matches how the OpenStax nursing textbooks define them?
options: Basic measurements that reflect the body's essential functions and are used to monitor a patient's progress.
Laboratory tests that require a blood or urine sample.
Medications prescribed to control high blood pressure.
Insurance codes used to bill for a hospital stay.
questionBank.explanation: The OpenStax nursing texts describe vital signs as markers of the body's balanced state (homeostasis) that are essential for monitoring patient progress. They are bedside measurements, not lab tests, medications, or billing codes — which is what rules out the other three options.
questionBank.skill: Recalling the working definition of vital signs

questionBank.prompt: Mr. Kim's chart shows that his resting pulse usually sits in the mid-60s. During morning rounds, the nursing assistant measures his pulse at 96 beats per minute. What does this finding mean?
options: It is meaningless, because 96 is a perfectly normal adult pulse.
It is within the general adult range but a clear change from his baseline, so it should be checked further.
He is having a heart attack and needs emergency resuscitation right now.
The only possible explanation is that the equipment is broken.
questionBank.explanation: Ninety-six falls inside the adult reference range of 60–100, but the patient's own baseline is the mid-60s, and the change from baseline is what signals a possible problem. Dismissing it, assuming a heart attack without other evidence, or blaming the equipment all ignore the baseline-and-trend principle.
questionBank.skill: Applying baseline-versus-range reasoning to a pulse reading

questionBank.prompt: A patient care technician is listing the vital signs she will measure during her morning rounds. Which list contains all five standard vital signs?
options: Height, weight, body mass index, pain score, and appetite.
Pulse, blood pressure, pain score, temperature, and weight.
Temperature, pulse, respirations, blood pressure, and oxygen saturation.
Heart rate, oxygen saturation, temperature, pain score, and height.
questionBank.explanation: The five vital signs in nursing practice are temperature, pulse, respirations, blood pressure, and oxygen saturation. Height, weight, and body mass index are anthropometric measurements, and pain — sometimes called the sixth vital sign — is a separate assessment, which rules out the other lists.
questionBank.skill: Naming the five vital signs

questionBank.prompt: A father is worried because his newborn daughter's resting heart rate is 130 beats per minute, which he knows would be fast for an adult. What is the most accurate response?
options: A heart rate of 130 means she needs to see a cardiologist immediately.
All people, regardless of age, should have a resting heart rate between 60 and 100.
The monitor must be broken, because no healthy baby's heart beats that fast.
Newborns naturally have much faster heart rates — 130 is within the normal range for her age.
questionBank.explanation: Normal vital signs vary across the life span. A newborn's resting heart rate normally runs about 100–160 beats per minute, so 130 is expected for her age even though the same number would be fast for an adult. The other options treat the adult range as universal, which is exactly the mistake the age-variation idea corrects.
questionBank.skill: Applying age-based normal ranges to a vital sign reading

questionBank.prompt: During a home visit, a nurse checks Ms. Rivera, who is recovering from pneumonia. Compared with her last visit, her temperature has risen from 98.2°F to 100.6°F and her oxygen saturation has dropped from 97 percent to 93 percent. Which response best applies the 'changes are the message' idea?
options: No action is needed because both readings are close to the adult reference ranges.
Tell her to take a hot bath right away to bring the temperature down.
Document the change from her baseline and report it to the provider, since both numbers moved together in a concerning direction.
Assume the pulse oximeter is inaccurate because she is wearing nail polish.
questionBank.explanation: Both numbers moved away from this patient's own baseline in the same concerning direction — fever up, oxygen down — which is the classic signal to check, document, and report. Ignoring the change because the values are near ranges, giving unsafe advice, or blaming equipment without evidence all miss the message.
questionBank.skill: Analyzing a change in vital signs against a patient's baseline

title: Temperature
in30Seconds: Body temperature is the body's heat signal. It reflects the balance between heat the body makes and heat it loses — a balance that shifts with illness, exercise, the environment, and the time of day. The normal adult range is roughly 97–99°F (36.1–37.2°C). Above that range is a fever, usually a sign the body is fighting something. Below about 95°F is hypothermia, dangerously low. One reading is one clue, not a verdict.
whyItMatters: Temperature is the fastest clue a caregiver can gather about what is happening inside the body. A climbing temperature can be the first sign of an infection before other symptoms appear, and a dropping one can signal danger in a cold-exposed or very ill patient. For nursing and allied health students, temperature is also part of the vital signs family — heart rate, respiratory rate, blood pressure, and oxygen level — that is checked in almost every patient encounter. Reading it correctly matters in practice: a number taken from the wrong site, at the wrong time of day, or right after hot coffee can mislead. Learning what temperature does — and does not — tell you is the difference between reacting to a number and understanding a patient.
learningObjectives: Define body temperature as the balance between heat the body produces and heat it loses, following the OpenStax description.
State the normal adult temperature range of roughly 97–99°F (36.1–37.2°C) and explain why normal varies by person, time of day, and measurement site.
Name the five common measurement sites — oral, rectal, axillary, tympanic, and temporal — and state one factual feature of each.
Distinguish fever, a temperature above the normal range that is a response to illness, from hypothermia, a temperature too low, usually below 95°F.
Explain how illness, exercise, environment, and time of day each change body temperature.
Analyze a temperature reading as one clue within a fuller assessment rather than a verdict by itself.

collegeVersion.heading: The heat signal
collegeVersion.body: Body temperature is a measurement with a simple meaning: it reflects the balance between heat the body produces and heat the body loses. OpenStax's Clinical Nursing Skills puts it plainly — body temperature reflects the balance between heat produced and heat lost, with heat produced during muscle movement and the normal physical and chemical processes of metabolism. Think of the body as a working furnace: muscles, the heart, and the liver all generate heat as they do their jobs, and the body continuously sheds that heat to the surroundings through the skin and the breath. When production and loss stay in rough balance, temperature holds steady. When one side moves — a bout of exercise raises production; a cold room raises loss — the number moves with it. Temperature is one of the four main measurements nurses monitor routinely, alongside heart rate, respiratory rate, and blood pressure, which is why it is counted among the vital signs.

collegeVersion.heading: The normal range — and why it moves
collegeVersion.body: There is no single correct number for body temperature. The long-taught average is 98.6°F (37°C), and the normal adult range is roughly 97°F to 99°F (36.1°C to 37.2°C) — a band MedlinePlus reports from studies of normal variation and OpenStax calls the normothermia range. Normal temperature differs from person to person and shifts with age, activity, and the time of day. In adults it is usually lowest in the early morning and climbs later in the day, following the body's circadian rhythm. The measurement site matters too: an axillary (armpit) reading tends to run about 1°F lower than an oral one, and a rectal reading about 0.5 to 1°F higher. A number that is normal for one person at one time and place may be unusual for another — which is why normal is a range, not a point.

collegeVersion.heading: Where temperature is measured
collegeVersion.body: Temperature can be measured at several places on the body, and each site has its own facts. Oral: a thermometer under the tongue is the most common route and averages about 98.6°F, but the person must be able to hold it still. Rectal: the most accurate route and the standard for infants, but also the most invasive. Axillary: under the armpit, minimally invasive and often used for young children, reading about 1°F lower than oral. Tympanic: a probe in the ear canal, quick and widely used, reading slightly higher than oral. Temporal: an infrared scan across the forehead, quick and noninvasive, usable even on a sleeping child. MedlinePlus notes that mercury glass thermometers are no longer recommended — the glass can break and mercury is a poison — and electronic thermometers are the usual choice. The site matters when interpreting the number, because each route samples a slightly different part of the body's heat.

collegeVersion.heading: Fever and hypothermia
collegeVersion.body: A fever is a body temperature above the normal range. MedlinePlus defines it plainly: a fever is a body temperature that is higher than normal, and it is not a disease — it is usually a sign that the body is trying to fight an illness or infection. Many references use a reading over 100.4°F (38°C) as the commonly cited fever threshold. The honest framing matters here: fever is a response, not always a problem. The body raises its temperature as part of fighting off infection, which is why a fever is not automatically something to fear or to treat. Hypothermia is the opposite departure: body temperature too low. MedlinePlus describes hypothermia as low body temperature, usually below 95°F (35°C), a danger that can follow prolonged cold exposure.

collegeVersion.heading: What changes a temperature reading
collegeVersion.body: Four everyday forces move the number. Illness: infection commonly raises temperature as the body fights the invader. Exercise: working muscles generate heat, so temperature climbs during and shortly after activity. Environment: a hot room or heavy clothing holds heat in, while cold air, wind, or wet clothing pull it out — prolonged cold exposure can drive temperature below normal into hypothermia. Time of day: the circadian rhythm makes temperatures lowest in the early morning and higher later in the day. Age and individual factors also matter, but these four are the everyday ones a caregiver sees shift a reading.

collegeVersion.heading: One clue, not a verdict
collegeVersion.body: The reality check: a single temperature reading is one clue, not a verdict. It gains meaning only in context — the site it was taken from, the time of day, what the person was doing, and most of all the rest of the assessment: how the patient looks, feels, and what the other vital signs say. A reading of 100.2°F after a long jog is not the same as 100.2°F at 7 a.m. in a resting patient. Caregivers treat temperature as part of a pattern, which is exactly why it is taught alongside the other vital signs.

vocabulary.definition: A measurement of how much heat the body holds, reflecting the balance between heat produced and heat lost.
The band of readings considered typical for healthy adults, roughly 97–99°F (36.1–37.2°C), which varies by person, time of day, and site.
A body temperature above the normal range, usually a sign that the body is fighting an illness or infection rather than a disease itself.
A dangerously low body temperature, usually below 95°F (35°C), often following prolonged cold exposure.
The measurement site under the tongue, the most common route for taking a temperature.
The armpit measurement site, minimally invasive and often used for young children, reading about 1°F lower than oral.
The ear-canal measurement site, read with a probe placed in the ear.
The forehead measurement site, read with an infrared scan across the skin.
The body's internal daily cycle, which makes temperature lowest in the early morning and higher later in the day.
The core measurements of body function — temperature, heart rate, respiratory rate, and blood pressure — checked routinely in patient care.

eli10.simplifiedExplanation: Your temperature tells you how much heat your body is holding. Your body makes heat all the time — when you move, when your heart beats, even when you digest food — and it also lets heat escape into the air around you. When making and losing stay even, your temperature stays put, right around 97 to 99 degrees Fahrenheit for most adults. A reading above that range is a fever, and it usually means your body is working to fight off an infection — a fever is a response, not the illness itself. A reading below about 95 degrees is hypothermia, which is dangerously low. Your temperature also moves with the time of day, dips in the early morning, climbs later, and rises when you exercise or when the room is hot. One reading is a clue, never the whole story.
eli10.analogy: Think of your body like a pot of water on a stove. The burner adds heat; the lid and the open air let it escape. Turn the burner up — illness or exercise — and the water warms. Open the window on a freezing day — cold exposure — and it cools. A steady flame and a mostly closed pot keep the water at the same comfortable temperature, the way your body holds near 98.6°F. The thermometer is your peek at the pot: it tells you the balance right now, not why the burner changed.
eli10.analogyLimits: A pot of water has no thermostat: it heats and cools passively. Your body actively manages its temperature — the brain senses the balance and responds, raising heat by shivering or shedding it by sweating — so the number is the result of active control, not just physics. Also, a thermometer reading comes from one site (ear, forehead, or armpit) and is only a sample; the pot analogy suggests one perfect reading, but real readings vary slightly by where you take them and what the person was doing.

workedExample: Priya is a first-semester nursing student on a medical-surgical unit. At 7 a.m. she takes Mr. Adams's temperature orally: 98.8°F. At 2 p.m., right after his physical therapy session, she rechecks and gets 99.4°F. Instead of recording a fever, Priya thinks in context: the morning reading came at the daily low point, and the second came right after exercise, which raises heat production. Both numbers sit inside the 97–99°F normal range, and Mr. Adams feels well. She charts both readings with the times, notes the activity, and reports that his temperature is within normal limits for the day.

commonMistakes.mistake: 98.6°F is the one correct normal temperature for everyone.
commonMistakes.correction: Normal is a range — roughly 97–99°F (36.1–37.2°C) for adults — and it varies by person, age, time of day, and measurement site. A reading of 98.9°F can be perfectly normal for one person and unusual for another.

commonMistakes.mistake: A fever is a disease that must always be brought down.
commonMistakes.correction: A fever is a response, usually the body fighting an illness or infection, not the illness itself — MedlinePlus states fever is not a disease but a sign. Whether to treat it depends on the person, the height of the temperature, and the cause.

commonMistakes.mistake: Any reading above 98.6°F means the patient is sick.
commonMistakes.correction: Temperature naturally rises later in the day and with exercise, and readings differ by site — axillary runs lower than oral, rectal higher. A single number means something only alongside the site, the time, and the rest of the assessment.

commonMistakes.mistake: The oral route works for every patient.
commonMistakes.correction: Oral readings need a patient who can hold the thermometer still under the tongue, and hot or cold drinks can distort the result. Infants and patients who cannot follow directions are usually measured another way, often axillary or rectal.

compareContrast.distinction: Fever is temperature above the normal range — usually a response to illness. Hypothermia is temperature too low, usually below 95°F (35°C), a danger often linked to cold exposure. They are opposite departures from the same normal range.
Oral is the most common route, averages about 98.6°F, and needs patient cooperation. Axillary is under the armpit, minimally invasive and good for young children, and reads about 1°F lower than oral.

Rectal is the most accurate route and the standard for infants but is invasive. Temporal scans the forehead with infrared, is quick and noninvasive — usable even on a sleeping child — and trades some accuracy for convenience.

keyTakeaway: Body temperature measures the balance between heat the body makes and heat it loses; normal is a range near 97–99°F, and a single reading is one clue within the whole assessment, not a verdict.

questionBank.prompt: A student nurse is studying how the body manages heat. Which statement correctly describes what a body temperature reading measures?
options: The balance between heat the body produces and heat the body loses.
The amount of heat the body gains from food eaten in the last hour.
The difference between skin temperature and room temperature.
The volume of blood the heart pumps each minute.
questionBank.explanation: OpenStax's Clinical Nursing Skills states that body temperature reflects the balance between heat produced and heat lost. The other options describe food intake, room conditions, and cardiac output — none of which is what a temperature reading measures.
questionBank.skill: Recognizing the working definition of body temperature

questionBank.prompt: A nursing assistant measures a patient's oral temperature ten minutes after the patient drank a large mug of hot coffee. The reading is 99.6°F (37.6°C). What is the most sensible next step?
options: Document the reading as a fever immediately.
Recognize the reading may be inflated by the hot drink and recheck the temperature after a short wait.
Tell the patient to take aspirin to bring the temperature down.
Record the reading as proof of hypothermia.
questionBank.explanation: Hot drinks can distort an oral reading, so a temperature taken right after coffee should be rechecked after a short wait rather than treated as a fever. The reading is above normal, not below it, and giving medication without assessment is never the immediate step.
questionBank.skill: Applying site-and-activity context to interpret an oral reading

questionBank.prompt: A nurse needs a temperature reading for a six-month-old infant who cannot hold a thermometer in her mouth. Which site is the most accurate choice for an infant?
options: Oral
Axillary
Rectal
Temporal
questionBank.explanation: The rectal route is the most accurate and is considered the standard for infants, though it is the most invasive. Oral needs cooperation the infant cannot give, and axillary and temporal are less accurate alternatives used for convenience.
questionBank.skill: Choosing the appropriate measurement site for an infant

questionBank.prompt: A patient's oral temperature is 101.2°F (38.4°C). The patient feels tired but has no other symptoms. Which interpretation fits the evidence?
options: The temperature is below the normal range, so the patient is hypothermic.
The reading is a normal early-morning variation.
The thermometer must be broken because the patient feels fine.
The temperature is above the normal range — a fever, which is a response that usually means the body is fighting an illness or infection.
questionBank.explanation: 101.2°F sits above the normal range and above the commonly cited 100.4°F fever threshold. MedlinePlus describes fever as a sign that the body is fighting an illness or infection — not a disease and not proof the thermometer is broken. It is not hypothermia and not a normal early-morning dip.
questionBank.skill: Interpreting an above-range reading with the honest fever framing

questionBank.prompt: On a cold winter night, a person who fell asleep outdoors is brought to the clinic. A tympanic thermometer reads 93.8°F (34.3°C). What does this reading most likely indicate?
options: A normal fluctuation caused by the time of day.
Hypothermia — a body temperature well below the normal range, usually below about 95°F (35°C).
A fever caused by an infection.
A rise in temperature from recent exercise.
questionBank.explanation: 93.8°F is far below both the normal range and the 95°F hypothermia threshold, and the cold-exposure story fits. Time-of-day swings stay inside the normal range, a fever runs above it, and exercise raises temperature rather than lowering it.
questionBank.skill: Analyzing a low reading in a cold-exposure scenario

quickCheck.explanation: OpenStax's Clinical Nursing Skills states that body temperature reflects the balance between heat produced and heat lost. The other options describe food intake, room conditions, and cardiac output — none of which is what a temperature reading measures.

quickCheck.prompt: A nursing assistant measures a patient's oral temperature ten minutes after the patient drank a large mug of hot coffee. The reading is 99.6°F (37.6°C). What is the most sensible next step?
options: Document the reading as a fever immediately.
Recognize the reading may be inflated by the hot drink and recheck the temperature after a short wait.
Tell the patient to take aspirin to bring the temperature down.
Record the reading as proof of hypothermia.
quickCheck.explanation: Hot drinks can distort an oral reading, so a temperature taken right after coffee should be rechecked after a short wait rather than treated as a fever. The reading is above normal, not below it, and giving medication without assessment is never the immediate step.
quickCheck.skill: Applying site-and-activity context to interpret an oral reading

quickCheck.prompt: A nurse needs a temperature reading for a six-month-old infant who cannot hold a thermometer in her mouth. Which site is the most accurate choice for an infant?
options: Oral
Axillary
Rectal
Temporal
quickCheck.explanation: The rectal route is the most accurate and is considered the standard for infants, though it is the most invasive. Oral needs cooperation the infant cannot give, and axillary and temporal are less accurate alternatives used for convenience.
quickCheck.skill: Choosing the appropriate measurement site for an infant

title: Pulse
in30Seconds: Your pulse is the wave of blood you can feel each time your heart beats — a heartbeat pushes blood through your arteries, and where an artery runs close to the skin, you can feel that push. The normal resting pulse for an adult is about 60 to 100 beats per minute, though athletes and children sit outside that band. A pulse tells you three things: how fast the heart beats, whether the beats come evenly, and how strong each beat feels. Fast is tachycardia; slow is bradycardia.
whyItMatters: The pulse is the cheapest, fastest window into the heart that exists — no machine required. It is one of the first things checked in an emergency because a pulse means blood is moving and the heart is pumping. In everyday care, a resting pulse that climbs, drops, or turns uneven can be the first clue to fever, dehydration, anxiety, or a medication's effect. Learning to read a pulse well matters for the student heading into any clinical rotation, and for anyone who wants to notice changes in their own body before they become big problems.
learningObjectives: Define the pulse as the wave of blood felt each time the heart beats, using the attributed working definition.
State the adult resting reference range of about 60-100 beats per minute and explain why athletes and children differ.
Name five pulse sites — radial, carotid, brachial, femoral, pedal — and locate each one.
Distinguish the three things a pulse tells you: rate, rhythm, and strength.
Apply the terms bradycardia and tachycardia to a given resting pulse reading.
Explain how exercise, emotion, illness, and medications can change pulse rate.

collegeVersion.heading: What the pulse actually is
collegeVersion.body: The pulse is the wave of blood you can feel each time the heart beats. Every heartbeat pushes a pulse of blood out of the heart and into the arteries, and wherever an artery runs close to the surface of the skin, that push can be felt with the fingertips. OpenStax's Clinical Nursing Skills puts it this way: blood flow caused by the beating heart can be detected where arteries occur close to the surface of the skin. MedlinePlus frames the same reality as a count — the pulse is the number of heartbeats per minute. Both descriptions point at the same thing: the pulse is the heart's rhythm of life made touchable. That is why it is assessed so often. Along with breathing, the pulse is one of the first vital signs checked in an emergency, because it demonstrates that the heart is pumping and blood is moving. In routine care it is measured to establish a baseline and then rechecked to catch changes early.

collegeVersion.heading: The normal range — and the honest note
collegeVersion.body: For a resting adult, the reference range is about 60 to 100 beats per minute. That number comes from sources like MedlinePlus, which lists 60 to 100 beats per minute for adults and seniors, and OpenStax, which gives the same adult range. Two honest qualifications belong next to that number. First, athletes: a well-trained athlete often rests in the 40s to 60s because a stronger, more efficient heart pumps more blood with each beat, so fewer beats are needed. MedlinePlus lists trained athletes at 40 to 60, and OpenStax says athletes and adolescents can rest as slow as 40 to 50. Second, age: children normally have faster resting pulses that gradually slow toward the adult range — a newborn's resting pulse can run 70 to 190 beats per minute. The 60-100 band is a population reference for resting adults, not a universal rule for every person at every moment.

collegeVersion.heading: The sites
collegeVersion.body: The pulse can be felt wherever an artery passes close to the skin, and clinicians name the sites by the artery underneath. The radial pulse sits at the wrist, on the thumb side of the forearm, and is the usual choice for routine adult checks because it is easy to reach and comfortable for the patient. The carotid pulse lies on the neck, to the side of the windpipe; it carries blood toward the brain and is often checked first in emergencies — and only one side is pressed at a time, so blood flow to the head is never squeezed from both sides. The brachial pulse is found in the inner arm at the elbow crease, the site used when taking a blood pressure with a stethoscope. The femoral pulse is in the groin, where a large artery serves the leg. The pedal pulse — more formally the dorsalis pedis — sits on the top of the foot and is the preferred lower-leg site in adults and children. Each site is a place where the same heartbeat can be felt, just at a different distance from the heart.

collegeVersion.heading: Rate, rhythm, and strength
collegeVersion.body: Feeling a pulse is one action, but it delivers three pieces of information. Rate is the count: how many beats per minute. This is the number charted as the pulse, and it answers the question of how fast the heart is working. Rhythm is the pattern: do the beats arrive evenly, like a metronome, or do they skip, stutter, or cluster? A regular rhythm is expected; an irregular rhythm can be a sign that something in the heart's electrical system deserves attention. Strength is the force of each beat — the volume of blood moving through the artery. A healthy pulse feels firm and springy. A weak, thready pulse suggests reduced blood flow, as with dehydration; a bounding, very strong pulse can occur when blood backs up in the circulation. Reading all three together — not just the count — is what makes the pulse useful.

collegeVersion.heading: Bradycardia, tachycardia, and what moves the needle
collegeVersion.body: Two words describe the speed of a resting pulse. Bradycardia means a resting pulse slower than 60 beats per minute. Tachycardia means a resting pulse faster than 100 beats per minute. Both terms describe the rate, not a diagnosis: a marathon runner with a resting pulse of 52 is not sick, and a nurse's pulse of 105 during a stressful shift is not automatically heart disease. What changes the pulse? Exercise raises it — muscles demand more blood. Emotion raises it too: fear and anxiety rev the heart, while relaxation lets it settle. Illness can raise it — fever, infection, dehydration, and low oxygen all push the rate up as the body works harder. And medications change it: some prescribed drugs slow the heart, others speed it. The pulse is a live dial, and knowing which way it moves — and why — is the skill.

vocabulary.definition: The wave of blood felt each time the heart beats, counted as heartbeats per minute where an artery runs near the skin.
The number of times the heart beats in one minute; the pulse count equals the heart rate.
The pulse felt at the wrist on the thumb side, the usual site for a routine adult pulse check.
The pulse felt on the neck beside the windpipe, carrying blood to the brain and often checked first in emergencies.
The pulse felt in the inner arm at the elbow crease, the site used with a stethoscope when taking blood pressure.
The pulse felt in the groin where the large femoral artery supplies the leg.
The pulse on the top of the foot (dorsalis pedis), the preferred lower-leg pulse site in adults and children.
A resting pulse slower than 60 beats per minute; the term names the rate, not a diagnosis.
A resting pulse faster than 100 beats per minute; the term names the rate, not a diagnosis.
The pattern of the pulse beats — whether they arrive evenly and predictably or irregularly.

eli10.simplifiedExplanation: Your heart is a pump about the size of your fist. Every time it squeezes, it shoves a wave of blood into your arteries — the tubes that carry blood around your body. Some of those tubes run close to the surface, like the one at your wrist, and when the wave passes, you can feel it with your fingers. That felt wave is your pulse. Counting how many waves arrive in a minute tells you how fast the pump is running — usually 60 to 100 times a minute for a resting adult. The beats should come evenly, and each should feel firm but not hard. A pulse that is too slow is called bradycardia; too fast is tachycardia. Exercise, worry, fever, and medicine can all change the speed, so the pulse is a quick way to hear what the heart is doing right now.
eli10.analogy: Think of a pulse as the heartbeat of a drum line you can feel through the ground. The drummer strikes the drum, and a moment later the ground shudders under your feet. You never see the drum, but the shudder tells you the drummer is playing, how fast, and how hard. Your heart is the drummer, your arteries are the ground, and your fingertips are the place where the shudder arrives. One finger on the wrist is like one foot on the ground: you feel every strike.
eli10.analogyLimits: A drumbeat reaches every patch of ground at nearly the same instant, but a pulse wave travels through arteries at different speeds and fades with distance — a pedal pulse at the foot is fainter than the carotid pulse at the neck. Also, the ground shudder only tells you about the drum; the pulse only tells you about blood movement. It does not show blood pressure, oxygen, or the electrical health of the heart, which is why a pulse check is one vital sign among several, not the whole picture.

workedExample: Nadia is a nursing student on her first clinical day. Her instructor asks her to check the resting pulse of Mr. Osei, a 54-year-old patient admitted for observation. Nadia asks Mr. Osei to sit quietly, then places her index and middle fingers on the radial artery at his wrist. She feels a firm, even beat. She counts for 30 seconds, gets 44 beats, and multiplies by 2: 88 beats per minute. She notes rhythm — regular, like a metronome — and strength — full and springy. Before charting, she checks his record: his usual resting pulse has hovered in the mid-80s for the past two days. Her reading matches his baseline, so 88 is unremarkable for him even though it is a specific number, not an average. She charts pulse 88, radial, regular, strong, and tells her instructor the patient's pulse is within his own usual range.

commonMistakes.mistake: Treating a pulse of 58 as 'bradycardia, therefore sick.'
commonMistakes.correction: Bradycardia names a rate below 60, not a diagnosis. A trained athlete resting at 52 can be perfectly healthy because a stronger heart pumps more per beat. The label should prompt a closer look at the person, not an automatic alarm.

commonMistakes.mistake: Pressing both carotid pulses at the same time.
commonMistakes.correction: The carotid arteries feed the brain, and pressing both sides at once can squeeze off blood flow to the head and cause fainting. Check one side at a time, gently, as OpenStax and MedlinePlus both advise.

commonMistakes.mistake: Only counting the beats and ignoring rhythm and strength.
commonMistakes.correction: The count is half the story. An uneven rhythm or a weak, thready beat can be the more important finding, so every pulse check includes all three: rate, rhythm, and strength.

commonMistakes.mistake: Judging a pulse against the population range instead of the patient's own baseline.
commonMistakes.correction: A rate of 96 is inside the 60-100 adult range, but if the patient's usual resting pulse is 65, 96 is a real change worth investigating. Individual trends matter more than the population band.

commonMistakes.mistake: Thinking a fast pulse during exercise is a sign of illness.
commonMistakes.correction: Exercise is supposed to raise the pulse — working muscles demand more blood. What matters is the resting pulse: it should settle back into the person's usual range after activity.

compareContrast.distinction: The pulse is the felt wave of blood at the skin; heart rate is the number of beats per minute. They measure the same thing — the pulse count equals the heart rate — but the pulse is the touchable version of the number.
Bradycardia is a resting pulse below 60 beats per minute; tachycardia is above 100. Both describe the speed of the rate only, and neither is a diagnosis by itself.

The radial pulse at the wrist is the routine site for comfortable, everyday checks. The carotid pulse on the neck is larger and closer to the heart, making it the first place checked in emergencies to confirm the heart is pumping — always one side at a time.

keyTakeaway: The pulse is the heart's telegram: a felt wave that tells you, in seconds, how fast the heart beats, how evenly it beats, and how strongly blood is moving — best read against the person's own baseline, not the population average.

questionBank.prompt: A nursing student is asked to explain what the pulse actually is before taking one. Which description matches the attributed working definition?
options: The wave of blood you can feel each time the heart beats, where an artery runs close to the skin.
The pressure of blood against the artery walls while the heart rests between beats.
The amount of oxygen the blood carries to the body's tissues.
The sound of the heart valves closing, heard with a stethoscope.
questionBank.explanation: The working definition: the pulse is the wave of blood felt each time the heart beats, detected where an artery passes close to the skin (OpenStax; MedlinePlus counts it as heartbeats per minute). The other options describe blood pressure between beats, oxygen content, and heart sounds — different measurements.
questionBank.skill: Recalling the working definition of the pulse

questionBank.prompt: A 45-year-old patient rests quietly while a nursing assistant counts a radial pulse of 52 beats per minute. The patient is a marathon runner with no complaints. What is the most accurate interpretation?
options: Tachycardia — the pulse is dangerously fast and must be reported immediately.
A normal finding — trained athletes often rest in the 40s to 60s because their hearts pump more blood per beat.
Bradycardia — a pulse below 60 always means the heart is failing.
An unreliable reading — a resting pulse can never be below 60 in an adult.
questionBank.explanation: MedlinePlus lists well-trained athletes at 40-60 bpm and OpenStax notes athletes and adolescents can rest at 40-50 bpm because greater stroke volume means fewer beats are needed. Bradycardia and tachycardia name rates, not diagnoses; 52 is not tachycardia, and below 60 does not automatically mean a failing heart.
questionBank.skill: Applying the reference range with the athlete caveat

questionBank.prompt: A nurse needs a quick confirmation that a patient's heart is pumping during an emergency response. Which site and technique are most appropriate?
options: The pedal pulse on the top of the foot, pressed firmly for 30 seconds.
Both carotid pulses at the same time, to get a stronger signal.
The carotid pulse on one side of the neck, pressed gently.
The radial pulse at the wrist, counting for a full two minutes.
questionBank.explanation: OpenStax identifies the carotid pulse as the emergency site to verify the presence of a pulse, and both OpenStax and MedlinePlus warn that only one carotid side is pressed at a time so blood flow to the brain is not restricted. The other options use wrong sites, both sides at once, or needless extra time.
questionBank.skill: Applying site selection and the one-side carotid rule

questionBank.prompt: A patient's resting pulse has hovered near 64 beats per minute for several days. This morning it reads 96, and the patient is visibly anxious about an upcoming procedure. Which analysis is most sound?
options: No concern is warranted because 96 is inside the adult reference range.
The patient has bradycardia and needs immediate cardiac monitoring.
The anxiety is irrelevant; a 32-beat jump always means a heart rhythm problem.
The rate is within the population range but is a real change from this patient's baseline — anxiety is a plausible cause worth rechecking.
questionBank.explanation: OpenStax's trends point is exactly this: a rate normal for the population can still be a change for a specific patient, and OpenStax lists fear and anxiety as factors that raise the pulse. Option A ignores the baseline shift, B misuses bradycardia (below 60), and C overstates what one reading can prove.
questionBank.skill: Analyzing a pulse change against the patient's baseline

Radial — neck; carotid — wrist; brachial — groin; femoral — foot; pedal — inner elbow.

questionBank.explanation: The standard pairing (OpenStax; MedlinePlus): radial at the wrist, carotid on the neck, brachial in the inner elbow crease, femoral in the groin, and pedal (dorsalis pedis) on the top of the foot. The other options scramble the sites.

title: Respirations
in30Seconds: Respirations are the breaths a person takes per minute — the count of each rise and fall of the chest. For a resting adult, the usual reference range is about 12 to 20 breaths per minute, though sources give slightly different edges and ranges vary with age and activity. Each breath has two parts: inhalation, breathing in, and exhalation, breathing out. When nurses check respirations they look at rate, depth, and pattern — and they count quietly, because people who know they are being watched may breathe differently.
whyItMatters: Of all the vital signs, respirations are the easiest to miss: no thermometer, no cuff, just a quiet count of the chest rising and falling. Yet the count is information — a resting adult breathing 28 times a minute is telling you something a pulse or temperature may not. Changes in breathing can be the first signal of trouble, and the way a person breathes — fast or slow, shallow or deep, regular or irregular — adds detail no other vital sign gives. For students, learning to count respirations well, without making the patient self-conscious, is an early professional skill that shows up on clinical checklists and licensing exams.
learningObjectives: Define respirations as the breaths a person takes per minute, following the MedlinePlus and OpenStax reference definitions.
State the adult resting reference range of about 12 to 20 breaths per minute, and explain that normal ranges vary with age and activity.
Name the two parts of a breath — inhalation and exhalation — and state what each one does.
Distinguish the three characteristics nurses notice when assessing respirations: rate, depth, and pattern.
Apply the quiet-counting technique: measure respirations without the patient's awareness, and explain why the count is done that way.
Analyze a scenario and identify how exercise, emotion, illness, or pain could change a person's breathing.

collegeVersion.heading: A working definition: the breath count
collegeVersion.body: Respirations are the breaths a person takes per minute. The National Library of Medicine's MedlinePlus describes the respiratory rate as the measure of your breathing, and the OpenStax Clinical Nursing Skills text defines it as the breaths per minute. The word is used two ways in care settings: it is the act of breathing itself, and it is the count — how many times a person breathes in one minute. Each complete breath is one cycle: the chest rises, the chest falls. When a nurse records 18 on a vital-signs flow sheet, the entry means the patient breathed 18 times during the minute counted. Respirations are one of the four classic vital signs — temperature, pulse, respirations, and blood pressure — the basic measures of body function caregivers track to see how a person is doing.

collegeVersion.heading: The reference range, with the honest caveat
collegeVersion.body: For a resting adult, the usual reference is about 12 to 20 breaths per minute. OpenStax's Clinical Nursing Skills gives the adult range as 12 to 20; MedlinePlus lists 12 to 18. The two references agree closely and differ only at the upper edge — a fair warning against treating any single number as sacred. The honest note is this: normal depends on who is breathing. Newborns breathe 30 to 60 times a minute, toddlers 20 to 30, school-age children 14 to 22, and the OpenStax text notes that rates gradually shift to the adult range in late childhood or early adolescence. Activity moves the count too: breathing speeds up with hard exercise and settles back down at rest. A count outside the adult range is a cue to look closer and report — a signal, not a diagnosis.

collegeVersion.heading: The two parts of a breath
collegeVersion.body: Each breath has two named parts. Inhalation is breathing in: the chest expands and air moves into the lungs. Exhalation is breathing out: the chest relaxes and air moves out. The OpenStax respiratory-system section states the pair plainly as inhalation (breathing in) and expiration (breathing out); exhalation and expiration are the same word, and you will hear both in practice. In the vital-signs room the nurse need not analyze how the lungs do their work; that depth belongs to the biology classroom. What matters here is recognizing the cycle — one rise, one fall — because the count is built from complete cycles, not from single movements.

collegeVersion.heading: What to notice: rate, depth, and pattern
collegeVersion.body: When a nurse checks respirations, three features describe what is happening. Rate is the count — how many breaths per minute. Depth is how full each breath is: shallow breaths barely move the chest, while deep breaths move it clearly. Pattern is the rhythm — whether breaths come at regular intervals or irregularly. The OpenStax skill text lists exactly these: the breaths per minute, the rhythm, and the depth of respiration. All three matter together. A patient can breathe 16 times a minute — a perfectly ordinary rate — and still be breathing so shallowly that the chest barely moves, which is why a number alone never tells the whole story. Unlabored breathing, the text notes, is quietly audible at most; a normal breath makes little sound.

collegeVersion.heading: What changes the count
collegeVersion.body: Breathing responds to the body's demands, and everyday forces move the count. Exercise raises it: MedlinePlus notes that mild breathing changes can come from something as simple as hard exercise. Emotion moves it too — the OpenStax text lists anxiety and fear among the causes of a faster rate. Illness can change it in either direction, and MedlinePlus warns that slow or fast breathing can be a sign of a serious breathing problem. Pain changes it as well: the OpenStax text notes that shallow breathing occurs with pain. None is mysterious — each is the body adjusting — but every one is information. The nurse's job is to notice the change, connect it to what the patient is doing or feeling, and record what was actually seen.

collegeVersion.heading: The quiet count
collegeVersion.body: Respirations are counted without the patient noticing, and the reason is honest and practical. The OpenStax skill text explains that there is no need to let the patient know the respiratory rate is being obtained, because the knowledge could cause the patient to unknowingly alter their breathing pattern. Breathing is unusual among the vital signs: it is partly voluntary. People can hold their breath, sigh, or breathe faster on purpose, and a patient who knows the count is happening may do exactly that without meaning to. So the nurse uses a small sleight of hand: after counting the pulse, she keeps her fingers on the wrist and shifts her gaze to the chest, watching it rise and fall while she counts. The patient sees a nurse finishing the pulse check; the nurse gets an accurate number.

collegeVersion.heading: The quiet vital sign
collegeVersion.body: Here is the reality check. Temperature needs a thermometer, blood pressure needs a cuff, and the pulse needs fingers on a wrist — but respirations need nothing but observation, which makes them the quietest of the vital signs and the easiest to skip. The quiet has a cost: because nothing beeps and no number pops up on a screen, the count can be recorded without being truly taken. The remedy is the same as for every vital sign: take it deliberately, every time. MedlinePlus calls the respiratory rate the measure of your breathing — and the measure is only as good as the looking. A patient's breaths per minute, noticed carefully, are a stream of information: the rate, the depth, the pattern, and what they change with.

vocabulary.definition: The breaths a person takes, counted per minute; the act of breathing and the count of it.
The number of breaths taken in one minute.
Breathing in: the chest expands and air moves into the lungs.
Breathing out: the chest relaxes and air moves out of the lungs; also called expiration.
In respiratory assessment, how many breaths a person takes per minute.
How full each breath is — whether breathing is shallow or deep.
The rhythm of breathing — whether breaths come at regular or irregular intervals.
Faster-than-normal breathing, above the adult resting reference range of about 20 breaths per minute.
Slower-than-normal breathing, below the adult resting reference range of about 12 breaths per minute.
The basic measures of body function — temperature, pulse, respirations, and blood pressure — used to check a person's condition.

eli10.simplifiedExplanation: Respirations are simply the breaths you take — one breath in, one breath out — and the count of those in a minute. When a nurse checks them, she is really counting how often your chest rises and falls. Most adults at rest breathe about 12 to 20 times a minute, though babies breathe much faster and a runner breathes faster than someone sitting still. The nurse also notices whether the breaths are full or shallow and whether they come in a steady rhythm. The trick is that people change their breathing when they know it is being watched, so nurses count quietly, as if they were still finishing the pulse check.
eli10.analogy: Counting respirations is a little like birdwatching. A bird that notices you watching freezes, calls, or flies — you no longer see how it behaves on its own. So you watch from the corner of your eye, pretending to do something else. The nurse does the same: fingers resting on the wrist as if the pulse count were still going, eyes on the chest, counting each rise and fall. The patient, like the bird, does not know he is being observed, so the nurse gets the true behavior — the real breathing, unaltered by being watched.
eli10.analogyLimits: A startled bird flies away for good, but a patient's breathing settles back to normal once he stops thinking about it — the change is brief, not permanent. Birdwatchers hide to see nature untouched; nurses count quietly only to get an accurate number, and the moment the count is done they can talk openly about breathing. And unlike a bird, a patient breathes on purpose when he chooses — which is exactly why the quiet count exists.

workedExample: Priya, a first-year nursing student, is taking vital signs on Mr. Hale, who is resting after a morning procedure. She counts his pulse for a stretch of time, then keeps her fingers on his wrist and shifts her gaze to his chest, watching it rise and fall as she counts. She records each complete cycle — one rise, one fall — as a single breath. In a minute he breathes 18 times, evenly and at an ordinary depth, so she writes 18 breaths per minute on the flow sheet and moves on to the blood pressure cuff. She never told him she was counting his breathing, and he never knew — the count reflected how he truly breathes at rest.

commonMistakes.mistake: Announcing the count: 'I'm going to count your breathing now.'
commonMistakes.correction: Breathing is partly voluntary, so telling a patient you are counting invites an altered pattern — faster, slower, or deeper than usual. Count quietly while appearing to finish the pulse check, then record the true number.

commonMistakes.mistake: Counting the rise and the fall as two breaths.
commonMistakes.correction: One breath is one complete cycle: the rise (inhalation) plus the fall (exhalation) together count as a single breath. Counting each movement separately doubles the number.

commonMistakes.mistake: Recording only the number and skipping depth and pattern.
commonMistakes.correction: Respirations are described by rate, depth, and pattern together. A normal count can hide shallow or irregular breathing, so all three belong in the assessment.

commonMistakes.mistake: Treating any count outside the range as dangerous on its own.
commonMistakes.correction: The range is a reference for resting adults, not a rule. Age, activity, and the patient's own baseline all matter — an unusual count is a cue to look closer and report, not a diagnosis.

commonMistakes.mistake: Counting respirations while the patient is talking or moving.
commonMistakes.correction: Speech and motion change the count. The number is most meaningful when the patient is at rest, breathing quietly — the state the reference range describes.

compareContrast.distinction: Rate is how many breaths a person takes per minute; depth is how full each breath is. The two can move independently — a fast rate can come with shallow breaths, which is why both are assessed.

Both are counts per minute, but the pulse is automatic while respirations are partly voluntary — people can change their breathing when they think about it. That is why respirations are counted without the patient's awareness.
Tachypnea is breathing faster than the adult resting reference (above about 20 breaths per minute); bradypnea is breathing slower (below about 12). Both are directional terms, not diagnoses.

keyTakeaway: Respirations — the breaths a person takes per minute — are the quiet vital sign: count them without the patient noticing, and read them as rate, depth, and pattern, because a change in breathing is often the first clue that something else is going on.

questionBank.prompt: A nursing student is learning to assess vital signs. Her instructor asks what the term respirations refers to in the vital-signs set. Which answer is correct?
options: The number of breaths a person takes per minute
The number of heartbeats felt at the wrist in a minute
The amount of oxygen carried by the blood, shown by a finger probe
The force of blood pushing against the artery walls
questionBank.explanation: Respirations are the breaths per minute — each rise-and-fall cycle counts as one breath. Option B describes the pulse, C describes oxygen saturation, and D describes blood pressure; all three are separate vital signs with their own lessons.

questionBank.prompt: While taking vital signs on Mr. Kim, a nursing assistant counts his pulse and then keeps her fingers on his wrist while quietly watching his chest rise and fall. Why does she count his respirations this way?
options: Because the pulse count is more accurate when it is taken twice
Because she needs to see whether both sides of the chest move equally
Because she is waiting for the blood pressure cuff to finish its reading
Because a patient who knows his breathing is being watched may change his breathing pattern
questionBank.explanation: Respirations are partly voluntary, so a patient who knows the count is happening may unknowingly breathe faster, slower, or deeper. Counting quietly — while appearing to finish the pulse check — keeps the number accurate. The other options describe reasons that do not match the technique.
questionBank.skill: Applying the quiet-counting technique and explaining why it exists

questionBank.prompt: A resting adult patient breathes 16 times in one minute with easy, even breaths. How does this count compare with the usual adult resting reference range?
options: It is above the range, so the breathing is abnormally fast
It is below the range, so the breathing is abnormally slow
It falls within the usual range of about 12 to 20 breaths per minute
It is exactly at the boundary where breathing is considered abnormal
questionBank.explanation: The adult resting reference is about 12 to 20 breaths per minute (OpenStax; MedlinePlus lists 12 to 18), and 16 sits comfortably inside it. Options A and B place the count outside the range, and D misreads a normal count as a boundary case.
questionBank.skill: Comparing a measured count with the adult reference range

questionBank.prompt: A nurse counts a patient's respirations and records 14 breaths per minute, but she also notes that the breaths are shallow and uneven. Why does she record more than just the number 14?
options: Because the reference range is calculated from depth and pattern rather than from the count
Because respirations are described by rate, depth, and pattern together, and a normal rate can hide shallow or irregular breathing
Because shallow breathing always means the count was taken incorrectly
Because depth and pattern matter only when the rate is abnormal
questionBank.explanation: Respirations are assessed as rate, depth, and pattern together — a rate inside the range does not by itself rule out a problem. Options A and C misunderstand what the range describes, and D ignores that depth and pattern are part of every respiratory assessment.
questionBank.skill: Applying the rate-depth-pattern framework to a real assessment

questionBank.prompt: A patient hurries up two flights of stairs to reach the clinic and is breathing quickly when the nurse begins vital signs. Which reasoning best explains what the nurse should conclude?
options: The fast breathing is a sign of illness, because any quick breathing is abnormal
The fast breathing proves the patient's resting rate is permanently elevated
Physical activity raises the breathing rate, so the count should be taken at rest to reflect the true resting value
The patient is breathing quickly only because he knows his breathing is being watched

Option A overreads a normal response as illness, B mistakes a temporary change for a permanent one, and D confuses the awareness effect with the effect of exercise.
