title: Pathophysiology Basics
in30Seconds: Pathophysiology is the study of how disease changes the body's normal function. Health is a working balance; disease disrupts it. Disease follows patterns — genetic, infectious, inflammatory, degenerative, and traumatic — and every illness has a timeline of onset, course, and outcome. Signs are what others can observe; symptoms are what the patient feels. Nurses study pathophysiology because understanding the why behind an illness tells them what to watch.
whyItMatters: Every symptom a nurse meets — a fever, a cough, a complaint of pain — points back to something happening inside the body, and pathophysiology is the subject that connects the two. It explains why a disease produces the signs and symptoms it does. Academically, it is the bridge between the science of the body and every clinical skill that follows. Practically, a nurse who understands the mechanism knows what to look for, what to ask, and which changes matter most — which is why assessment, the first step of the nursing process, depends on it. The cellular-injury, inflammation, and fluid-and-electrolyte lessons build directly on this foundation.
learningObjectives: Define pathophysiology as the study of how disease changes the body's normal function, with the concept attributed to its source.
Distinguish health as a working balance from disease as a disruption of that balance.
Name the five common disease patterns — genetic, infectious, inflammatory, degenerative, and traumatic — and give an original example of each.
Distinguish signs from symptoms, using what can be observed versus what the patient feels.
Describe a disease's timeline in terms of onset, course, and outcome.
Apply the “why guides what to watch” argument to explain why nurses study pathophysiology.

collegeVersion.heading: What pathophysiology is
collegeVersion.body: Pathophysiology is the study of how disease changes the body's normal function. The National Library of Medicine's MeSH vocabulary captures the concept precisely: pathophysiology concerns “disordered function in disease states.” Notice what that means. The subject is not the disease itself, and it is not normal anatomy or physiology; it is the meeting point — how a disease takes something that works and makes it stop working. Etiology, the cause or origin of a disease, is the related question pathophysiology answers alongside mechanism: why did this begin, and what does it do once it begins? A nurse who understands pathophysiology can look at an illness and name what has gone wrong, which is the first step toward knowing what to watch.

collegeVersion.heading: Health as balance, disease as disruption
collegeVersion.body: Health is best understood as a working balance. The body's systems — breathing, circulation, immunity, healing — keep one another in check, and health is what it feels like when that balance holds. The World Health Organization's founding constitution defines health as a state of complete physical, mental, and social well-being, not merely the absence of disease. Disease, by contrast, is a disruption: something tips the balance, and normal function gives way to disordered function. The disruption can be large or small, sudden or slow, but the definition stays the same. Health is the balance working; disease is the balance broken.

collegeVersion.heading: Five patterns of disease
collegeVersion.body: Most diseases follow one of five patterns. Genetic disorders are conditions caused by changes in one or more genes — a child born with cystic fibrosis carries a gene variant that disrupts the lungs' normal function. Infectious diseases are caused by germs: bacteria, viruses, fungi, and parasites, with strep throat a familiar bacterial example. Inflammatory disease involves the body's protective immune response to injury or infection — the warmth and swelling around a splinter in a fingertip show the pattern in miniature. Degenerative disease is gradual breakdown over time; in osteoarthritis, the cartilage that cushions a knee wears away until bone meets bone. Traumatic disease begins with physical injury, such as the stretched ligament of a sprained ankle from a fall. Each pattern points to a different kind of cause, and therefore a different thing to watch. Cellular injury and inflammation each have their own lessons; this is the map, not the territory.

collegeVersion.heading: Signs and symptoms
collegeVersion.body: The National Cancer Institute's dictionary draws the line cleanly. A sign is something found during a physical exam or as a result of a laboratory or imaging test — evidence a health care provider can observe, such as a fever, a rash, or a high blood pressure reading. A symptom is something a person feels or experiences that may indicate disease — pain, nausea, fatigue — and only the person experiencing it can report it. Symptoms do not show up on medical tests. A person with a urinary tract infection might run a fever that a thermometer measures, a sign, while the same person feels drained and achy in a way only they can describe, a symptom. The distinction shapes nursing language: notes record signs, patients report symptoms, and both are data.

collegeVersion.heading: The timeline of disease
collegeVersion.body: Every disease has a timeline with three parts. Onset is how quickly it begins: a sprained ankle announces itself in an instant, while osteoarthritis creeps in over years. Course is how it runs: acute illnesses are short and intense, while chronic diseases last a year or more and demand ongoing attention. Outcome is how it ends — recovery, long-term management, or lasting disability. The timeline matters because it predicts what to expect. Sudden onset calls for quick watching; a chronic course calls for steady watching; and when a disease is found early, treatment is often easier — one reason screening looks for disease before symptoms appear.

collegeVersion.heading: Why nurses study this
collegeVersion.body: Nursing care begins with assessment, the systematic collection and analysis of data about the patient and the first step of the nursing process. Assessment only works if the nurse knows what data to collect, and that knowledge comes from pathophysiology. Understanding why a disease happens tells you what to watch: the nurse who knows that chronic lung disease narrows the airways watches breathing effort and oxygen levels, and the nurse who knows an infection is caused by germs watches the fever and the signs the germ produces. Pathophysiology is not the whole of nursing — observation, communication, and the care team complete the picture — but it is the reason the picture makes sense.

vocabulary.definition: The study of how disease changes the body's normal function; the National Library of Medicine's MeSH vocabulary frames the concept as disordered function in disease states.
A state of complete physical, mental, and social well-being, in the World Health Organization's founding definition, not merely the absence of disease.
A disruption of the body's normal working balance, marked by disordered function in the body.
The cause or origin of a disease, such as the germ behind an infection.
Evidence of disease that can be observed or measured by another person, such as a fever, a rash, or a high blood pressure reading.
Something a person feels or experiences that may indicate disease, such as pain or fatigue, which only the patient can report.
Describing a disease that begins sharply and runs a short, intense course.
Describing a disease that lasts a year or more and requires ongoing medical attention or limits daily activities.

eli10.simplifiedExplanation: Pathophysiology is the study of how disease changes the body's normal function — the story of what goes wrong when someone gets sick. Healthy bodies keep everything in balance; disease tips that balance over. Diseases tend to follow one of five patterns: they can be passed down in genes, caused by germs, driven by the body's own protective response to injury, a slow wearing-out of tissue, or the result of a physical injury. Every illness also has a timeline: how fast it starts, how it runs, and how it ends. And every illness shows up in two kinds of evidence — signs, which other people can see or measure, and symptoms, which only the sick person feels. Nurses study all of this because knowing why a disease happens tells them what to watch for in the patient in front of them.
eli10.analogy: Think of the body as a working kitchen. Health is the kitchen running smoothly: recipes followed, ingredients fresh, pots where they belong. Pathophysiology is what happens when something goes wrong. A missing ingredient is a genetic disorder; spoiled food is an infectious disease; a pan fire is inflammation; a worn-out oven is a degenerative disease; a dropped pot is trauma. Signs are what you can see from the doorway — smoke, spills, a burned hand. Symptoms are what the cook feels but you cannot see — the heat, the ache, the nausea.
eli10.analogyLimits: The kitchen breaks down as a picture of disease because the body is alive and self-repairing — it fights back, heals, and adapts, while a kitchen stays broken until someone fixes it. Disease also rarely follows one neat pattern; real illnesses often mix causes, and what looks like a missing ingredient in one person can be a worn-out oven in another.

workedExample: Mr. Alvarez, 58, is admitted with a two-day fever and a cough that is bringing up thick mucus. The admitting nurse, Priya, uses pathophysiology to decide what to watch. The fever and the mucus suggest an infectious pattern — germs multiplying in the airways — so she watches his breathing effort, oxygen level, and temperature trend, and she asks when the cough began (onset: sudden, over two days). The thermometer reads 101.8°F: a sign, measurable by anyone. Mr. Alvarez says he feels weak and achy: symptoms only he can report. When the sputum culture grows bacteria, the etiology — the cause — is confirmed. The course is acute, and because the cause was found early, the likely outcome is recovery. Priya's understanding of the why told her exactly what to watch from the first moment.

commonMistakes.mistake: “Signs and symptoms are the same thing, just different words.”
commonMistakes.correction: A sign can be observed or measured by someone else — a fever on a thermometer, a rash, a high blood pressure reading. A symptom is felt and reported only by the patient — pain, fatigue, nausea. A patient can have symptoms with no visible signs, or signs with no symptoms.

commonMistakes.mistake: “Chronic means the disease is severe or fatal.”
commonMistakes.correction: Chronic describes time, not severity: chronic diseases last a year or more and require ongoing attention. A chronic condition can be mild, and an acute illness can be dangerous.

commonMistakes.mistake: “If the exam and tests are normal, the patient must be fine.”
commonMistakes.correction: Symptoms do not show up on medical tests and cannot be observed by others. A patient can feel genuinely unwell while the measurable evidence is unremarkable — the patient's report is data too.

commonMistakes.mistake: “Pathophysiology lets the nurse name the diagnosis alone.”
commonMistakes.correction: Pathophysiology explains why disease happens and guides what to watch, but assessment, teamwork, and the provider's evaluation complete the picture. Understanding the mechanism is not the same as making the diagnosis.

compareContrast.distinction: A sign is observable or measurable by others — fever, rash, high blood pressure. A symptom is felt and reported only by the patient — pain, fatigue, nausea. The same illness usually produces both.
Acute describes a short, intense course that begins sharply; chronic describes a disease lasting a year or more that needs ongoing attention. Time is the difference, not seriousness.

Health is a working balance of the body's systems — complete well-being in the WHO's framing, not merely the absence of disease. Disease is a disruption of that balance, and the shift between the two can be gradual.

keyTakeaway: Pathophysiology is the why behind every symptom: understanding how disease changes the body's normal function tells the nurse what to watch, what to ask, and which changes matter.

questionBank.prompt: A nursing student is asked in class to give the working definition of pathophysiology. Which answer is correct?
options: The study of how disease changes the body's normal function.
The study of how the body is put together and how its parts work.
The study of how medicines move through and act on the body.
The study of how often diseases occur in a population.
questionBank.explanation: Pathophysiology is the study of how disease changes the body's normal function — what the National Library of Medicine's MeSH vocabulary calls disordered function in disease states — which option A states. Option B describes anatomy and physiology, option C describes pharmacology, and option D describes epidemiology.

questionBank.prompt: A patient tells the nurse, “I feel pain in my chest and I've been exhausted all week.” The exam, chest X-ray, and blood tests are all normal. How should the nurse classify what the patient is reporting?
options: Signs, because the patient described them in detail.
Etiology, because they point to the cause of the illness.
Symptoms, because they are felt by the patient and cannot be observed or measured by anyone else.
Both signs and symptoms, because the tests were normal.
questionBank.explanation: The patient's reports are symptoms — things a person feels or experiences that only the patient can report and that do not show up on tests, matching the National Cancer Institute's definition. Option A is wrong because signs are observable or measurable by others, option B confuses symptoms with the cause (etiology), and option D is wrong because nothing here was observed or measured.
questionBank.skill: Applying the sign-versus-symptom distinction to a patient report

questionBank.prompt: During rounds, a nurse sees a rash on a patient's arm while the patient says, “I feel achy and my stomach is upset.” Which statement correctly labels what the nurse and the patient have each noticed?
options: The rash is a symptom because the nurse can see it; the achiness is a sign because the patient feels it.
The rash is a sign because it can be observed by others; the achiness and upset stomach are symptoms because only the patient feels them.
Both are signs because they are both part of a physical exam.
Both are symptoms because the patient is the one experiencing them.
questionBank.explanation: The rash is a sign — evidence found on physical exam that others can observe — while achiness and an upset stomach are symptoms, felt and reported only by the patient, per the National Cancer Institute's definitions. Option A swaps the two labels, option C wrongly calls the patient's feelings signs, and option D wrongly calls the visible rash a symptom.
questionBank.skill: Classifying clinical findings as signs or symptoms

questionBank.prompt: A 70-year-old patient has had knee pain for several years that started gradually. An X-ray shows the joint's cartilage has worn away and the bones are rubbing together. Which disease pattern does this best illustrate?

Infectious, because a germ could have caused the wear.
Traumatic, because the joint is damaged.
Degenerative, because the tissue broke down gradually over time.
questionBank.explanation: Osteoarthritis illustrates the degenerative pattern — gradual breakdown of tissue over time, with the cartilage cushion wearing away until bones rub together, as MedlinePlus describes. Option A is wrong because nothing here suggests a change in genes, option B is wrong because no germ is involved, and option C is wrong because the damage came from gradual wear, not a single injury.
questionBank.skill: Matching a clinical picture to a disease pattern

questionBank.prompt: Mr. Chen slips on a wet stair and lands hard on his ankle. Minutes later it is swollen and painful, and the provider finds a stretched ligament. Which disease pattern best describes what happened?

Traumatic, because a physical injury — the fall — caused the damage.
Infectious, because the swelling means germs entered the joint.
Inflammatory, because inflammation is the disease itself.

Option A is wrong because no gene change is involved, option C is wrong because swelling alone does not mean infection, and option D confuses the body's protective response, a sibling topic, with the cause of the injury.

title: Cellular Injury
in30Seconds: Cellular injury is damage to cells that disrupts their normal function. It can come from a lack of oxygen, toxins, infection, trauma, or extreme heat and cold. Some injuries are reversible — the cell recovers; others are irreversible, ending in cell death. Injured cells swell, change, and release signals, and the body answers with repair and regeneration. Understanding what injures cells — and how they die — explains the symptoms behind most illnesses.
whyItMatters: Every illness that a nurse meets starts at the same place: cells being pushed past what they can tolerate. Academically, cellular injury is the bridge between normal physiology and the disease patterns introduced in pathophysiology basics — it is the microscopic root of most illness. Practically, recognizing how an injury happens — oxygen cut off, toxin exposure, infection, a burn — tells the nurse what to watch and what questions to ask. Looking forward, the same logic extends through inflammation, infection control, and every system-based course that follows, because treatments from oxygen therapy to wound care exist to limit injury and support repair.
learningObjectives: Define cellular injury as damage to cells that disrupts their normal function, with the concept attributed to its source.
Name the major causes of cellular injury — lack of oxygen, toxins, infection, trauma, and heat and cold — and give an original example of each.
Distinguish reversible injury, in which the cell recovers, from irreversible injury, in which the cell dies.
Distinguish apoptosis, programmed cell death, from necrosis, accidental cell death that triggers inflammation.
Describe what injured cells do and how the body responds with inflammation, repair, and regeneration.
Apply the injury-pattern idea to explain why a patient's symptoms follow the mechanism of the injury.

collegeVersion.heading: What cellular injury is
collegeVersion.body: When a cell is pushed beyond what it can tolerate, it is injured. The working definition used here: cellular injury is damage to cells that disrupts their normal function. It is the same disruption of ordered function that pathophysiology describes at the level of the whole body, now seen at the level of the cell — which is why the pathophysiology-basics lesson calls this territory beneath its map. Injury is a spectrum. At one end, a cell is stressed but intact; at the other end, it dies. The National Cancer Institute's dictionary marks the endpoint: necrosis, it says, refers to the death of living tissues. Everything between a stressed cell and a dead one is what this lesson maps.

collegeVersion.heading: Five common causes of injury
collegeVersion.body: Most cellular injury comes from one of five causes. Lack of oxygen: when a coronary artery narrows, the heart muscle downstream is starved of fuel — the mechanism behind a heart attack. Toxins: poisons damage cells directly, whether a caustic cleaner splashed on skin, alcohol in excess, or carbon monoxide from a faulty heater. Infection: bacteria and viruses injure the cells they invade, which is why a strep throat leaves the throat lining raw. Trauma: physical force tears and crushes tissue, as when a fall fractures a bone and damages the flesh around it. Heat and cold: a kitchen scald cooks skin cells, and prolonged cold freezes them, as in the frostbitten fingertips of a hiker caught outdoors. One cause, one mechanism, and each points to a different thing to prevent.

collegeVersion.heading: Reversible or irreversible
collegeVersion.body: The most important question about any injury is whether the cell can recover. In reversible injury the damage is mild enough that the cell returns to normal once the cause is removed — a muscle cell briefly short of oxygen recovers when blood flow returns. In irreversible injury the damage passes the point of no return, and the cell dies. Cells die in two distinct ways. Apoptosis is programmed cell death: a series of molecular steps inside the cell lead to its own orderly death, and the body uses the process to remove unneeded or abnormal cells, which is why the NCI dictionary calls it programmed cell death. Necrosis is accidental cell death: living tissue dies from injury, spills its contents, and triggers inflammation. The difference matters clinically, because inflammation is the body's alarm system.

collegeVersion.heading: What injured cells do
collegeVersion.body: Injured cells are not passive. They swell, because the pumps that keep water out of the cell fail when energy runs low. Their internal structure changes — organelles distort, and the cell's shape and appearance under a microscope alter. They release signals: the contents of damaged cells, and distress molecules they actively send out, alert the immune system that something is wrong. And they stop doing their jobs: a muscle cell that cannot contract, a gland cell that cannot secrete. These changes are what a pathologist sees through the lens and what a nurse infers from how the patient behaves.

collegeVersion.heading: The body's response: repair and regeneration
collegeVersion.body: The body answers injury with a standard sequence. The first response is inflammation: it limits the extent of the injury, eliminates or blunts the cause, and sets the stage for healing — it is the subject of its own lesson. Then come two kinds of healing. Regeneration replaces the lost tissue with new cells of the same type and restores function, the way skin heals over a shallow scrape. Repair patches the damage with scar tissue that restores structure but not full function, the way a deep cut heals with a scar. Which one happens depends on the tissue: skin and liver regenerate well, while heart muscle and nerve cells mostly do not — for them, repair is the best the body can manage.

collegeVersion.heading: Why it matters clinically
collegeVersion.body: Injury patterns explain symptoms. The nurse who knows that a heart attack is oxygen-starved muscle dying beyond repair expects chest pain that rest does not ease, and knows the dying cells will soon stir up inflammation. The nurse who knows frostbite is cold killing tissue understands why the fingers throb as they rewarm. The nurse who knows a caustic chemical burns cells on contact washes the skin immediately. Cellular injury is the microscopic root of most illness: fever, pain, swelling, and organ failure all trace back to cells being pushed past their limits. Understanding the injury is the first step toward limiting it and supporting the body's repair.

vocabulary.definition: Damage to cells that disrupts their normal function, ranging from reversible stress to cell death.
A shortage of oxygen reaching the body's cells; the mechanism behind injury from lack of oxygen.
A poison — any chemical that damages cells, whether produced by living organisms or made by humans.
Cell damage from which the cell fully recovers once the cause is removed.
Cell damage past the point of no return that ends in the cell's death.
Programmed cell death: a series of molecular steps inside a cell lead to its own orderly death, one way the body removes unneeded or abnormal cells.
The death of living tissue from injury, which spills cell contents and triggers inflammation.
The replacement of damaged tissue by new cells of the same type.
The body's standard initial response to injury: it limits the injury's extent, blunts its cause, and begins repair and regeneration.

eli10.simplifiedExplanation: Cells are the body's smallest workers, and cellular injury is what happens when something pushes them past what they can handle. Five things do most of the damage: not enough oxygen, poisons, germs, physical force, and extreme heat or cold. Some damage is minor — take the cause away and the cell bounces back; that is reversible injury. Some damage is fatal: the cell dies. When cells die on purpose, in a neat, orderly way the body controls, it is called apoptosis — programmed cell death, how the body clears out unneeded or abnormal cells. When cells die by accident, bursting and spilling their contents, it is called necrosis, and it stirs up inflammation. Injured cells swell, look different, and send out alarm signals, and the body answers with repair and replacement. Most illnesses start right here, at the level of the cell.
eli10.analogy: Think of cells as workers in a busy kitchen, and cellular injury as the things that knock them off their game. No oxygen is a worker suffocating in a smoke-filled room; a toxin is a worker breathing fumes from a spilled cleaner; infection is a coworker spreading a cold; trauma is a dropped crate landing on someone's foot; heat and cold are a too-hot oven and a walk-in freezer. A reversible injury is a worker who needs a break and a glass of water and is back on the line in minutes. An irreversible injury is a worker who collapses and does not get back up — the kitchen staff must call for a replacement.
eli10.analogyLimits: Where the analogy breaks down: a kitchen can close for the night and reopen fresh, but the body never fully closes — cells keep working through injury, and the repair crew (inflammation) works while the damage is still happening. And unlike an employer who simply hires a new worker, the body can only replace some cells: heart muscle and nerve cells that die are gone for good.

workedExample: Mr. Patel, 64, is brought in with crushing chest pain that started while he was shoveling snow and has not eased with rest. The nurse, Dana, thinks in terms of cellular injury. The pain began with an oxygen shortage: a narrowed coronary artery cannot deliver enough blood to part of the heart muscle, so those cells are being starved. Because the shortage is severe and ongoing, the injury passes from reversible to irreversible: the muscle cells die, and the tissue dies with them — necrosis, which the NCI dictionary describes as the death of living tissues. The dying cells spill their contents, which Dana knows will trigger inflammation, the standard initial response to injury, in the hours ahead. The EKG and a blood test for troponin, a protein released by dying heart muscle, confirm the pattern. The persistent pain is not random; it is the injury pattern announcing itself.

commonMistakes.mistake: “Apoptosis and necrosis are the same thing — both are just cell death.”
commonMistakes.correction: Apoptosis is programmed cell death: an orderly, molecularly driven death the body uses to remove unneeded or abnormal cells. Necrosis is accidental cell death of living tissue that spills its contents and triggers inflammation. The distinction shapes what the nurse expects to see — necrosis brings an inflammatory response, apoptosis usually does not.

commonMistakes.mistake: “Any cell injury is permanent.”
commonMistakes.correction: Most injuries are reversible: remove the cause — restore oxygen, wash off the toxin — and the cell recovers. Only damage past the point of no return is irreversible and ends in cell death.

commonMistakes.mistake: “Inflammation is a disease in its own right.”
commonMistakes.correction: Inflammation is the body's standard initial response to injury: it limits the extent of the damage, blunts the cause, and sets up repair and regeneration. It is a response with a job, not a separate illness — and it gets its own lesson.

commonMistakes.mistake: “Lost cells are always replaced, so the body heals completely.”
commonMistakes.correction: Regeneration — new cells of the same type — restores function, but not every tissue can do it. Heart muscle and nerve cells generally do not replace themselves; for them the body falls back on repair, scar tissue that restores structure but not full function.

compareContrast.distinction: Reversible injury is damage the cell survives — remove the cause and the cell returns to normal. Irreversible injury passes the point of no return and ends in cell death. Reversibility is the first question a clinician asks about any injury.

Apoptosis is programmed, orderly cell death the body uses to clear unneeded or abnormal cells; necrosis is accidental cell death of living tissue that spills contents and triggers inflammation. One is controlled demolition, the other is a collapse.

Regeneration replaces damaged tissue with new cells of the same type and restores function; repair patches the damage with scar tissue that restores structure but not full function. Skin and liver regenerate well; heart muscle and nerve cells mostly rely on repair.

keyTakeaway: Cellular injury is the microscopic root of most illness: knowing what injures cells, whether the damage is reversible, and how cells die tells the nurse what to watch and why symptoms appear.

options: Damage to cells that disrupts their normal function.
The immune system's reaction to germs and foreign substances.
The division of cells to replace tissue that has worn out.
The study of how medicines change the way cells behave.

questionBank.prompt: During a heart attack, part of the heart muscle is cut off from oxygen. The starved muscle cells die, spill their contents, and trigger inflammation in the surrounding tissue. Which term names this kind of cell death?
options: Apoptosis
Regeneration
Reversible injury
Necrosis
questionBank.explanation: This is necrosis — accidental cell death of living tissue that triggers inflammation, exactly what the NCI dictionary describes as the death of living tissues. Option A is apoptosis, the body's orderly, programmed cell death; option B is replacement by new cells of the same type; option C is damage the cell recovers from. The inflammation is the giveaway: necrosis stirs it up, apoptosis does not.
questionBank.skill: Applying the necrosis–apoptosis distinction to a clinical scenario.

questionBank.prompt: A man who works outdoors in winter develops numb, painful fingertips after spending hours in below-freezing cold. His provider tells him the cold damaged his skin cells. Which cause of cellular injury does this illustrate?
options: Lack of oxygen
Heat and cold
Trauma
Toxins
questionBank.explanation: The fingertip damage came from extreme cold, one of the classic causes of cellular injury — heat and cold damage cells directly, as in burns and frostbite. Option A, lack of oxygen, is a different mechanism; option C, trauma, is physical force such as a blow or a cut; option D, toxins, is chemical damage. The temperature is the injurious agent here.
questionBank.skill: Matching a described injury to its cause.

questionBank.prompt: A laboratory worker accidentally splashes a strong cleaning chemical on her forearm, and the skin cells it touches are damaged and die on the spot. Which cause of cellular injury is at work?
options: Trauma
Infection
Toxins
Lack of oxygen
questionBank.explanation: The chemical is a toxin — a poisonous substance that damages cells directly, one of the five common causes of cellular injury. Option A, trauma, means physical force; option B, infection, means damage by germs; option D, lack of oxygen, starves cells of fuel. A caustic chemical burns cells by chemical action, which is the toxin mechanism.
questionBank.skill: Applying the toxin cause to a chemical-exposure scenario.

questionBank.prompt: A patient with a heart attack reports chest pain that began suddenly and has not improved with rest. Using the injury-pattern idea, which explanation best accounts for the pain?
options: The pain means the heart muscle is regenerating new cells.
The pain proves the injury is reversible and the cells will recover.
The pain is produced by the repair process, not by the injury itself.
The pain reflects heart muscle cells injured beyond repair that have died.
questionBank.explanation: Persistent pain that rest does not ease is the clinical signature of irreversible injury — the starved heart muscle cells have died, and the body's inflammatory response to that necrosis follows. Option A is wrong because regeneration replaces cells rather than causing pain, and heart muscle regenerates poorly; option B is wrong because pain that persists signals damage past the point of no return; option C confuses the body's later repair response with the source of the pain, which is the injured, dying tissue itself.
questionBank.skill: Analyzing a symptom pattern through the reversible–irreversible injury mechanism.

title: Inflammation
in30Seconds: Inflammation is the body's protective response to injury or infection — a coordinated alarm that contains damage, summons immune cells, and starts repair. The classic signs are redness, heat, swelling, pain, and loss of function. Acute inflammation, like a paper cut healing in days, is short and purposeful. Chronic inflammation, which lingers for months or years, can contribute to disease. Nurses read these signs as information about what is happening beneath the surface.
whyItMatters: A nurse meets inflammation every shift — the red hot ankle after a fall, the swollen throat of a patient with strep, the warmth around an IV site. It is the body's oldest alarm system, and it is also a clue. The five classic signs tell a story about blood flow, vessel leakiness, and immune activity that a nurse can read without any equipment. Understanding what inflammation is for — and when it overstays its welcome — separates a meaningful observation from a confusing one. It is also the foundation for the infection-control and wound-care skills that follow in the curriculum.
learningObjectives: Define inflammation as the body's protective response to injury or infection, with the definition attributed to its sources.
Name the five classic signs of inflammation and explain the underlying cause of each.
Distinguish acute inflammation from chronic inflammation, using original examples of each.
Explain what inflammation does for the body: containing damage, summoning immune cells, and starting repair.
Describe the relationship between inflammation and the immune system, including fever as a systemic sign.
Apply the “fire alarm, not the fire” framing to judge when inflammation is helpful and when it becomes harmful.

collegeVersion.heading: What inflammation is
collegeVersion.body: Inflammation is the body's protective response to injury or infection. MedlinePlus's medical encyclopedia describes it plainly: inflammation occurs when tissues are injured by bacteria, trauma, toxins, heat, or any other cause. The National Cancer Institute's dictionary adds the mechanism in one line: the body releases chemicals that trigger an immune response to fight off infection or heal damaged tissue. Notice what both definitions share — inflammation is a response, not an invader. It is something the body does, and it does it on purpose. A scraped elbow turns red and warm not because the scrape is failing but because the body has switched on a program of defense and repair. The response is the same whether the trigger is a splinter, a sprain, or a throat infection: injured tissue sends out chemical signals, and the body answers.

collegeVersion.heading: The five classic signs
collegeVersion.body: Textbooks have taught the same five signs for generations: redness, heat, swelling, pain, and loss of function. Each one follows from what the response is doing. Redness happens because blood vessels widen, sending more blood to the injured area. Heat happens for the same reason — the extra blood carries warmth from deep in the body to the surface, which is why an inflamed joint feels hot to the touch. Swelling happens because the widened vessels become leaky, letting fluid move out of the blood and into the tissue. Pain happens partly because that swelling presses on nerves and partly because the chemicals of inflammation sensitize them. Loss of function is the natural result: a swollen finger does not bend easily, and a sore knee does not want to bear weight. The signs are not five separate problems. They are five views of the same process — more blood, leakier vessels, and fluid where it does not belong.

collegeVersion.heading: What inflammation actually does
collegeVersion.body: Inflammation has three jobs, and they follow in order. First, it contains the damage. Fluid and clotting factors move into the injured area and wall it off, so a local problem stays local. Second, it summons immune cells. The same chemical signals that widen vessels also act as a call for phagocytes — white blood cells that engulf germs and debris. MedlinePlus describes the clean-up directly: phagocytes move into the area, swallow up foreign matter, dead tissue, and bacteria, and pus collects as the battle ends — a mixture of dead tissue, dead bacteria, and spent white cells. Third, it starts repair. With the threat contained and the debris cleared, the body can begin rebuilding. None of this is glamorous, and much of it is uncomfortable, but it is the body's own first-aid kit, stocked and ready at every injury.

collegeVersion.heading: Acute versus chronic
collegeVersion.body: Acute inflammation is the response that starts fast, does its job, and ends. Cut your finger on a piece of paper, and within minutes the area reddens and swells; within days the cut has closed and the redness fades. The National Cancer Institute's definition makes the endpoint explicit: once the injury or infection is healed, the inflammatory process ends. Chronic inflammation is different — it lingers for months or years, sometimes long after the original trigger is gone. The same dictionary notes the cost: chronic inflammation can damage healthy cells, tissues, and organs. A person with years of joint pain is not experiencing one long paper cut; the inflammatory program that should switch off is still running. The contrast matters clinically because acute inflammation is usually a sign of healing at work, while chronic inflammation is often a problem in its own right.

collegeVersion.heading: The immune connection
collegeVersion.body: Inflammation is the immune system's first responder, not a separate system. The chemicals released by damaged cells — histamine, bradykinin, and prostaglandins, in MedlinePlus's list — do two things at once: they widen and loosen the vessels, and they recruit the white cells that actually destroy invaders. Fever shows the connection on a whole-body scale. MedlinePlus notes that a fever is not a disease; it is usually a sign that the body is fighting an illness or infection, and higher temperatures make it harder for many bacteria and viruses to survive. The warmth of a single inflamed joint and the warmth of a feverish patient are the same logic at different scales. Immunologists study the details of which cells talk to which; nurses study what the conversation looks like from the outside.

collegeVersion.heading: When inflammation turns harmful
collegeVersion.body: Because inflammation is protective, it is tempting to treat every trace of it as good news. The honest picture is more complicated. Chronic inflammation contributes to disease — the National Cancer Institute says it can damage healthy cells, tissues, and organs — and long-standing inflammation is one piece of the story in conditions such as heart disease, diabetes, and arthritis. This is not a reason to fear inflammation, and it is not a reason to skip the topic; it is a reason to be precise. Acute inflammation is a fire alarm: loud, useful, and meant to stop ringing once the fire is out. Chronic inflammation is the alarm that never stops, and a fire alarm that never stops is itself a problem. The nurse's job is to read the signal, ask what it is telling them, and notice when it has been ringing too long.

vocabulary.definition: The body's protective response to injury or infection, driven by chemicals that widen blood vessels and summon immune cells to the affected tissue.
A short-lived inflammatory response that begins quickly and ends once the injury or infection heals.
Long-lasting inflammation that can persist for months or years and can damage healthy cells, tissues, and organs.
A white blood cell that moves into an inflamed area and engulfs germs, dead tissue, and debris.
The fluid that collects when inflammation is fighting infection, made of dead tissue, dead bacteria, and spent white blood cells.
A chemical released by damaged cells that widens and loosens blood vessels during the inflammatory response.
A classic sign of inflammation caused by widened blood vessels sending more blood into the injured area.
A classic sign of inflammation caused by leaky vessels letting fluid move from the blood into the tissue.
A body temperature higher than normal, usually a sign that the body is fighting an illness or infection rather than a disease itself.
A classic sign of inflammation in which the injured part does not move or work as easily as usual, such as a swollen finger that will not bend.

eli10.simplifiedExplanation: Inflammation is how your body protects itself when something hurts it. When tissues get injured — by a cut, a germ, a burn, or a hard knock — they send out chemical signals, and the body answers by sending extra blood and fluid to the area. That is why an injured spot turns red, feels warm, swells up, and hurts. The swelling and pain are annoying, but they are the body containing the damage, calling in white blood cells to clean up, and starting to repair. Most inflammation is short: it finishes its job and stops. Sometimes it lingers for a long time, and then it can cause harm instead of helping.
eli10.analogy: Think of inflammation as a fire alarm in a building. The alarm is not the fire — it is the warning system that tells everyone to act. When a small fire starts in a wastebasket, the alarm rings, water sprays, and the damage stays small. That is acute inflammation: noisy, effective, and over quickly. But an alarm that never stops ringing — after the fire is out, day after day — stops being helpful. It keeps people on edge and wears the building out. Chronic inflammation is the alarm that will not shut off.
eli10.analogyLimits: The alarm is a good picture of the warning role, but it misses how active inflammation is. A fire alarm only warns; inflammation also fights — it sends white blood cells that destroy germs and starts the repair work itself. And unlike an alarm, which is either ringing or silent, inflammation comes in degrees, from a mild ache to a raging response.

workedExample: Jonas, 19, scrapes his elbow on the gym floor. Within minutes the scrape is red and warm; by evening it is swollen and tender, and bending the elbow hurts. His roommate calls it infected. His nurse mother, visiting, points instead to what the signs mean: widened vessels brought the redness and heat, leaky vessels caused the swelling, and the tenderness is the chemicals of inflammation sensitizing the nerves. The scrape is doing what injuries do — containing the damage and calling in white blood cells to clean up. By day four the redness has faded and the elbow bends again. The inflammation did its job and switched off, exactly as acute inflammation should.

commonMistakes.mistake: “Inflammation means infection.”
commonMistakes.correction: Inflammation is the body's response; infection is one possible trigger. A sprained ankle inflames without any germ involved. Infection can trigger inflammation, but not all inflammation is infection.

commonMistakes.mistake: “The redness, heat, and swelling are the problem, so the goal is to make them disappear.”
commonMistakes.correction: Those signs are the visible evidence of the body containing damage and starting repair. Treating the response without asking what triggered it misses the cause; the signs are information first.

commonMistakes.mistake: “Chronic means severe.”
commonMistakes.correction: Chronic describes duration, not intensity. Chronic inflammation means the response lingers for months or years; it can be low-grade and nearly silent, and that persistence is what allows it to damage tissues over time.

commonMistakes.mistake: “Fever is a disease that needs to be fought.”
commonMistakes.correction: A fever is usually a sign that the body is fighting an illness or infection — a whole-body extension of inflammation — not a disease itself. Treating the underlying cause matters more than treating the number on the thermometer.

compareContrast.distinction: Acute inflammation begins fast and ends when the injury heals — a paper cut that reddens for a few days. Chronic inflammation lingers for months or years and can damage healthy tissue — years of joint pain from a response that never switches off.
Redness and heat come from widened vessels carrying more blood to the area; swelling comes from those same vessels leaking fluid into the tissue. Both trace to the same vascular changes.

Inflammation is the body's response; infection is an invasion by germs. Infection often triggers inflammation, but inflammation can occur without infection — a sprain inflames with no germ involved — and the response is protective in both cases.

keyTakeaway: Inflammation is the body's protective response to injury or infection — a fire alarm, not the fire. The classic signs are its visible language, and the nurse's skill is reading what they say and noticing when the alarm rings too long.

questionBank.prompt: During clinical orientation, an instructor asks the group for the working definition of inflammation. Which answer is correct?
options: The process by which the body produces antibodies after a vaccination.
The gradual breakdown of tissue that happens with aging.
The body's protective response to injury or infection, in which chemicals widen blood vessels and summon immune cells.
The movement of medicines from the bloodstream into the tissues.
questionBank.explanation: Inflammation is the body's protective response to injury or infection — triggered when tissues are injured by bacteria, trauma, toxins, heat, or any other cause, as MedlinePlus's encyclopedia describes — which option C states. Option A describes antibody production, a later immune event; option B describes degeneration; option D describes drug distribution, a pharmacology concept.
questionBank.skill: Recognizing the working definition of inflammation

questionBank.prompt: A patient falls while getting out of bed and lands on her wrist. Twenty minutes later the wrist is red, warm, and swollen, and she is guarding it. The provider finds a sprain, not a break. Which statement best explains what the patient's signs represent?
options: The body's protective response to injury — widened vessels and leaking fluid — at work in a sprained wrist.
An infection has entered the wrist and is multiplying in the joint.
The injury destroyed the blood vessels, so blood is pooling under the skin.
The wrist is failing because the inflammatory response has worn out.
questionBank.explanation: A sprain — a stretched ligament from a fall — triggers acute inflammation: widened, leaky vessels produce the redness, heat, and swelling, per MedlinePlus's description of the response to tissue injury. Option B is wrong because a sprain involves no germ; option C is wrong because the vessels are leaky, not destroyed; option D is wrong because the response is protective and just beginning.
questionBank.skill: Applying the mechanism of acute inflammation to a sprain

questionBank.prompt: A nurse is caring for a patient whose knuckles have been swollen, warm, and painful for two years. The provider explains that the inflammatory process has been running continuously. Which conclusion about this patient's inflammation is most accurate?
options: It is acute inflammation, because it causes pain.
It is protective, because it will end once the current injury heals.
It is harmless, because the body would not maintain a harmful process.
It is chronic inflammation, and its long persistence can damage healthy tissue.
questionBank.explanation: Two years of continuous inflammation is chronic, and the National Cancer Institute's dictionary notes that chronic inflammation can damage healthy cells, tissues, and organs — so option D is right. Option A is wrong because duration, not pain, separates acute from chronic; option B is wrong because this response has not ended with healing; option C contradicts the documented harm of long-running inflammation.
questionBank.skill: Analyzing a clinical picture to classify inflammation as chronic and judge its significance

questionBank.prompt: A patient with a splinter in her palm asks why the area around it is red, warm, and swollen even though she cannot see any germs. What is the most accurate response?
options: The redness and warmth mean the splinter has carried bacteria deep into the hand.
The splinter injured the tissue, and the body's protective response widened the vessels and leaked fluid into the area.
The swelling is pus forming, which always means the wound is infected.
The signs will last for months because every injury causes chronic inflammation.
questionBank.explanation: Tissue injury alone — from trauma such as a splinter — triggers the response: damaged cells release chemicals that widen and loosen vessels, producing redness, warmth, and swelling, as MedlinePlus describes. Option A overreads: redness and warmth do not by themselves prove bacteria; option C is wrong because pus is a late battle sign, not the same as early swelling; option D is wrong because a simple splinter injury produces short-lived acute inflammation.
questionBank.skill: Explaining the vascular mechanism behind the classic signs

Redness, bleeding, bruising, numbness, and cramping.

title: Fluid and Electrolyte Basics
in30Seconds: Fluid and electrolyte balance is the body's way of keeping the right amount of water and dissolved minerals in the right places — inside cells, outside cells, and in the blood. Electrolytes such as sodium, potassium, calcium, and chloride carry an electric charge that muscles, nerves, and the heart depend on. The kidneys, hormones, and thirst keep the system in check. When it slips, dehydration or fluid overload follows, and nearly every body system feels the difference.
whyItMatters: Nurses meet fluid and electrolyte problems in nearly every patient population, and small imbalances can produce outsized symptoms — a modest potassium shift can disturb the heart's rhythm. Academically, this lesson is the frame for later clinical topics: intravenous therapy, kidney disease, and the pathophysiology of dehydration all assume you know what the compartments are and who regulates them. Practically, it explains everyday observations, like why a vomiting patient looks dry and tired or why a heart-failure patient gains weight from retained fluid. Looking ahead, you will meet these ideas again in pharmacology, where diuretics and electrolyte replacements are everyday tools.
learningObjectives: Define fluid and electrolyte balance as the body's regulation of water and dissolved minerals inside and outside cells, following MedlinePlus and OpenStax.
Explain what electrolytes are and match sodium, potassium, calcium, and chloride to their main jobs.
Distinguish the three fluid compartments — intracellular, extracellular, and intravascular (blood plasma) — by location and share of body fluid.
Describe how the kidneys, hormones, and thirst keep fluid and electrolyte balance, and what happens when that regulation is overwhelmed.
Apply the concepts to classify a patient scenario as dehydration or fluid overload and explain why imbalance matters clinically.

collegeVersion.heading: The body's internal sea
collegeVersion.body: About 60 percent of an adult's body weight is water, according to the Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health — enough to think of the body's fluid as an internal sea that every cell floats in. That fluid is not pure water: it is water with substances dissolved in it, and the dissolved minerals called electrolytes are the most important of them. Fluid and electrolyte balance is the body's way of keeping the right amount of water and minerals in the right places. MedlinePlus puts the rule simply: the amount of water you take in should equal the amount you lose, and when something upsets that balance you end up with too little water (dehydration) or too much (overhydration). OpenStax's Fundamentals of Nursing makes the same point at the bedside: the body must maintain a strict balance between fluid levels and electrolyte concentrations for normal processes to occur.

collegeVersion.heading: What electrolytes are
collegeVersion.body: Electrolytes are minerals that carry an electric charge when dissolved in water or body fluids, including blood — the definition MedlinePlus uses. The charge is the point: muscles contract, nerves signal, and the heart keeps its rhythm because electrolytes carry that charge across cell membranes. Four get the most attention in nursing. Sodium, the most abundant electrolyte outside cells, helps control the amount of fluid in the body and supports nerve and muscle function. Potassium, the most abundant inside cells, helps cells, the heart, and muscles work properly. Calcium helps make and keep bones and teeth strong and is needed for muscle contractions, nerve impulses, and blood clotting. Chloride helps control the amount of fluid in the body and supports healthy blood volume and blood pressure. The nutrition subject owns the dietary depth on electrolytes — food sources and intake guidance — and this lesson only points there.

collegeVersion.heading: The three fluid compartments
collegeVersion.body: Body fluid lives in three neighborhoods. Intracellular fluid is the fluid inside the body's cells, and it holds about two-thirds of all body fluid. Extracellular fluid is everything outside the cells, about one-third of the total, and it includes the fluid that surrounds the cells (interstitial fluid). Intravascular fluid — blood plasma — is the liquid part of blood, the fluid that carries blood cells and dissolved substances through the vessels, and it belongs to the extracellular compartment. Fluid moves between compartments constantly; that movement is how water and electrolytes reach the cells that need them.

collegeVersion.heading: Who keeps the balance
collegeVersion.body: Three partners keep the balance. The kidneys are the main regulators: they filter the blood and decide how much water and how many electrolytes to keep or release, which is why OpenStax says total body fluid is regulated by the renal system. Hormones give the orders — when fluid is low, antidiuretic hormone (ADH) tells the kidneys to reabsorb water, and aldosterone helps regulate sodium and potassium. Thirst is the intake side of the system: it is the body's signal that water is running low, prompting drinking. MedlinePlus notes one wrinkle: some older adults lose their sense of thirst, so the signal is not equally reliable in everyone.

collegeVersion.heading: Too little and too much
collegeVersion.body: Two common failures of the system. Dehydration is losing more fluid than the body takes in, so the body does not have enough fluid to work properly — MedlinePlus's definition. Vomiting, diarrhea, fever with heavy sweating, and simply not drinking enough are the usual causes. Fluid volume overload, also called hypervolemia, is the opposite: the body retains an excessive amount of fluid, often because the heart, kidneys, or liver cannot move it out — heart failure, kidney failure, and cirrhosis are the classic settings. An electrolyte imbalance, meanwhile, means one or more electrolytes are too low or too high in the blood.

collegeVersion.heading: Why it matters clinically
collegeVersion.body: The stakes are high because the system is shared: one imbalance drags many systems down at once. Consider a concrete chain: a patient with heart failure takes a diuretic that pushes potassium out through the kidneys; two days of vomiting add more potassium loss; potassium drifts below normal; and the heart, which depends on potassium to contract and keep its rhythm, becomes irritable. The patient feels weak and notices a fluttering heartbeat — a small lab change with a large effect. OpenStax warns that even slight abnormalities in electrolyte values can have serious consequences, and when homeostasis fails the body is at risk of organ dysfunction. This is why nurses track intake and output, watch for dry mouth or swollen ankles, and order electrolyte panels: the balance is invisible, but its failures are not.

vocabulary.definition: The state the body maintains when the amount of water and dissolved minerals (electrolytes) in its fluid compartments stays within a normal range.
A mineral that carries an electric charge when dissolved in water or body fluids; examples include sodium, potassium, calcium, and chloride.
The body fluid found inside the body's cells; it holds about two-thirds of the body's fluid.
The body fluid found outside the cells, including the fluid that surrounds the cells and the liquid part of blood.
The liquid component of blood, the fluid that carries blood cells and dissolved substances through the vessels.
The condition of losing more fluid than the body takes in, so the body lacks enough fluid to work properly.
The condition in which the body retains an excessive amount of fluid, often linked to heart, kidney, or liver problems.
A hormone that signals the kidneys to reabsorb water when the body's fluid level is low.
A hormone that helps the kidneys regulate sodium and potassium, which in turn helps control fluid balance.
The process by which the body keeps its internal conditions, including fluid and electrolyte levels, within a stable range.

eli10.simplifiedExplanation: Your body is mostly water — about 60 percent of an adult's weight — and that water carries dissolved minerals called electrolytes: sodium, potassium, calcium, and chloride. These minerals carry an electric charge, and your muscles, nerves, and heart use that charge to do their jobs. The fluid lives in three neighborhoods: inside cells, outside cells, and in the blood. The kidneys do most of the bookkeeping, hormones such as ADH and aldosterone send the orders, and thirst tells you when to drink. When water and minerals drift out of balance, you get too little fluid (dehydration) or too much (fluid overload), and cells start working poorly.
eli10.analogy: Imagine the body as a city with a water system. The mains are the blood, the buildings are the cells, and the dissolved minerals are like the minerals in drinking water — invisible, but the pumps and pipes depend on them. The kidneys are the treatment plant, deciding what to keep and what to flush. The hormones are the dispatchers, and thirst is the gauge that warns the city when the reservoir runs low.
eli10.analogyLimits: The city-water analogy breaks down because the body's pipes are alive: fluid crosses cell membranes, and electrolytes are actively pumped in and out — a city does not pump minerals against the current. And the body cannot simply top up the reservoir: adding water without the right minerals, or minerals without water, can make the problem worse.

workedExample: Mr. Alvarez, 74, arrives at the clinic after two days of vomiting and diarrhea. The nurse, Priya, notes his mouth is dry, his urine is dark and scant, and he says he feels dizzy when he stands. She recognizes the pattern: fluid loss is exceeding intake, so he is dehydrated. She reviews his medicines — he takes a diuretic for high blood pressure — and flags him for a basic metabolic panel, a blood test that checks electrolytes such as sodium and potassium. While waiting, she offers small sips of oral rehydration fluid. Priya's mental model: the balance tipped, the kidneys could not keep up, and the plan is to replace what was lost without overshooting.

commonMistakes.mistake: Drinking more water fixes every fluid problem.
commonMistakes.correction: Too little water is only half the story. Fluid overload means the body has too much fluid, often because the heart or kidneys cannot move it out, and adding water can worsen swelling and strain. Balance also means matching water with electrolytes, not just volume.

commonMistakes.mistake: Electrolytes only matter for athletes.
commonMistakes.correction: Heavy sweating is one route of loss, but vomiting, diarrhea, fever, and medicines such as diuretics shift electrolytes in anyone. An older adult with the flu can lose potassium as surely as a marathon runner.

commonMistakes.mistake: If a person feels thirsty, hydration is fine.
commonMistakes.correction: Thirst is a real signal, but it is not an early one, and MedlinePlus notes that some older adults lose their sense of thirst — they can be dehydrated without feeling it.

commonMistakes.mistake: Fluid overload just means someone drank too much water.
commonMistakes.correction: Usually it means the body is retaining fluid it cannot move — heart failure, kidney failure, and cirrhosis are the common causes. Drinking too much water can contribute, but retention is the usual story.

compareContrast.distinction: Intracellular fluid is inside the body's cells and holds about two-thirds of body fluid; extracellular fluid is outside the cells and holds the remaining third, including the fluid around cells and the liquid part of blood.
Dehydration is losing more fluid than the body takes in, leaving too little to work properly; overload is retaining too much fluid, often because the heart or kidneys cannot move it out.

An electrolyte is a mineral that carries an electric charge when dissolved, and nerves, muscles, and the heart depend on that charge; plain water is the solvent, carrying the minerals but carrying no charge of its own.
The kidneys regulate the output side — how much water and how many electrolytes the body keeps or releases; thirst handles the input side, signaling when to drink. Both must work for balance to hold.

keyTakeaway: Fluid and electrolyte balance is the body's internal chemistry set: water plus charged minerals, kept in the right compartments by kidneys, hormones, and thirst. When the recipe drifts, dehydration or fluid overload follows — and nearly every system feels it.

questionBank.prompt: A nursing student is reviewing the definition of electrolytes for a class quiz. Which statement matches how MedlinePlus and OpenStax describe them?
options: Minerals that carry an electric charge when dissolved in water or body fluids.
Vitamins that the body stores in fat tissue for later use.
Proteins that carry oxygen through the bloodstream.
Sugars that provide quick energy to working muscles.
questionBank.explanation: Electrolytes are minerals — sodium, potassium, calcium, and chloride among them — that carry an electric charge when dissolved in body fluids (MedlinePlus; OpenStax). B describes fat-soluble vitamins, C describes oxygen-carrying proteins, and D describes carbohydrates.

questionBank.prompt: During a class discussion, a student asks where most of the body's fluid is located. Which answer is correct?
options: In the blood vessels, because blood is mostly liquid.
Inside the body's cells, in the intracellular compartment.
In the space around the brain and spinal cord.
Split evenly among cells, blood, and tissues.
questionBank.explanation: About two-thirds of body fluid sits inside the cells (intracellular), with roughly one-third outside (OpenStax). A is wrong because blood plasma is only part of the extracellular third, C is wrong because that fluid makes up less than one percent, and D misstates the split.
questionBank.skill: Locating the major fluid compartments

questionBank.prompt: A patient has had diarrhea for two days, is drinking very little, and now has a dry mouth, dark urine, and dizziness when standing. Which condition does this best describe?
options: Fluid volume overload, because the intestines are full of fluid.
A hormone problem, because ADH is being released too often.
An electrolyte surplus, because diarrhea adds sodium to the blood.
Dehydration, because fluid loss is exceeding fluid intake.
questionBank.explanation: MedlinePlus defines dehydration as losing more fluid than the body takes in, leaving too little fluid to work properly — diarrhea, poor intake, dry mouth, dark urine, and dizziness fit that picture. A describes the opposite problem, B misattributes the cause, and C is false because diarrhea depletes electrolytes rather than adding them.
questionBank.skill: Classifying a clinical picture as dehydration

questionBank.prompt: A patient with heart failure has gained several pounds, and the nurse notes swollen ankles and shortness of breath when lying flat. The patient says, “I barely drank anything today.” Which explanation is most accurate?
options: The patient must be dehydrated because intake was low.
The patient's thirst mechanism has failed completely.
The body is retaining fluid it cannot move, so fluid volume overload has developed despite low intake.
The kidneys are releasing too much water into the urine.
questionBank.explanation: Fluid volume overload is excessive retention of fluid, and heart failure is a classic risk because the heart and kidneys cannot move fluid out of the tissues (OpenStax). A misreads low intake as dehydration, B is unsupported, and D describes the opposite of retention.
questionBank.skill: Reasoning about why fluid overload develops despite low intake

questionBank.prompt: Which pair correctly matches an electrolyte with its main job in the body?

Potassium — builds the skeleton and keeps teeth strong.
Calcium — makes up the liquid part of blood.
Chloride — carries oxygen from the lungs to the tissues.

B and C swap jobs (calcium builds bones and teeth; potassium supports cells, heart, and muscles), and D describes oxygen transport, which is not an electrolyte job.
