title: Ethics in Psychological Research
in30Seconds: Research ethics are the rules that protect the people who take part in psychological studies and keep the science honest. The American Psychological Association's working standard is simple: participants must be treated fairly and without harm, and findings must be reported honestly. In practice that means informed consent before a study begins, strict limits on deception, a full debriefing when the study ends, confidentiality for every participant's data, and review-board approval before research with people can start.
whyItMatters: Psychology's findings are only as trustworthy as the way they were gathered. A study built on pressure, secrecy, or mistreatment produces knowledge no one should act on — which is why every serious psychology program teaches the rules before the methods. The same rules will follow you further than the classroom. If you ever read research to make a decision, you benefit from knowing participants were protected. If you ever design a study — even a small class project — you will be the one responsible for consent, disclosure, and confidentiality. And if you take part in research yourself, as many students do, the rules describe your rights: what you should be told, what you can refuse, and what must happen before you leave.
learningObjectives: Define research ethics and state the APA's working standard: participants must be treated fairly and without harm, and findings must be reported honestly.
Explain informed consent as a participant's voluntary agreement based on understanding, including the right to decline or withdraw at any time.
Describe when deception is allowed in research and why participants who were deceived must receive a full debriefing afterward.
Identify what an institutional review board (IRB) does and why its approval is required before research with human participants proceeds.
Analyze the historical cases — the Tuskegee syphilis study and Milgram's obedience research — that shaped today's ethics rules, and apply the rules to an original research scenario.

collegeVersion.heading: What research ethics are
collegeVersion.body: Research ethics are the values, principles, and standards that guide how studies are designed, carried out, and reported. The APA Dictionary of Psychology defines them exactly that way, and its entry on ethics makes the standard concrete for research: participants must be treated fairly and without harm, and investigators must report results and findings honestly. Honest reporting matters as much as fair treatment: invented or hidden findings corrupt the knowledge everyone else builds on. The APA's Ethical Principles of Psychologists and Code of Conduct turns the same commitments into a working professional code, and the APA Dictionary notes that research ethics require studies with human participants to be evaluated by an institutional review board. The working definition for this lesson is the APA's: treat participants fairly and without harm, and report honestly.

collegeVersion.heading: Informed consent
collegeVersion.body: Informed consent is a participant's voluntary agreement to take part, given with real understanding of what the study involves. The APA Dictionary defines it as voluntary agreement based on understanding of a procedure's nature, its potential benefits and possible risks, and the available alternatives, and it notes that participants are free to decline or to withdraw at any time. The U.S. Office for Human Research Protections describes the same idea in three moves: researchers must disclose the information needed for an informed decision, make sure participants understand it, and protect voluntariness so that no one is coerced or unduly influenced. In practice, consent is documented with a signed form before the study starts, describing what participation involves, noting risks, and stating that involvement is voluntary and can be discontinued without penalty. An original example: a researcher recruiting for a study on study habits must tell participants how long the session runs and what they will be asked to do, and they can leave at any moment with no consequence. A signature from someone rushed, pressured, or misled is not informed consent — it is paperwork.

collegeVersion.heading: Deception and debriefing
collegeVersion.body: Deception is any distortion or withholding of fact with the purpose of misleading others. The APA Dictionary's example is the classic case: not disclosing the true purpose of an experiment to a participant. Sometimes deception is necessary, because participants who know the exact question may change their behavior and ruin the results — OpenStax's example is a researcher concealing an interest in how clothing affects opinions. But deception is tightly bounded: never harmful, and when a study uses it, participants must receive a full debriefing — complete, honest information about the purpose, how the data will be used, and why the deception was necessary. The APA Dictionary defines debriefing as giving participants in a completed research project a fuller explanation of the study than was possible before or during the research. The best-known historical example is Stanley Milgram's obedience research at Yale in 1963: 40 men were led to believe they were taking part in a study to improve learning and memory and told to deliver electric shocks — in 15-volt steps up to 450 volts — to a learner whenever the learner erred. The learners were confederates who never received shocks, and 65% of participants continued to the maximum voltage. Participants were deceived about the true purpose — the real question was obedience to authority — which is why the study is taught in ethics discussions as the standard example of deception and why disclosure afterward is a rule, not a courtesy.

collegeVersion.heading: Confidentiality
collegeVersion.body: Confidentiality protects the information participants reveal in confidence. The APA Dictionary describes it as a professional-ethics principle shielding research participants and survey respondents against unauthorized access to what they share, and OpenStax notes that the consent form guarantees collected data remain completely confidential. In practice, answers, scores, and identifying details are stored and reported so no unauthorized person can link them to the person who gave them. An original example: in a study of stress among first-year students, the researcher may know who said what, but the published paper reports only group patterns and the raw data stay in locked files. Confidentiality is what makes honest answers possible; people will not tell the truth about sensitive topics if their identities can leak.

collegeVersion.heading: The review board — and the honest framing
collegeVersion.body: Before research with human participants can proceed, it must pass through an institutional review board (IRB). The APA Dictionary calls the IRB a committee that reviews research proposals for ethical acceptability; it helps protect participants and is mandatory at any U.S. institution receiving federal funds for research. OpenStax adds that its approval is generally required before an experiment can proceed. The honest framing: these rules exist because people were hurt before the rules did. In the Tuskegee syphilis study, the U.S. Public Health Service recruited rural Black men in Tuskegee, Alabama, in 1932, promising free medical care, meals, and burial insurance; 600 men took part. Those who tested positive for syphilis were never told they had it, penicillin was withheld even after it became a recognized treatment in 1947, and the study ran for 40 years — ending in 1972 only after the national press exposed it. The outrage led to the National Research Act of 1974 and to today's strict guidelines, and the Belmont Report of 1979 distilled three principles — respect for persons, beneficence, and justice — that still anchor U.S. oversight of human-subjects research. Milgram's study is part of the same history: a landmark finding about obedience, and a reminder of what deception looks like and why the rules require full disclosure afterward.

vocabulary.definition: The values, principles, and standards that guide researchers in designing studies, carrying them out, and reporting findings (APA Dictionary of Psychology).
A participant's voluntary agreement to take part in a study, based on understanding its nature, risks, and benefits; participants may decline or withdraw at any time.
Misleading participants or withholding information about a study, typically its true purpose; allowed only when necessary for valid results and never harmful.
The fuller explanation of a study given to participants after it is complete, covering the true purpose and how the data will be used.
Protecting the information participants share in confidence from unauthorized access or disclosure.
A committee that reviews research proposals involving human participants for ethical acceptability before the research can proceed.
Done by free choice; participation in research is always voluntary, and participants can withdraw without penalty.
To leave a study at any time without penalty; the right to withdraw is part of informed consent.

eli10.simplifiedExplanation: Research ethics are the rules that keep studies with people honest and safe. Before a study starts, participants must be told what they are agreeing to, and they can say no or walk away at any time — that is informed consent. Some studies need to hide part of their purpose, because knowing it would change how people behave; that is deception, and it is only allowed when it does not hurt anyone. When the study ends, the researcher must explain the true purpose — that is debriefing. Personal data stay protected — that is confidentiality. And none of it starts until a review board says yes. In one line: tell people what they are in for, do not hurt them, come clean afterward, and protect their information.
eli10.analogy: Think of a research participant as a house guest. A good host says what is for dinner before anyone sits down (informed consent), does not film the guest through a hidden camera (no secret data collection), and thanks them at the door with the full story of the evening (debriefing). The guest came freely and can leave whenever they like.
eli10.analogyLimits: The analogy breaks down because a guest can spot a bad host and walk out, while a participant often cannot tell how much is being kept from them — deception is hidden by design. So research leans on formal safeguards: a review board that approves the study in advance, written rules, and mandatory disclosure afterward. Good manners protect guests; rules protect participants.

workedExample: Designing a study with deception, the right way. Maya wants to study whether people judge a speaker's honesty differently when the speaker breaks eye contact. If she announces the real question, participants will watch the speaker's eyes on purpose, and her results will be meaningless. So she proposes deception: participants will be told the study is about how well people remember spoken information. Before anything happens, her university's IRB must approve the plan. At recruitment, participants get an honest consent form covering the session, the risks (none beyond ordinary conversation), and the right to withdraw at any time. During the study, the deception touches only the stated purpose — nothing harmful. Afterward, every participant is debriefed: told the true purpose, why it was hidden, and how the data will be used. Their responses stay confidential.

commonMistakes.mistake: Informed consent is just getting a signature.
commonMistakes.correction: The signature documents consent; the consent itself is the participant's voluntary agreement based on understanding. A form signed by someone who was rushed, pressured, or misled gives the researcher paperwork, not informed consent — the APA Dictionary defines consent by understanding and voluntariness, not by ink.

commonMistakes.mistake: Deception is never allowed in research.
commonMistakes.correction: Deception is allowed when it is necessary to protect the integrity of the results and it causes no harm — but participants must receive a full debriefing afterward (OpenStax Psychology 2e). The rule bans harmful or unnecessary deception, not all concealment of purpose.

commonMistakes.mistake: Consent and debriefing are the same conversation, just at different times.
commonMistakes.correction: They are different acts with different content. Consent happens before the study: agreeing to take part with understanding of what it involves. Debriefing happens after: a fuller explanation of the study — especially the true purpose and why deception was used — owed to every participant once the research is complete (APA Dictionary).

commonMistakes.mistake: A study with no physical risk needs no review board.
commonMistakes.correction: The IRB weighs ethics, not just physical danger. At any U.S. institution receiving federal research funds, an IRB is mandatory, and it reviews proposals involving human participants — including surveys and studies whose only risks are psychological or social — before the research proceeds (APA Dictionary; OpenStax).

compareContrast.distinction: Consent comes before the study: the participant agrees to take part with understanding of what it involves. Debriefing comes after: the fuller explanation of the study — especially the true purpose — that participants are owed once the research is complete.

Deception withholds or distorts specific information, typically the study's purpose, to keep results valid — and it is bounded: never harmful, always disclosed in the debriefing. A lie about risks or about what participants will experience crosses the line because it destroys the understanding that informed consent depends on.

Research ethics are field-specific rules that govern how studies are designed, run, and reported (APA Dictionary). Moral philosophy asks broader questions about what is right and wrong in general — a separate discipline that this lesson does not attempt to cover.

keyTakeaway: Research ethics protect the people who make psychology possible: every participant is a volunteer who must be treated fairly and without harm, informed before the study, and fully explained to afterward — because people were hurt before these rules existed.

questionBank.prompt: During recruitment for a study on sleep habits, a researcher tells potential participants that they may leave the study at any time, even after signing the form. Which principle is the researcher honoring?
options: Debriefing
The right to withdraw, which is part of informed consent
Confidentiality
Deception
questionBank.explanation: The APA Dictionary defines informed consent as voluntary agreement in which participants are free to decline or withdraw from the research at any time, so the promise reflects informed consent. Debriefing is the explanation given after the study, confidentiality protects data, and deception means misleading participants.
questionBank.skill: Recalling that informed consent includes the right to withdraw at any time

questionBank.prompt: A study used deception because telling participants the true purpose would have changed their behavior. What must the researcher do when the study ends?
options: Nothing, because the participants signed consent forms
Erase all records so participants cannot be identified
Provide a full debriefing: the true purpose, why the deception was necessary, and how the data will be used
Ask participants to sign a second consent form for the deception
questionBank.explanation: OpenStax Psychology 2e states that when deception is involved, participants must receive a full debriefing upon conclusion — complete, honest information about the purpose, why the deception was necessary, and how the data will be used. The other options skip the required disclosure.
questionBank.skill: Recalling that deception requires a full debriefing after the study

questionBank.prompt: Priya wants to study how people react to being left out of a group. She plans to tell participants they are playing a strategy game and to reveal the real purpose only at the end. Which condition must her study meet for that deception to be acceptable?
options: Participants must never learn the true purpose, so the results stay clean
The deception must continue after the study ends, to protect other participants
The deception must replace informed consent entirely
The deception must not be harmful, and participants must receive a full debriefing afterward
questionBank.explanation: Deception is permitted only when it is necessary to keep results valid, must not be harmful, and must be followed by a full debriefing in which the true purpose is disclosed (OpenStax Psychology 2e; APA Dictionary). The other options describe permanent concealment, which the rules do not allow.
questionBank.skill: Applying the rules that bound deception in research to a new scenario

questionBank.prompt: A critic claims researchers can police their own ethics and that formal oversight is unnecessary. Which historical case most directly refutes that claim?
options: The Tuskegee syphilis study, in which the U.S. Public Health Service withheld treatment from men who were never told they had the disease, until the press exposed it in 1972
The Asch conformity studies, in which participants judged the lengths of lines
Milgram's obedience study, in which participants believed they were delivering shocks to a learner
Ebbinghaus's memory experiments, in which he tested himself on nonsense syllables
questionBank.explanation: Tuskegee is the case where researchers inside a respected institution caused decades of harm with no effective internal check — the study ended only when the national press exposed it in 1972, and the outrage led to the National Research Act of 1974 (OpenStax Psychology 2e). The other studies are famous for different findings and do not show that same failure of self-policing.
questionBank.skill: Analyzing historical cases as evidence for why research oversight exists

questionBank.prompt: A university that receives federal research funding wants to run a short, no-risk survey about students' study habits. No deception is involved. Which of the following still applies under the rules in this lesson?
options: Nothing — a study with no risk needs no oversight
The proposal still needs IRB review, and participants still give informed consent, with their data kept confidential
The researcher may skip consent but must debrief participants afterward
The IRB must approve the survey, but once it starts, participants may not withdraw
questionBank.explanation: An institutional review board is mandatory at any U.S. institution receiving federal funds for research, informed consent applies to participation in research generally, and consent documents guarantee confidentiality (APA Dictionary; OpenStax). None of the other options matches those requirements.
questionBank.skill: Applying IRB, consent, and confidentiality rules to a low-risk study

title: Historical Thinking
in30Seconds: Historical thinking is what it means to reason like a historian instead of memorizing dates. You treat every account as something a person made for a reason, so you ask who wrote it, when, and why (sourcing), read it in its own time and place (contextualization), and check it against other sources (corroboration). The big idea: history is an evidence-based interpretation you can argue for, not a fixed list of facts to recite.
whyItMatters: Almost every college course asks you to build a claim from imperfect evidence, and history is where that habit is taught directly. Learning to source, contextualize, and corroborate turns you from a passive receiver of facts into someone who can weigh conflicting accounts and defend a conclusion. These are also everyday survival skills: the same moves that test a Civil War letter test a viral post, a political ad, or a news story of uncertain origin. Employers and citizenship alike reward people who can ask where a claim comes from, judge whether it is trustworthy, and change their minds when better evidence appears.
learningObjectives: Define historical thinking and distinguish it from memorizing dates and facts
Explain the historical-reading skills of sourcing, contextualization, corroboration, and close reading, and attribute them to the Stanford History Education Group
Distinguish established historical facts from interpretation, and explain why disciplined accounts can still differ
Apply sourcing, contextualization, and corroboration to a specific document or scenario
Analyze why comparing multiple sources produces a more trustworthy account than relying on one

collegeVersion.heading: From memorizing the past to investigating it
collegeVersion.body: Most people leave school history thinking the subject is a settled list of names, dates, and battles to be recalled on a test. Working historians experience it very differently. To them the past is not directly visible; it survives only in traces — letters, laws, photographs, ledgers, oral testimony, ruins — each made by a particular person or institution for a particular purpose. Historical thinking is the disciplined set of habits for turning those traces into a defensible account of what happened and what it meant. The cognitive scientist Sam Wineburg, who founded the Stanford History Education Group in 2002, put the gap bluntly: historians critically analyze documents and probe the motives of the people who made them, while students of history are too often 'relegated to searching for facts.' Closing that gap is the whole point of this lesson. Historical thinking does not throw out dates — you still need to know that the U.S. Constitution was drafted in 1787 — but it treats a date as the beginning of a question, not the end of one.

collegeVersion.heading: The core moves: sourcing, contextualization, corroboration
collegeVersion.body: The Stanford History Education Group's 'Reading Like a Historian' curriculum organizes historical reading around a small set of skills, and three of them do most of the work. Sourcing means looking at a document's origin before its content: who created this, when, for whom, and why? A general's after-action report, a soldier's private diary, and a newspaper's front page can describe the same battle very differently, and knowing the author's position and purpose tells you how to weigh each. Contextualization means reading a source inside its own time and place rather than through present-day assumptions — recognizing that a word, a law, or a silence meant something specific in, say, 1850 that it does not mean now. Corroboration means never resting a conclusion on a single account: you compare sources, note where they agree, and pay special attention to where they diverge, because the disagreements often reveal bias, error, or a perspective you had missed. A fourth skill, close reading, runs underneath all three — attending carefully to a source's exact claims, word choices, and the evidence it offers for them.

collegeVersion.heading: History as interpretation, not a fixed list of facts
collegeVersion.body: The deepest idea in historical thinking is that history is interpretation built from evidence. That does not mean 'anything goes.' Historians separate established facts — the Battle of Hastings occurred in 1066; six million Jews were murdered in the Holocaust — from interpretation, which asks why events happened, how they connected, and what they meant. On questions of interpretation, well-trained historians using the same documents can reach different, defensible conclusions, because they weigh causes differently or ask different questions. This is why a history essay makes an argument and marshals evidence rather than simply listing what happened. It also explains why historical accounts change over time: new sources surface, and later generations ask questions earlier ones ignored — recovering, for example, the experiences of enslaved, colonized, and indigenous people who were written out of older 'master narratives.' A claim is stronger not because an authority asserts it but because the evidence supports it and it survives comparison with rival accounts.

collegeVersion.heading: Turning the moves into a routine
collegeVersion.body: Historical thinking becomes practical when you make it a repeatable routine. The Library of Congress teaches a simple three-step version for any primary source: Observe (collect what you actually notice), Reflect (connect it to what you already know), and Question (decide what you still need to find out). The National Archives teaches a parallel progression — meet the document, observe its parts, make sense of it, then use it as historical evidence — and stresses that the steps stay the same for a photograph, a map, a cartoon, or a treaty. The value of a fixed routine is that it slows you down at exactly the moment you are tempted to accept a striking source at face value. In practice, working a source means asking of it: Who made this and why? What was going on when it was made? What does it actually claim, and in what words? And what do other sources say about the same thing? Answer those, and you are no longer memorizing history — you are doing it.

vocabulary.definition: The disciplined practice of reasoning about the past the way historians do — asking questions and building evidence-based interpretations from surviving sources — rather than memorizing facts.
Considering a document's origin — who made it, when, for whom, and why — and judging its trustworthiness before relying on what it says.
Understanding a source within the time, place, and circumstances in which it was created, rather than through present-day assumptions.
Comparing a source against other sources to establish what is probable and to notice where accounts of the same event agree or diverge.
Careful attention to a source's exact claims, word choices, and the evidence and reasoning it offers to support them.
A record created by a participant or witness at the time under study, such as a letter, photograph, or official document.
An evidence-based explanation of why past events happened and what they meant, which can reasonably differ among historians.
The distinction between what can be established as having happened (and when) and the arguable question of why it happened and what it signified.
Judging or reading the past solely by present-day standards and assumptions, which distorts what a source meant in its own time.

eli10.simplifiedExplanation: Imagine three friends each tell you why they were late to a party. You do not just believe the first one — you notice who is talking and why they might shade the story, you remember what was going on that day, and you compare all three to figure out what probably really happened. Historians do exactly that with letters, photos, and records left from long ago. They ask who made something and why, picture the time it came from, and check it against other clues. History is less like a list of facts to memorize and more like being a detective who has to explain the past and show the evidence.
eli10.analogy: Doing history is like being a detective at a crime scene where every clue was left behind by someone who had their own reasons. You cannot just take one witness's word; you ask who each witness is, what they could see, and whether their stories line up.
eli10.analogyLimits: The analogy breaks down because a detective usually expects one true solution to convict a suspect, while historians accept that thoughtful people can reach different, defensible interpretations of the same evidence — and there is no confession or courtroom verdict to settle it for good.

workedExample: Suppose you are handed a printed 1850s advertisement offering a reward for the return of a person who escaped slavery. A memorizer notes the date and moves on. A historical thinker sources it first: who paid for this notice, and why? The enslaver, to reclaim someone as property and to warn others — so the ad is evidence of the slaveholder's aims, not a neutral report. Contextualization places it under the Fugitive Slave Act of 1850, which legally compelled such recaptures, explaining why the notice could be printed openly. Close reading of its wording and the details it lists reveals what the enslaver knew and valued. Finally, corroboration sets it beside a very different source — a formerly enslaved person's narrative — to reconstruct the same system from the other side. One document, four moves, and a far richer, better-supported account than any date alone could give.

commonMistakes.mistake: Believing historical thinking means abandoning dates and facts.
commonMistakes.correction: You still need accurate facts and chronology; historical thinking uses them as the starting point for questions and interpretation, not as the finish line.

commonMistakes.mistake: Treating a source as a neutral window onto the past.
commonMistakes.correction: Every source was made by someone for a purpose. Sourcing — asking who made it and why — comes before trusting what it says.

commonMistakes.mistake: Concluding that because history is interpretation, all opinions about the past are equally valid.
commonMistakes.correction: Interpretations still have to fit the evidence and survive comparison with other sources; a claim contradicted by the record is simply weaker or wrong.

commonMistakes.mistake: Judging a source only by today's assumptions (presentism).
commonMistakes.correction: Contextualization asks what a word, law, or action meant in its own time before you evaluate it, which is different from excusing injustice.

commonMistakes.mistake: Trusting a single dramatic source because it feels convincing.
commonMistakes.correction: Corroboration requires checking it against other accounts; the places where sources disagree are often the most revealing.

compareContrast.distinction: Memorizing treats the past as a fixed list of facts to recall; historical thinking treats it as an interpretation you build and defend from evidence.
A fact is what can be established as having happened and when; an interpretation is the arguable claim about why it happened and what it meant.
Sourcing evaluates one document by its origin and purpose; corroboration compares several documents against one another to test what is probable.

keyTakeaway: Historical thinking means investigating the past like a historian — sourcing, contextualizing, and corroborating evidence to build an interpretation you can argue for — rather than memorizing a fixed list of dates and facts.

title: What Historians Do
in30Seconds: The past is everything that ever happened; history is the account historians build from the traces that survived. That work is a craft: ask a focused question, find and weigh sources, interpret the evidence, and argue a case. Because sources are partial and the people asking change, interpretations get revised, and two careful historians can read the same event differently. History is less a fixed list of facts than a disciplined, evidence-based conversation about the human past.
whyItMatters: Knowing how history is made changes how you read everything that claims to describe the past, from a textbook to a documentary to a viral post. It lets you tell an established fact from an argument about meaning, and to ask the questions a historian would: Where does this come from? Who made it, and why? What is left out? Academically, this is the foundation the rest of a history course builds on, and it transfers to any field that reasons from evidence. Practically, it builds the habit of checking a claim against its sources rather than trusting whoever tells the story most confidently. And it prepares you for the fact that good history is revised, not because it was wrong, but because new evidence and new questions keep arriving.
learningObjectives: Distinguish the past (everything that happened) from history (the evidence-based account historians construct)
Describe the historian's research process: asking a question, finding and evaluating sources, interpreting evidence, and building an argument
Define historiography and explain why historical interpretations change over time
Distinguish primary from secondary sources and explain why each must be read critically
Analyze a scenario to identify why two historians might reach different, defensible interpretations of the same event

collegeVersion.heading: History is not the same as the past
collegeVersion.body: It is tempting to treat history as a fixed record of what happened, a list of dates and names waiting to be memorized. That confuses two different things. The past is everything that ever occurred, most of which left no trace and is gone for good. History is the account that historians reconstruct from the fraction of the past that survived: documents, objects, buildings, images, memories, and data. Because that surviving evidence is always partial, history is not a transcript of the past but a disciplined interpretation of it. This is why the discipline is defined by a method rather than by a body of settled facts. Facts matter enormously, and many are firmly established, but the work of history is turning scattered evidence into a supported account of what happened and, harder still, why. Keeping the two apart is the single most useful habit in the subject: 'the past' is the territory, and 'history' is the map that people draw of it, always at some scale, always leaving things out, always drawn by someone with a point of view.

collegeVersion.heading: The craft: question, sources, evidence, argument
collegeVersion.body: Historians do not simply 'know' the past; they investigate it, and the investigation follows a recognizable shape. It begins with a question, something focused enough to answer with evidence, such as how a community experienced a war rather than the unanswerable 'what was the war like.' The question guides the search for sources, the surviving materials that might bear on it. Historians then evaluate those sources, asking who made each one, for whom, and why, because a source is a piece of evidence about its maker as much as about its subject. Next comes interpretation: weighing what the evidence can and cannot show, noticing gaps and silences, and testing one source against others. Finally the historian constructs an argument or a narrative, a claim about what happened and what it meant, supported by the evidence and open to challenge by anyone who reads the same sources. This is why history is a form of reasoning, not memorization. Two students given the same documents should be able to argue for different readings, and the better argument is the one that accounts for more of the evidence and hides less of it.

collegeVersion.heading: Reading sources: primary, secondary, and critical
collegeVersion.body: The raw materials of the craft are sources, and historians sort them into two broad kinds. A primary source was created during the period under study, an eyewitness or a direct product of the moment: a letter, a treaty, a photograph, a tax roll, a pot, a song. A secondary source comes later and retells, analyzes, or interprets that period, such as a modern biography or a scholarly article. The line can blur, since a source can be primary for one question and secondary for another, but the distinction shapes how a source is used. Neither kind is simply believed. Reading a source critically means attending to its author, its intended audience, its purpose, and the context that produced it, then asking what the source is in a position to know and what it might distort or omit. A wartime poster and a soldier's diary both come from the same conflict, yet they were made for different reasons and reveal different things. Corroboration, checking a claim against independent sources, is how historians move from what a single document asserts to what they can reasonably conclude.

collegeVersion.heading: Historiography: why history gets rewritten
collegeVersion.body: If history were just the past copied down, it would never change. It changes constantly, and the study of how history has been written and rewritten is called historiography. There are several reasons interpretations shift. New evidence surfaces, as archives open or long-ignored materials are read for the first time. New questions get asked, often about people earlier historians overlooked, such as the enslaved, the colonized, workers, women, and indigenous communities. And the historians themselves change, bringing the concerns of their own moment to old events. The result is that the same well-documented event can carry very different meanings from different vantage points. Few historians doubt that Columbus reached the Caribbean in 1492, but whether that encounter is best understood as a discovery or an invasion, and how it was experienced by the people already living there, has been thoroughly rethought. Competing scholarly accounts are therefore normal and healthy, not a sign that history is unreliable. Revision is what a living discipline does; a field that never reconsidered its conclusions would have stopped investigating.

collegeVersion.heading: History among its neighbors
collegeVersion.body: History shares the study of the human past with several evidence-based fields and increasingly works alongside them. Archaeology reconstructs the past chiefly from material remains, objects, structures, and physical traces, which makes it indispensable for times and places that left few or no written records. Related fields such as anthropology, geography, economics, and the digital analysis of large datasets feed the same effort from other angles. The American Historical Association's shared vocabulary for this kind of thinking, sometimes summarized as the 'five C's', names the concepts historians lean on across all these collaborations: change over time, context, causality, contingency, and complexity. What tends to distinguish history within this family is its central reliance on interpreting sources of every kind, especially the textual record, to build explanatory arguments about human choices and their consequences. The boundaries are practical rather than rigid, and the strongest work often crosses them, but the historian's particular contribution is turning surviving evidence into a reasoned, contestable account of why things happened as they did.

vocabulary.definition: The disciplined, evidence-based study and interpretation of the human past, expressed as accounts that historians construct from surviving sources.
Everything that actually happened, most of which left no surviving trace; it is the subject that history tries to reconstruct, not history itself.
Any surviving material a historian uses as evidence about the past, such as a document, object, image, building, or dataset.
A source created during the period under study, standing close in time to the events, such as a letter, treaty, photograph, or artifact.
A later account that retells, analyzes, or interprets a period, usually at a distance of time or place, such as a modern biography or scholarly article.
The reasoned conclusion a historian draws from evidence about what happened and what it meant, always open to challenge by others reading the same sources.
The study of how history has been written and rewritten over time, including how and why interpretations of the same events change.
Checking a claim in one source against independent sources to judge how well the evidence supports a conclusion.
The evidence-based study of the human past chiefly through material remains such as objects and structures, closely related to history and vital where written records are scarce.

eli10.simplifiedExplanation: The past is everything that ever happened, and almost all of it is gone. History is what people called historians manage to figure out from the bits that stuck around, like old letters, tools, pictures, and buildings. They don't just memorize it. They act like detectives: they ask a clear question, hunt for clues, check who left each clue and why, and then explain what they think happened and why. Because clues are always missing, two honest historians can look at the same clues and tell slightly different stories. And when someone finds a new clue or asks a new question, the story gets updated. That updating is normal, not a mistake.
eli10.analogy: Think of a detective piecing together what happened in a room after everyone has left. They can't watch it happen; they only have what got left behind, a coffee cup, a note, a muddy footprint. So they line up the clues, ask who left each one and why, and build the most careful explanation that fits all of them. If a new clue turns up under the couch, a good detective changes the story to match. Historians do the same thing with letters, records, and objects instead of coffee cups.
eli10.analogyLimits: The detective usually hunts for one right answer, a single 'who did it,' and once the case is closed it stays closed. History is rarely that tidy. Many historical questions are about meaning and causes, not a single culprit, so more than one careful answer can be reasonable at the same time. And a historical 'case' is never permanently closed: new evidence and new questions keep reopening it, which is why history is rewritten rather than solved once and filed away.

workedExample: Imagine two historians studying the same event: a factory town's strike in 1912. They read the same box of sources, a mill owner's ledgers, the local newspaper, a set of workers' letters, and city police reports. The first historian asks why the strike failed and leans on the ledgers and police reports, arguing that the company simply outlasted the workers financially. The second asks how the strikers themselves understood their fight and leans on the letters, arguing that the strike built a lasting sense of solidarity even though it 'failed' on paper. Neither is making things up; each question steers attention toward different evidence, and each reads the shared sources critically, noting that the newspaper depended on mill advertising and that the police reports recorded arrests, not motives. Both accounts are defensible, and both could be revised if a strikers' union archive surfaced later. That is history as a craft: the same past, honestly interpreted, yielding more than one supported story.

commonMistakes.mistake: Treating history and the past as the same thing.
commonMistakes.correction: The past is everything that happened; history is the account historians reconstruct from surviving evidence. History is always partial and interpreted, because most of the past left no trace.

commonMistakes.mistake: Assuming history is just memorizing settled facts.
commonMistakes.correction: Facts matter, but the discipline is a method: asking questions, evaluating sources, interpreting evidence, and arguing a case. The reasoning is the point, not the recall.

commonMistakes.mistake: Believing that when historians disagree, one of them must be lying or wrong.
commonMistakes.correction: Because evidence is partial and questions differ, more than one careful interpretation can be defensible. Disagreement over meaning is normal scholarship, distinct from disputing an established fact.

commonMistakes.mistake: Thinking that rewriting history means earlier historians got everything wrong.
commonMistakes.correction: Interpretations are revised because new evidence surfaces, new questions get asked, and new perspectives emerge. Revision is what a healthy discipline does, not proof the earlier work was worthless.

commonMistakes.mistake: Taking a source at face value because it is old or firsthand.
commonMistakes.correction: Every source is read critically for its author, audience, intent, and context. A firsthand account still has a purpose and blind spots, and its claims are corroborated against other sources.

compareContrast.distinction: The past is everything that happened, most of it lost; history is the evidence-based account historians build from what survived, always partial and interpreted.
A primary source was created during the period studied; a secondary source is a later work that retells, analyzes, or interprets that period.
A fact is what can be firmly documented (what happened, when); an interpretation is a supported argument about why it happened and what it meant, which can be revised.
Both study the human past from evidence; history relies heavily on interpreting sources including the textual record, while archaeology works chiefly from material remains.

keyTakeaway: History is not the past itself but a disciplined, evidence-based interpretation of it: historians ask questions, evaluate sources, and argue supported accounts, and those accounts are legitimately revised as new evidence, questions, and perspectives appear.

questionBank.prompt: Which statement best captures the difference between 'the past' and 'history' as a discipline?
options: There is no difference; the two words mean exactly the same thing
The past is the evidence-based account historians write, while history is everything that happened
The past is everything that happened, while history is the account historians reconstruct from surviving evidence
The past is only what is written down, while history is only what is spoken aloud
questionBank.explanation: The past is everything that occurred, most of it lost; history is the interpreted account historians build from the evidence that survived. Option B reverses the two terms. Option A denies a distinction the discipline depends on. Option D invents a written-versus-spoken split that is not what the terms mean.
questionBank.skill: Distinguishing the past from history

questionBank.prompt: A historian is beginning a new project. Which sequence best reflects the historian's research process?
options: Memorize accepted dates, then repeat them accurately in a narrative
Decide the conclusion first, then discard any sources that disagree with it
Collect every object from a period, then display them without commentary
Ask a focused question, find and evaluate sources, interpret the evidence, and build a supported argument
questionBank.explanation: The craft moves from a focused question to finding and weighing sources, interpreting them, and constructing an argument open to challenge. Option A reduces history to memorization. Option B describes cherry-picking, the opposite of evaluating evidence. Option C collects without the interpretation that makes it history.
questionBank.skill: Describing the historian's research process

questionBank.prompt: You are handed a soldier's 1915 diary and a 2010 scholarly book about the same war. How should each be classified?
options: Both are secondary sources because both discuss the war
The diary is a primary source and the book is a secondary source
The diary is a secondary source and the book is a primary source
Neither is a source until it has been published by a museum
questionBank.explanation: A primary source is created during the period studied, like the 1915 diary; a secondary source, like the 2010 book, retells or interprets the period from a distance. Option A ignores that the diary is from the moment. Option C reverses the categories. Option D invents a publication requirement that does not define a source.
questionBank.skill: Classifying primary and secondary sources

questionBank.prompt: In historiography, what is the main reason the same well-documented event can be interpreted differently over time?
options: New evidence, new questions, and new perspectives lead historians to reevaluate earlier interpretations
Historians are required to disagree with anyone who came before them
The facts of what happened physically change as years pass
Older interpretations are always discarded because they were dishonest
questionBank.explanation: Historiography describes how interpretations shift as archives open, new questions arise (often about overlooked people), and later historians bring present concerns. Option B invents a rule of mandatory disagreement. Option C is impossible; established facts do not change, their interpretation does. Option D wrongly assumes earlier work was dishonest rather than working from less evidence.
questionBank.skill: Explaining why interpretations change (historiography)

questionBank.prompt: Two historians read the same box of sources about a 1912 strike and reach different but well-supported conclusions. What does this best illustrate about the discipline?
options: At least one of the historians must be fabricating evidence
History cannot produce reliable knowledge because answers vary
The sources should be ignored since they led to disagreement
Different questions and partial evidence can yield more than one defensible interpretation of the same past
questionBank.explanation: Because evidence is partial and each historian asks a different question, both can build defensible, evidence-based arguments, which is normal scholarship. Option A assumes disagreement means fabrication. Option B confuses interpretive range with unreliability. Option C would abandon the evidence that makes history possible.
questionBank.skill: Analyzing why defensible interpretations can differ

title: Primary Sources
in30Seconds: A primary source is firsthand evidence: an object, document, or recording made at the time of an event by someone who witnessed or took part in it. Letters, laws, photographs, artifacts, and oral histories are all primary sources. They put you as close to the past as evidence allows, but each one is partial and shaped by its maker, so historians read them carefully and check them against other sources.
whyItMatters: Primary sources are the raw material of history. Every credible claim about the past traces back to evidence created at the time, so knowing how to find, read, and question a primary source is the skill that separates informed judgment from repeating what others assert. The same habit transfers well beyond history class: evaluating an original document, dataset, or recording rather than a summary of it is central to research, journalism, law, and everyday media literacy. Learning to ask who made a source, when, and why builds the discipline of checking evidence before believing a story about it.
learningObjectives: Define a primary source as firsthand evidence created at the time of the events studied.
Distinguish a primary source from a secondary source in a specific case.
Identify the major types of primary sources, from documents to artifacts to oral histories.
Apply sourcing questions (who, when, why, for whom) to analyze a primary source.
Explain why a single primary source is rarely enough and must be corroborated.

collegeVersion.heading: What makes a source "primary"
collegeVersion.body: A primary source is firsthand evidence: an object or document that comes directly from the time period being studied, created by someone who witnessed or took part in the events. A soldier's wartime letter, a treaty as it was signed, a census ledger, a photograph taken on the day, a pharaoh's statue carved during his reign — each is primary for the period it comes from. What matters is not the format but the relationship in time: the source was produced within the events, not written about them afterward. This is the key line against a secondary source, which is created after the fact and interprets or analyzes primary evidence — a modern biography of that pharaoh, a textbook chapter on a war, a documentary. Historians use both. Primary sources supply the direct evidence; secondary sources supply context and the accumulated interpretation of earlier scholars, a body of work called historiography. Because a primary source is defined by its relationship to a question, the same item can be primary for one inquiry and secondary for another: a 1950s history textbook is a secondary source about the events it describes, but a primary source for how history was taught in the 1950s.

collegeVersion.heading: The main types of primary sources
collegeVersion.body: Primary sources come in far more forms than the written page. Written documents are the most familiar: letters, diaries, laws, treaties, speeches, newspapers, and government records. Material culture — artifacts and objects such as tools, coins, buildings, clothing, and works of art — is primary evidence too, and often the only evidence for societies that left few or no written records. Images carry their own testimony: photographs, maps, paintings, posters, and political cartoons each capture how people saw and depicted their world. Oral histories — recorded interviews and testimony — preserve firsthand memory, especially for communities whose experiences were left out of official documents. Finally, quantitative records and data — censuses, tax rolls, ship manifests, price lists, and ledgers — let historians measure patterns across whole populations. The National Archives, for instance, provides analysis worksheets for nine distinct document types, including photographs, artifacts, maps, cartoons, sound recordings, and artwork, a reminder that evidence about the past is not limited to text.

collegeVersion.heading: Reading a primary source: sourcing
collegeVersion.body: You cannot take a primary source at face value; you have to interrogate it. Historians call the first step sourcing: before deciding what a document proves, ask who created it, when and where, why it was made, and for whom — its intended audience. A public proclamation written to justify a war reveals a government's official story, not necessarily what happened; a private diary reveals one person's candid view, not the whole event. Two widely used frameworks put this into practice. The Library of Congress teaches Observe, Reflect, Question: note the concrete details you can see or hear, interpret them using what you already know, then list the questions the source raises. The National Archives uses a parallel four-step sequence — meet the document, observe its parts, try to make sense of it, and use it as historical evidence — asking at each stage who wrote it, who received it, when, and why. Both frameworks slow you down so you make inferences from evidence rather than jumping to conclusions.

collegeVersion.heading: Strengths and limits: why one source is rarely enough
collegeVersion.body: Primary sources are valuable precisely because they are close in time to the events; the analogy is a court trial held quickly, while witness memory is still fresh. But proximity is not the same as objectivity. Every primary source is partial: it captures one vantage point, was made for a purpose, and often survives only because someone chose to preserve it — which means whole perspectives, especially those of the poor, the enslaved, the colonized, and the illiterate, can be missing from the record. A single source can be mistaken, one-sided, or deliberately misleading, and it cannot tell you what it does not contain. This is why historians corroborate: they compare a source against other independent sources, weigh agreements and contradictions, and treat a claim as well founded only when several lines of evidence support it. A primary source is where analysis begins, not where it ends. Recognizing the perspective built into a source, and building interpretations from that evidence, are skills the related topics on bias and perspective and on evidence and interpretation take further.

vocabulary.definition: Firsthand evidence — an object, document, or recording — created at the time of the events being studied by a witness or participant.
An account created after the fact that interprets, analyzes, or summarizes primary sources, such as a textbook or a scholarly biography.
Analyzing a source by identifying who made it, when and where, why, and for what audience, before using it as evidence.
Checking a claim by comparing a source against other independent sources to see whether they agree.
Physical objects and artifacts — tools, coins, buildings, art, clothing — used as primary evidence about the people who made and used them.
Recorded firsthand testimony or memory gathered through interviews, often preserving experiences absent from written records.
The origin and chain of custody of a source — where it came from and how it survived — which affects how much it can be trusted.
The study of how historians have interpreted and written about a topic over time.
A source's built-in slant, arising from the maker's viewpoint, interests, or purpose, that shapes what it records and omits.

eli10.simplifiedExplanation: A primary source is a piece of the past that was made while the past was actually happening. If your grandmother writes in her diary on the day something happens, that diary is a primary source. If a writer reads a stack of old diaries fifty years later and writes a book about them, the book is a secondary source. Primary sources aren't only writing — they can be a photograph, an old coin, a song, a map, or a recorded interview. To use one well, you become a detective: figure out who made it, when, and why they made it. That last question matters a lot, because people make things for reasons. A poster telling everyone the king is wonderful was made to make the king look good, so it tells you what the king wanted people to believe, not necessarily the truth. That is why detectives never trust just one clue. They gather several and see which story all the clues point to together.
eli10.analogy: Think of primary sources like the clues at the scene of a mystery. A fingerprint, a note, or a security photo comes straight from the event, so a good detective studies each one — but never trusts a single clue by itself and always checks whether the clues agree.
eli10.analogyLimits: The analogy breaks down because a crime scene has one hidden truth a detective can solve, while history is usually about many valid perspectives, not a single answer. Historical sources also can't be dusted for prints or cross-examined; many are lost forever, and the ones that survive were often kept by the powerful, so the 'evidence' is unevenly preserved in a way a fresh crime scene is not.

workedExample: Suppose you are researching a 1911 factory fire. You find three primary sources: a fire-department incident report filed that week, a letter a surviving worker wrote to her sister two days later, and a newspaper photograph of the building taken during the blaze. Source each one. The incident report was written by officials to record cause and code violations, so it is strong on facts like the time and the locked exits but silent on how workers experienced it. The letter is firsthand and vivid but shaped by grief and by one person's limited view from inside. The photograph shows the scale of the fire but not why the exits failed. No single source is complete, and each carries its maker's purpose. By corroborating them — matching the report's locked-exit finding against the survivor's account of a jammed door and the photo's smoke pattern — you build an interpretation resting on several independent lines of evidence rather than on any one document alone.

commonMistakes.mistake: Treating a primary source as automatically true or objective because it comes from the time.
commonMistakes.correction: Firsthand does not mean unbiased. Every source has a maker with a viewpoint and a purpose; being close to the event makes a source valuable evidence, not a neutral fact.

commonMistakes.mistake: Assuming primary sources are only written documents.
commonMistakes.correction: Artifacts, photographs, maps, art, recordings, oral histories, and datasets are all primary sources — often the only evidence for societies that left few written records.

commonMistakes.mistake: Deciding a source is primary or secondary by its format alone (for example, 'a book is always secondary').
commonMistakes.correction: Classification depends on the question. A published book is a secondary source about the events it describes but a primary source for the ideas and attitudes of the time it was written.

commonMistakes.mistake: Building an argument on a single source because nothing contradicts it.
commonMistakes.correction: Silence is not confirmation. One source is partial and may simply omit what challenges it, so historians corroborate across multiple independent sources before trusting a claim.

commonMistakes.mistake: Confusing sourcing with summarizing what a document says.
commonMistakes.correction: Summarizing repeats the content; sourcing analyzes the source — who made it, when, why, and for whom — which is what lets you judge how much to trust the content.

compareContrast.distinction: A primary source is created within the events by a witness or participant; a secondary source is created afterward and interprets or analyzes primary evidence. Good research uses both.
Summarizing restates what the source says; sourcing steps back to ask who made it, when, why, and for whom, which is what lets you weigh its reliability.
Both can be primary sources, but written records carry explicit statements, while artifacts, buildings, and objects testify indirectly and are often the only evidence for non-literate societies.

keyTakeaway: A primary source is firsthand evidence made at the time of the events; it puts you closest to the past but is always partial and shaped by its maker, so historians source it (who, when, why, for whom) and corroborate it against other sources before trusting what it says.

questionBank.prompt: What makes a source a primary source?
options: It is the most reliable and unbiased account available on the topic
It was created at the time of the events by someone who witnessed or took part in them
It was written by a professional historian using careful methods
It summarizes and interprets earlier records for a general audience
questionBank.explanation: A primary source is defined by its relationship in time: it is firsthand evidence produced within the events by a witness or participant. It is not defined by reliability (primary sources are often biased), by professional authorship, or by summarizing others — the last describes a secondary source.
questionBank.skill: Defining a primary source

questionBank.prompt: A historian is studying the American Civil War. Which of the following would they classify as a primary source?
options: A 2010 college textbook chapter about the war's major battles
An encyclopedia entry summarizing the causes of the war
A biography of a Civil War general written in 2005
A letter a soldier wrote home to his family during the war
questionBank.explanation: The soldier's wartime letter was created within the events by a participant, making it a primary source. The textbook, encyclopedia entry, and modern biography were all written after the fact and interpret earlier evidence, so they are secondary sources.
questionBank.skill: Classifying a source as primary vs. secondary

questionBank.prompt: When historians "source" a primary document, what are they primarily asking?
options: Who created it, when, why, and for whom it was intended
How long the document is and what language it is written in
Whether present-day experts agree with its conclusions
How many copies of the document still survive today
questionBank.explanation: Sourcing means analyzing the origin and purpose of a source — its author, date, motive, and intended audience — before using it as evidence. Length and language, modern agreement, and survival counts may be noted but are not what sourcing centers on.
questionBank.skill: Applying the sourcing questions

questionBank.prompt: A single diary kept by one plantation owner is the only surviving account of daily life on a particular estate. What is the best conclusion a historian should draw about using it?
options: Because it was written at the time, the diary is objective and can be reported as fact
Because no other source contradicts it, the diary can be treated as the complete truth
It is valuable firsthand evidence but partial and one-sided, so its claims should be corroborated where possible
Because it is only one source, it proves nothing and should be set aside
questionBank.explanation: The diary is genuine firsthand evidence, so it is not worthless — but it reflects one perspective and omits the enslaved and other people's experiences. Being written at the time does not make it objective, and the absence of a contradicting source is not confirmation. The sound move is to use it critically and corroborate it.
questionBank.skill: Evaluating the limits of a single primary source

questionBank.prompt: A historian studying public opinion in 1925 uses a newspaper editorial from that year arguing for a new law. In this use, the editorial is best described as:
options: A secondary source, because editorials express opinion rather than fact
A tertiary source, because newspapers compile information from many places
Neither primary nor secondary, because opinion pieces are not evidence
A primary source, because it is firsthand evidence created at the time of the opinion being studied
questionBank.explanation: For the question of 1925 public opinion, the editorial comes directly from the period and phenomenon under study, so it is a primary source — even though it is opinion. Whether a source is primary depends on the research question, not on whether it contains opinion or is a newspaper.
questionBank.skill: Recognizing that primary/secondary status depends on the research question

title: Secondary Sources
in30Seconds: A secondary source is an account created after the fact that analyzes, interprets, or summarizes primary evidence. It sits one step removed from the events: think textbooks, scholarly books, journal articles, biographies, and documentaries. Secondary sources are where historians make arguments about what happened and why. The same item can even be primary or secondary depending on the question you ask of it.
whyItMatters: Most of what you read in a history course is secondary: textbooks, monographs, and journal articles that build an argument from primary evidence. Knowing that these are interpretations, not neutral records, changes how you read them. You start asking who wrote this, what evidence they used, whether other scholars agree, and how the argument has shifted over time. That habit protects you from mistaking one confident book for settled fact, and it is the foundation of every research paper, literature review, and evidence-based claim you will make in college and beyond.
learningObjectives: Define a secondary source as a later account that interprets, analyzes, or summarizes primary evidence.
Distinguish secondary sources from primary sources and classify common examples.
Explain why the same item can be primary or secondary depending on the research question.
Apply criteria—peer review, citation, author expertise, publisher—to judge a secondary source's reliability.
Analyze how historians build on and argue with earlier scholarship (historiography).

collegeVersion.heading: What makes a source secondary
collegeVersion.body: A secondary source is a work created after the events it describes that analyzes, interprets, or summarizes evidence rather than recording the events firsthand. It sits one step removed from what happened. A primary source—a soldier's diary, a treaty, a census return, a photograph taken at the scene—comes directly from the moment under study. A secondary source is what a later author writes about that moment, usually by gathering and reasoning over many primary sources. When a historian reads dozens of letters, land records, and newspapers and then writes a book explaining why a rebellion began, the letters are primary and the book is secondary. The defining features are timing (created afterward) and function (it interprets rather than simply witnesses). Both matter: a memoir written decades later is still close to primary because its author participated in the events, whereas a scholar's monograph about those same events is secondary because its author is analyzing evidence from the outside.

collegeVersion.heading: The common forms you will meet
collegeVersion.body: In college the secondary sources you handle most are textbooks, scholarly monographs (single-topic academic books), peer-reviewed journal articles, biographies written after their subject's life, documentaries, dissertations, and book or exhibition reviews. Each carries a different weight. A textbook synthesizes a broad consensus for teaching and rarely makes an original argument. A journal article or monograph, by contrast, advances a specific claim and defends it with cited evidence. A documentary interprets a subject for a general audience—though it often embeds primary material, such as archival footage or interviews, which can be primary sources in their own right. Recognizing the form tells you what to expect: how original the argument is, how much evidence stands behind it, and how much interpretive distance separates the author from the events. Some frameworks add a third label, 'tertiary,' for reference works such as encyclopedias and textbooks that compile secondary scholarship; the primary/secondary line remains the distinction that matters most.

collegeVersion.heading: Why classification depends on the question
collegeVersion.body: A source is not permanently primary or secondary; its status depends on the research question you bring to it. A biology textbook is a secondary source if you are studying biology, because it summarizes the field's findings. But if your project is the history of science education—how textbooks portrayed evolution across the twentieth century—that same textbook becomes a primary source, because it is now direct evidence from the period you are studying. A 1990 history of World War II is secondary evidence about the 1940s, yet a primary source about how historians in 1990 understood the war. This is one of the most useful ideas in the discipline: before you label a source, ask what you are trying to find out. The label follows the question, not the object.

collegeVersion.heading: Judging reliability and reading historiographically
collegeVersion.body: Because secondary sources make arguments, you have to evaluate them rather than accept them. Scholarly work is filtered by standards, chief among them peer review, in which other experts assess an article or book before publication. Strong positive signals include an author with relevant expertise, a university press or recognized scholarly publisher, full citations that let you trace the evidence, and appropriate currency for the topic. These are not guarantees, but they distinguish vetted scholarship from unsupported opinion. Reading well also means reading historiographically. Historiography is the study of how historians have interpreted a topic over time. Scholars are in conversation: they build on, extend, and dispute one another's work, and two careful historians can read the same records and reach opposite conclusions because interpretation is shaped by their questions, methods, and context. So the goal is not to find the one true book but to locate a source within its debate—what it argues, whom it answers, and what evidence it rests on. Historians apply the same scrutiny to any source: who made it, for what audience, with what intent, and whether other sources corroborate it.

vocabulary.definition: A work created after the events it describes that interprets, analyzes, or summarizes evidence rather than recording the events firsthand.
Firsthand or contemporary evidence produced by a participant or observer at the time of the events, such as a diary, treaty, or photograph taken at the scene.
A scholarly book that examines a single, focused topic in depth and advances an original argument.
A process in which experts in a field evaluate a manuscript's evidence and reasoning before it is published.
The study of how historians have interpreted and debated a topic over time, and of the methods they use.
Checking a claim against additional sources to see whether independent evidence supports it.
A reference work, such as an encyclopedia, that compiles and condenses secondary scholarship rather than making an original argument.
An evidence-based explanation of what past events meant or why they happened, which can reasonably differ between careful scholars.

eli10.simplifiedExplanation: Imagine a soccer game. The players on the field and the video of the match are the primary sources—they are the event itself. A secondary source is the sports reporter who watches the game afterward and writes an article explaining who played well and why the team won. The reporter was not scoring goals; they are studying what happened and making sense of it. In history, the diaries, laws, and photographs are the game, and the textbooks, biographies, and history books are the reporters. Two reporters can watch the exact same game and still disagree about which player was the reason for the win, because explaining is not the same as just recording.
eli10.analogy: A secondary source is like a movie review: the movie is the primary source, and the review is a later, thoughtful take on it. You can enjoy a review, but you know it is one critic's argument, not the film itself.
eli10.analogyLimits: The analogy understates the work behind good scholarship. A movie critic usually watches one film, but a historian's secondary source is built from many primary sources and is often checked by other experts through peer review before it is published—so it carries more evidence and vetting than a single opinion column.

workedExample: Suppose you are researching the 1889 Johnstown Flood. You gather survivors' letters, contemporary newspaper reports, and the Red Cross's relief records—these are primary sources. Then you read David McCullough's 1968 book about the flood: it is a secondary source, because it was written long after and interprets those primary materials into an argument about why the dam failed and who was responsible. Now change the question. If your new project is 'how did American popular history writing portray corporate responsibility in the 1960s,' McCullough's 1968 book flips roles and becomes a primary source—direct evidence from the period you are now studying. Same book, different classification, because the research question changed.

commonMistakes.mistake: Treating a source as permanently primary or secondary based on what it is.
commonMistakes.correction: The label depends on your research question. Ask what you are studying before you classify; the same textbook can be secondary for its subject and primary for a study of textbooks.

commonMistakes.mistake: Assuming a published history book states settled, neutral fact.
commonMistakes.correction: A secondary source is an argument built from evidence. Read it as one interpretation, and check what evidence supports it and whether other scholars agree.

commonMistakes.mistake: Judging reliability only by how confident or recent a source sounds.
commonMistakes.correction: Weigh peer review, cited references, author expertise, and publisher. Confidence and recency alone do not make a claim trustworthy.

commonMistakes.mistake: Confusing a memoir written decades later with a secondary source.
commonMistakes.correction: A participant's later memoir is still close to primary because its author lived the events; a secondary source is written by someone analyzing the events from outside.

commonMistakes.mistake: Thinking that if two historians disagree, one must simply be wrong.
commonMistakes.correction: Interpretation legitimately varies. Careful scholars can reach different conclusions from the same evidence; the point is to weigh their arguments, not to assume error.

compareContrast.distinction: A primary source is firsthand evidence from the time of the events; a secondary source is a later work that interprets or analyzes such evidence.
A textbook synthesizes broad consensus for teaching; a monograph advances an original, evidence-backed argument on a focused topic.
A secondary source analyzes primary evidence to make an argument; a tertiary source (e.g., an encyclopedia) compiles and condenses secondary work without an original thesis.

keyTakeaway: Secondary sources are later works that interpret primary evidence, so read them as arguments—checking who made them, what evidence backs them, and how they fit the wider scholarly debate—while remembering that a source's classification depends on the question you ask of it.

questionBank.prompt: Which statement best defines a secondary source in history?
options: An account created after the events it describes that analyzes or interprets primary evidence
A firsthand record made by a participant or eyewitness during the events
Any document that is stored in a government or university archive
A source that has been translated from its original language into English
questionBank.explanation: A secondary source is defined by timing (created afterward) and function (it interprets or analyzes evidence). Option B describes a primary source. Archives (C) hold both primary and secondary materials, so storage location does not decide the category. Translation (D) is unrelated to whether a source is primary or secondary.
