title: Colonial America
in30Seconds: Colonial America is the era when European settlers, mainly the English, built lasting colonies along eastern North America in the 1600s and 1700s. Beginning with Jamestown in 1607 and Plymouth in 1620, thirteen colonies grew into three regions with different economies, took land from Native nations, developed racialized slavery in the plantation South, and practiced local self-government through elected assemblies.
whyItMatters: The colonies are where the United States began, so their patterns still shape it. The regional split between a commercial North and a plantation South, the growth of racialized slavery, the dispossession of Native nations, and the habit of governing through elected assemblies all set up the American Revolution, the Constitution, and the conflicts that led to the Civil War. Studying this period teaches you to hold several truths at once: colonists built new self-governing communities while also displacing Indigenous peoples and enslaving Africans. That kind of honest, multi-sided reading is exactly the historical thinking later topics build on.
learningObjectives: Identify the founding of key colonies, including Jamestown (1607) and Plymouth (1620), and the motives behind them.
Distinguish the New England, Middle, and Southern colonial regions and explain how geography shaped their economies.
Explain how indentured servitude and, over time, racialized hereditary slavery developed in the colonies.
Describe how relations with Native nations shifted from trade and alliance to dispossession and war.
Analyze how colonial assemblies established traditions of representative self-government.

collegeVersion.heading: Founding the first colonies: Jamestown (1607) and Plymouth (1620)
collegeVersion.body: England came late to American colonization. After the failed Roanoke venture of the 1580s, its first permanent foothold was Jamestown, planted in 1607 on a Virginia river by the Virginia Company of London, a joint-stock company that sold shares to investors hoping for quick profit. Profit did not come quickly. Disease, brackish water, and food shortages produced the 'Starving Time' of 1609-1610, which killed most of the settlers. The colony survived only when John Rolfe began cultivating a marketable strain of tobacco around 1612; within a decade tobacco was Virginia's cash crop and its reason to keep expanding onto Native land. A different kind of colony took root farther north. In 1620 a group of English Separatists we now call the Pilgrims landed at Plymouth in present-day Massachusetts, seeking to worship apart from the Church of England. Before going ashore they signed the Mayflower Compact, a short agreement to govern themselves by common consent. A decade later a much larger Puritan migration built the Massachusetts Bay Colony under Governor John Winthrop; the 'Great Migration' of the 1630s brought thousands of families. Chesapeake colonies were founded chiefly to make money; New England colonies were founded chiefly around religious community. That contrast in motive shaped how each region grew.

collegeVersion.heading: Three regions, three economies
collegeVersion.body: By the eighteenth century the mainland colonies are usefully grouped into three regions, and geography explains much of what separated them. New England (Massachusetts, Connecticut, Rhode Island, New Hampshire) had thin, rocky soil and short growing seasons, so it leaned on small family farms, fishing, timber, shipbuilding, and seaborne trade rather than a single export crop. The Middle colonies (New York, taken from the Dutch in 1664; Pennsylvania, granted to William Penn in 1681; plus New Jersey and Delaware) had fertile land and became the 'breadbasket,' exporting wheat and other grains, and they held the most religiously and ethnically mixed populations. The Southern colonies (Maryland, chartered 1632; Virginia; the Carolinas, chartered 1663; and Georgia, chartered 1732) had warm climates and long growing seasons suited to labor-intensive cash crops grown on plantations: tobacco in the Chesapeake, and rice and indigo in the Carolina and Georgia Lowcountry, where planters drew directly on the enslaved-labor model of Barbados. The same crops that made the plantation South wealthy also made it the region most dependent on enslaved workers. Understanding the colonies means seeing them as different societies, not one uniform 'America.'

collegeVersion.heading: Labor, slavery, and a diverse society
collegeVersion.body: Colonial labor began largely with indentured servants: poor Europeans who traded four to seven years of work for passage across the Atlantic, often lured by headright grants of land to whoever paid their way. The first documented Africans in English North America were brought to Virginia in 1619; at that moment slavery was not yet a fixed legal institution, and some early Africans gained freedom. Over the seventeenth century that openness closed. A 1662 Virginia law made a child's status follow the enslaved or free condition of the mother, making bondage inheritable; after Bacon's Rebellion in 1676 unsettled the colony, Virginia passed further laws (1680, 1682) restricting Black people, and the Virginia Slave Codes of 1705 consolidated slavery into a lifelong, hereditary, racial status and even classed enslaved people as property. Racialized slavery, in other words, was built by law over decades, not present from the first ship. The result was a strikingly diverse and unequal colonial society: enslaved Africans, indentured servants, wealthy planters, small farmers, merchants, and many distinct Native nations, alongside religious communities from Puritans and Quakers to Catholics in Maryland. The deeper history of the Atlantic slave system and of U.S. slavery belongs to other topics; here the point is simply how and when the institution took hold.

collegeVersion.heading: Native nations: from alliance to dispossession and war
collegeVersion.body: Colonization did not happen on empty land. Every colony was planted among Native nations who had lived there for millennia, and the earliest relationships often mixed trade, diplomacy, and alliance. The Wampanoag leader Massasoit allied with Plymouth in 1621; Native knowledge and trade goods kept struggling colonies alive. But the colonists' hunger for farmland turned cooperation into conflict as settlement expanded. In New England the Pequot War of 1636-1637 ended in the massacre of Pequot people at Mystic. Two generations later, King Philip's War (1675-1676) pitted a coalition led by Metacom, the Wampanoag sachem the English called King Philip and a son of Massasoit, against the New England colonies. It was proportionally one of the deadliest wars in American history; Metacom was killed in August 1676, over a thousand Native people were sold into slavery, and survivors were pushed onto small reserved lands or absorbed into other nations. The broad pattern across the colonies was similar: early exchange giving way to land dispossession, epidemic disease, and war. An honest account of colonial America holds both the settlers' achievements and this dispossession in view at once.

collegeVersion.heading: The seeds of self-government
collegeVersion.body: One legacy of the colonial period outlasted the crops and the colonies themselves: the habit of local self-government. As early as 1619 Virginia's House of Burgesses met as the first elected representative assembly in England's American colonies, and the 1620 Mayflower Compact recorded settlers agreeing to govern by common consent. Over the next century nearly every colony developed an elected assembly that controlled local taxes and spending, even while a royal or proprietary governor represented authority from London and property qualifications kept the franchise narrow and male. These assemblies were not democracies in the modern sense, and they coexisted with slavery and dispossession. But the experience of colonists debating and voting on their own laws created expectations about representation and consent that, when Britain tightened control after 1763, would help spark the American Revolution. The colonial era is where those political traditions were rehearsed.

vocabulary.definition: The period from the early 1600s to the 1770s when European powers, chiefly England, established permanent settlements along eastern North America that later became the United States.
A business that raised money by selling shares to many investors who shared the profits and risks; the Virginia Company that founded Jamestown was one.
A plant grown mainly to be sold for profit rather than to feed the growers, such as the tobacco, rice, and indigo raised on Southern plantations.
A laborer who agreed to work without pay for a fixed number of years, usually in exchange for passage across the Atlantic, after which they were freed.
A policy granting a set amount of land, typically fifty acres, to anyone who paid for a settler's passage, which encouraged the import of servants and expansion onto Native land.
A system, hardened by colonial laws over the 1600s, that made enslavement a lifelong and inheritable condition assigned on the basis of African ancestry.
Virginia's assembly, first meeting in 1619, that was the earliest elected representative lawmaking body in England's North American colonies.
A 1620 agreement signed by Plymouth's settlers pledging to govern themselves by common consent, an early example of colonial self-government.
A devastating 1675-1676 conflict in which New England colonies fought a Native coalition led by the Wampanoag leader Metacom, ending in heavy Native losses and dispossession.

eli10.simplifiedExplanation: A long time ago, people from Europe, mostly from England, sailed across the ocean and started towns along the east coast of North America. The first ones that lasted were Jamestown in 1607 and Plymouth in 1620. Over time there were thirteen colonies, and they were not all the same. In the cold, rocky north people fished, cut timber, and traded. In the warm south people grew huge fields of tobacco and rice on farms called plantations and forced enslaved Africans to do the work. The land those colonies grew on already belonged to many Native nations, and as the colonies pushed outward there was trading at first and then terrible wars. One thing the colonists started that stuck around was voting: they picked people to make some of their own local laws.
eli10.analogy: Think of the colonies like three very different neighborhoods that grew up in one big new town, each shaped by its own land, weather, and the people who moved there.
eli10.analogyLimits: The neighborhood picture is friendly, but it hides the hardest facts. Real neighborhoods form on empty lots; these colonies were built on land taken from Native nations, and the Southern 'neighborhood' ran on the forced labor of enslaved people. It also makes the regions sound like free choices, when climate, distant kings, and brutal coercion did much of the shaping.

workedExample: Suppose you are handed two facts and asked to explain the difference between them: Massachusetts merchants in 1700 made their living from fishing fleets, shipyards, and trade, while Virginia planters the same year depended on enslaved Africans growing tobacco. Rather than treating this as random, a historian reasons from geography and law. New England's thin soil and short growing season could not support a profitable single crop, so its economy spread across the sea and small farms. Virginia's warm climate and long season made tobacco enormously profitable, and profitable plantation crops created demand for a large, permanent labor force. Colonial statutes such as Virginia's 1705 slave codes then locked that labor force into lifelong, hereditary, racial slavery. The two facts are not a coincidence; they are the predictable outcome of climate, crop, and law working together.

commonMistakes.mistake: Thinking all thirteen colonies were basically the same.
commonMistakes.correction: They fell into three distinct regions, with New England commerce and small farms, the Middle colonies' grain and diversity, and the plantation South differing sharply in economy and society.

commonMistakes.mistake: Assuming racialized slavery existed fully formed the moment Africans arrived in 1619.
commonMistakes.correction: In 1619 slavery was not yet a fixed legal institution; colonial laws across the 1600s, culminating in codes like Virginia's of 1705, gradually made it lifelong, hereditary, and racial.

commonMistakes.mistake: Picturing the colonies as planted on empty wilderness.
commonMistakes.correction: Every colony was built among established Native nations; relations moved from trade and alliance to land dispossession and wars such as the Pequot War and King Philip's War.

commonMistakes.mistake: Treating colonial assemblies as full democracies.
commonMistakes.correction: Assemblies like the House of Burgesses were elected but limited to propertied men and coexisted with slavery and dispossession; they were early steps toward representative government, not modern democracy.

commonMistakes.mistake: Confusing indentured servitude with slavery.
commonMistakes.correction: Indentured servants worked for a fixed term and were then freed, while enslaved people were held for life with a status passed to their children.

compareContrast.distinction: Jamestown was a for-profit venture of the joint-stock Virginia Company; Plymouth was founded by Separatists seeking to worship freely, giving the Chesapeake and New England colonies different founding motives.
Indenture was a temporary contract that ended in freedom; racialized slavery, hardened by colonial law, was lifelong, hereditary, and assigned by African ancestry.
New England relied on small farms, fishing, timber, and trade suited to poor soil; the South's warm climate supported cash-crop plantations worked by enslaved laborers.

keyTakeaway: Colonial America was not one uniform society but three regions shaped by geography, built through both self-governing assemblies and the dispossession of Native nations and the enslavement of Africans.

questionBank.prompt: Where and when did England establish its first permanent colony in North America?
options: Plymouth, in present-day Massachusetts, in 1620
Jamestown, in Virginia, in 1607
Charles Town, in Carolina, in 1670
St. Mary's City, in Maryland, in 1634
questionBank.explanation: Jamestown (1607), founded by the joint-stock Virginia Company, was England's first permanent North American colony. Plymouth (1620), Charles Town (1670), and Maryland's settlement (1634) all came later and are named as distractors with real but later dates.
questionBank.skill: Recalling the founding date and place of the first permanent English colony

questionBank.prompt: Why did a plantation economy dependent on enslaved labor develop in the Southern colonies but not in New England?
options: New England colonists were legally forbidden from owning enslaved people
The Southern colonies had no access to Atlantic shipping
Royal decree required the South to grow only export crops
The South's warm climate and long growing seasons suited labor-intensive cash crops like tobacco and rice, unlike New England's thin soil and short seasons
questionBank.explanation: Geography drove the difference: the South's climate favored plantation cash crops (tobacco, rice, indigo) that demanded large forced labor forces, while New England's poor soil and short seasons pushed it toward small farms, fishing, and trade. Enslaved people were held in New England too, so option A is false; the other options invent barriers and decrees.
questionBank.skill: Explaining how geography shaped divergent regional economies

questionBank.prompt: The Virginia House of Burgesses, first meeting in 1619, is historically significant mainly because it was —
options: the first elected representative legislative assembly in England's North American colonies
the first written constitution of the United States
a council appointed entirely by the English king with no elected members
an alliance council uniting the New England colonies against Native nations
questionBank.explanation: The House of Burgesses (1619) was the first elected representative assembly in the English colonies, an early root of colonial self-government. It was not a national constitution, not a wholly royal-appointed body, and had nothing to do with a New England military alliance.
questionBank.skill: Identifying the origin of representative self-government in the colonies

questionBank.prompt: When the first Africans arrived in Virginia in 1619 slavery was not yet a fixed legal institution, yet by 1705 Virginia law made it lifelong and hereditary. This change best illustrates that —
options: colonial slavery ended within a few decades of 1619
racialized slavery existed fully formed from the first English settlement
racial slavery was built gradually through colonial laws passed across the 1600s that hardened it into an inheritable status
enslaved and indentured laborers were treated identically throughout the colonial period
questionBank.explanation: Laws such as the 1662 inheritance statute, the post-1676 restrictions, and the 1705 Virginia Slave Codes show slavery being constructed step by step into a lifelong, hereditary, racial condition. It did not vanish (A), was not present fully formed in 1619 (B), and indentured servitude was legally distinct and time-limited (D).
questionBank.skill: Interpreting change over time in the legal construction of slavery

questionBank.prompt: Which pairing correctly matches a colonial region with its characteristic colonial-era economy?
options: New England paired with large tobacco and rice plantations worked by enslaved laborers
Middle colonies paired with grain farming that earned them the nickname 'breadbasket'
Southern colonies paired with fishing, shipbuilding, and small subsistence farms
Middle colonies paired with a single established church and almost no immigration
questionBank.explanation: The fertile Middle colonies exported wheat and grain and were called the 'breadbasket.' The other options swap the regions: plantations belonged to the South, fishing and shipbuilding to New England, and the Middle colonies were among the most religiously and ethnically diverse, not closed to immigration.
questionBank.skill: Applying the regional-economy framework to classify colonies

title: The American Revolution
in30Seconds: The American Revolution was the conflict in which thirteen British colonies broke from Britain and founded the United States. After the costly French and Indian War, Britain taxed the colonies without their consent, protest escalated from the Boston Massacre to the Boston Tea Party, and fighting began at Lexington and Concord in 1775. Congress declared independence on July 4, 1776; the war ended with the Treaty of Paris in 1783.
whyItMatters: The Revolution created the United States and gave the modern world an influential statement of natural rights and government by consent. Understanding it lets you read the founding documents critically rather than as slogans: you can trace how a tax dispute became a claim about human equality, and how that claim was applied unevenly. It also sharpens a core historical skill, separating what happened and when from why it mattered, and holding the Revolution's ideals and its exclusions in view at the same time. Almost every later argument about American citizenship, rights, and rebellion begins here.
learningObjectives: Explain how British war debt and post-1763 taxation led to the grievance of 'no taxation without representation.'
Sequence the key events from the Stamp Act (1765) through the Treaty of Paris (1783) with accurate dates.
Distinguish the Revolution's stated ideals from how it was experienced by enslaved people, women, Native Americans, and loyalists.
Analyze why Saratoga and the French alliance were turning points in the war.
Apply the concept of 'consent of the governed' to a primary-source grievance.

collegeVersion.heading: Causes: war debt, taxes, and the rights of British subjects
collegeVersion.body: The Revolution grew out of victory, not defeat. Britain won the Seven Years' War, known in North America as the French and Indian War, which ended in 1763 and left Britain dominant but deeply in debt. To help pay for defending and administering a larger empire, Parliament began raising revenue from the colonies: the Sugar Act of 1764, then the Stamp Act of 1765, a direct tax on printed materials. Colonists reacted sharply. Many accepted that Parliament could regulate trade but insisted it could not tax them internally, because they elected no members to it. Out of this came the slogan 'no taxation without representation.' The Townshend Acts of 1767 taxed imported goods and provoked boycotts and renewed protest. The dispute was not, at first, about leaving the empire. Colonists framed their case as a defense of the ordinary rights of British subjects, arguing that a subject could be taxed only with the consent of his elected representatives. Enlightenment ideas about natural rights and government resting on the consent of the governed gave this grievance a broader, more radical vocabulary.

collegeVersion.heading: From protest to rupture: Massacre, Tea Party, and Lexington
collegeVersion.body: Protest hardened into confrontation. British troops stationed in Boston clashed with a crowd, and the conflict turned deadly on March 5, 1770, in the killing that came to be called the Boston Massacre. Tensions eased briefly, then flared again over tea. The Tea Act of 1773 lowered the price of British East India Company tea but kept a tax colonists rejected on principle. On December 16, 1773, protesters boarded ships in Boston Harbor and destroyed the cargo in what became known as the Boston Tea Party. Parliament answered in early 1774 with the Coercive Acts, called the Intolerable Acts in the colonies, which closed the port of Boston and restricted Massachusetts self-government. These measures pushed the colonies toward common action. On April 19, 1775, British regulars marching to seize colonial military stores met militia at Lexington and Concord, and the first shots of the war were fired. Armed rebellion had begun more than a year before the colonies formally declared independence.

collegeVersion.heading: Independence and the ideas behind it
collegeVersion.body: As fighting spread, the Continental Congress moved from resistance toward separation. Richard Henry Lee introduced a motion for independence on June 7, 1776, and Congress assigned the drafting of a formal declaration to a committee, with Thomas Jefferson as principal author; Benjamin Franklin and John Adams reviewed his draft. Congress adopted the final text on July 4, 1776. The Declaration of Independence did two things at once. It listed specific grievances against the king to justify the break, and it grounded the right to rebel in a general principle: 'that all men are created equal, that they are endowed by their Creator with certain unalienable Rights,' and that governments derive 'their just powers from the consent of the governed.' That second move mattered far beyond 1776. By stating the case for independence as a claim about universal human rights and consent, the Declaration created a standard that later generations, including abolitionists and suffragists, would use to measure the nation against its own words.

collegeVersion.heading: The war's course and the Treaty of Paris
collegeVersion.body: The military struggle lasted eight years. Early campaigns went badly for the Continental Army under George Washington, but a major turning point came at Saratoga in New York, where the British general Burgoyne surrendered about five thousand soldiers on October 17, 1777. That victory convinced France, long hostile to Britain, that the American cause could succeed. France signed a Treaty of Alliance and a Treaty of Amity and Commerce with the United States on February 6, 1778, bringing money, troops, and a navy into the war and turning a colonial rebellion into a wider conflict. The decisive campaign came in 1781, when combined American and French forces trapped Lord Cornwallis at Yorktown, Virginia; he surrendered on October 19, 1781. Fighting wound down, and negotiators signed the Treaty of Paris on September 3, 1783, in which Britain recognized the independence of the United States. A war that began as a tax dispute ended with a new nation on the map.

collegeVersion.heading: Contradictions and limits
collegeVersion.body: The Revolution's ideals and its practice did not match, and honest history holds both in view. The Declaration proclaimed that all men are created equal, yet slavery continued in the new nation, and several of the men who signed the document enslaved people themselves. For the roughly one-fifth of the population who were enslaved, revolutionary liberty was a promise withheld; some sought freedom by joining whichever side offered it. Native American nations faced a different calculation: many allied with Britain, correctly fearing that an independent United States would expand westward onto their lands, and they were among the Revolution's clear losers. Women contributed to boycotts, war production, and the home front but gained no formal political rights. Loyalists, colonists who stayed loyal to the crown, were roughly a fifth of the population; many were harassed, dispossessed, or forced into exile. Recognizing these limits does not diminish the Revolution's importance. It explains why the struggle to make 'all men are created equal' real has continued long after 1783.

vocabulary.definition: The North American theater of the Seven Years' War, ending in 1763, whose costs left Britain in debt and motivated new colonial taxes.
The colonial argument that Parliament could not tax colonists who elected none of its members and had not consented to the tax.
A 1765 British law placing a direct tax on printed materials in the colonies; its repeal followed widespread protest.
The March 5, 1770 killing of colonists by British soldiers during a street confrontation in Boston.
The December 16, 1773 destruction of British East India Company tea in Boston Harbor in protest of the Tea Act.
The 1774 British laws punishing Massachusetts, including closing Boston's port, which pushed the colonies toward united resistance.
The document adopted July 4, 1776, drafted mainly by Thomas Jefferson, announcing the colonies' separation from Britain and its justifying principles.
The principle that a government's legitimate authority derives from the agreement of the people it rules.
Colonists who remained loyal to the British crown during the Revolution; many were dispossessed or exiled.
The September 3, 1783 agreement in which Britain recognized the independence of the United States and ended the war.

eli10.simplifiedExplanation: Britain had just fought an expensive war and wanted the colonies to help pay for it, so it added taxes. The colonists were angry not mainly because the taxes were large but because nobody had asked them, and they had no one speaking for them in the government that made the rules. Small protests grew into big ones, then into fighting. The colonists decided they would rather run their own country, so they wrote the Declaration of Independence saying people have rights no ruler can take away. After eight years of war, and help from France, they won and became the United States. But the same leaders who wrote that everyone is equal still allowed slavery and left many people out, which is a real part of the story too.
eli10.analogy: Imagine a landlord who keeps adding fees to your rent and changing the house rules, but never lets you into the meeting where those rules are decided. Eventually the tenants stop paying, hold their own meeting, and declare they are moving out to start a household of their own.
eli10.analogyLimits: The analogy captures the anger about being ruled without a voice, but it undersells the stakes and the unfairness inside the new household. Leaving a landlord is peaceful; the Revolution was an eight-year war that killed thousands. And the tenants who 'started their own household' did not extend their new freedom to everyone under their roof, since slavery continued and many people were excluded.

workedExample: Read one grievance from the Declaration: the colonists accuse the king of 'imposing Taxes on us without our Consent.' Work through why this line matters. First, identify the principle behind it: that rightful authority comes from the consent of the governed. Second, connect it to the earlier fight over the Stamp Act (1765) and Townshend Acts (1767), where colonists objected not to the amount of the tax but to being taxed by a Parliament they did not elect. Third, notice what the grievance does rhetorically: it reframes a specific policy dispute as a violation of a universal right, which justifies not just protest but separation. Finally, test the principle against the Revolution's own record. If consent is the standard, then enslaved people, women, and Native American nations were governed without their consent by the very republic that made the argument, which is exactly the tension later reformers pressed.

commonMistakes.mistake: Thinking the colonists rebelled because taxes were unusually high.
commonMistakes.correction: The core objection was constitutional, not financial: they held that Parliament could not tax them without their consent because they elected no representatives to it.

commonMistakes.mistake: Treating July 4, 1776 as the day the war was won or the day fighting started.
commonMistakes.correction: Fighting began at Lexington and Concord on April 19, 1775; July 4, 1776 is when Congress adopted the Declaration. The war continued until 1783.

commonMistakes.mistake: Assuming all colonists supported independence.
commonMistakes.correction: A large minority were loyalists who backed the crown, and many colonists were neutral; the population was divided, not unanimous.

commonMistakes.mistake: Presenting 'all men are created equal' as an accomplished fact of the new nation.
commonMistakes.correction: It was a stated ideal contradicted in practice by slavery and by the exclusion of women and Native Americans; the gap between ideal and reality is central to the history.

commonMistakes.mistake: Crediting the American victory to the colonists alone.
commonMistakes.correction: The French alliance of 1778, prompted by Saratoga, brought decisive money, troops, and naval power, seen most clearly at Yorktown in 1781.

compareContrast.distinction: The Massacre was a deadly street clash that produced martyrs and propaganda; the Tea Party was an organized, deliberate destruction of property to protest the Tea Act. One was violence against people, the other targeted goods.

Lee's motion for independence was introduced June 7 and approved before the wording was finished; July 4 is the date Congress adopted the final text, which is why it appears on the document and became the holiday.
Saratoga was the turning point that brought France into the war; Yorktown was the decisive final campaign that made British continuation untenable and led to peace.

keyTakeaway: The American Revolution turned a dispute over taxation without consent into a war for independence and a lasting claim that governments rest on the consent of the governed, a claim the new nation proclaimed while denying it to the enslaved, to women, and to Native peoples.

options: December 16, 1773
April 19, 1775
March 5, 1770
July 4, 1776
questionBank.explanation: OpenStax states conflict 'turned deadly on March 5, 1770.' December 16, 1773 is the Boston Tea Party, April 19, 1775 is Lexington and Concord, and July 4, 1776 is the adoption of the Declaration.

questionBank.prompt: Which battle is generally identified as the turning point that helped bring France into the war as a formal ally?
options: Saratoga (1777)
Yorktown (1781)
Lexington and Concord (1775)
Bunker Hill (1775)
questionBank.explanation: The British surrender at Saratoga on October 17, 1777 convinced France to sign a formal alliance on February 6, 1778. Yorktown (1781) was the decisive final campaign, and Lexington and Concord opened the war.
questionBank.skill: Identifying the strategic significance of Saratoga

questionBank.prompt: A student notes that colonists protested the Stamp Act even though it was a relatively small tax. Which reasoning best explains their objection?
options: They believed all taxation was inherently illegal under British law.
They wanted to break from Britain immediately and needed a pretext.
They objected only because the tax fell on tea and other luxuries.
They held that Parliament could not tax them without their consent, since they elected no members to it.
questionBank.explanation: The grievance was constitutional: 'no taxation without representation.' Colonists accepted trade regulation but denied that a Parliament they did not elect could tax them. They were not yet seeking independence, did not reject all taxation, and the Stamp Act taxed printed materials, not tea.
questionBank.skill: Explaining the constitutional basis of colonial protest

questionBank.prompt: Who was the principal drafter of the Declaration of Independence, and when did Congress adopt its final text?
options: Benjamin Franklin; July 2, 1776
Thomas Jefferson; July 4, 1776
John Adams; September 3, 1783
Richard Henry Lee; April 19, 1775
questionBank.explanation: Congress assigned the drafting to Thomas Jefferson, whose draft Franklin and Adams reviewed, and adopted the final text on July 4, 1776. Lee introduced the motion for independence on June 7; September 3, 1783 is the Treaty of Paris.
questionBank.skill: Attributing authorship and dating the Declaration

questionBank.prompt: Which statement best captures a central contradiction of the American Revolution?
options: It declared independence but never actually separated from Britain.
It proclaimed that 'all men are created equal' while slavery continued and women and Native Americans were excluded from its new freedoms.
It was won without any foreign assistance despite claims to the contrary.
It abolished slavery immediately but denied the vote to landowners.
questionBank.explanation: The Declaration's claim of universal equality coexisted with the continuation of slavery and the exclusion of women, Native Americans, and others. The colonies did separate from Britain, France's aid was decisive, and slavery was not abolished by the Revolution.
questionBank.skill: Evaluating the gap between the Revolution's ideals and its practice

title: The U.S. Constitution
in30Seconds: The U.S. Constitution, framed in Philadelphia in 1787, replaced the weak Articles of Confederation with a stronger national government. Its framers balanced competing interests through compromises, some of which protected slavery, such as counting enslaved people as three-fifths of a person for representation. The document rests on federalism, separation of powers, and checks and balances, and it can be amended. Ratified by 1788 and joined by the Bill of Rights in 1791, it remains the framework of American government.
whyItMatters: The Constitution is the oldest written national framework still in force, and understanding how it was made explains both its strengths and its original injustices. The 1787 compromises show how a working government can be assembled from conflicting interests, and how doing so entrenched slavery for decades. Studying the framing teaches you to read a founding document as a negotiated, revisable product of its time rather than a finished sacred text. Its amendment process is why later generations could abolish slavery and expand the vote, a pattern of change that still shapes American political debate today.
learningObjectives: Explain why the Articles of Confederation proved too weak to govern the new nation.
Describe the major compromises of the 1787 Constitutional Convention, including the Great Compromise and the compromises over slavery.
Distinguish federalism, separation of powers, and checks and balances as the Constitution's core structural principles.
Trace ratification and the Federalist and Anti-Federalist debate through to the Bill of Rights.
Analyze how the amendment process has let the Constitution change over time.

collegeVersion.heading: Why the first framework failed: the Articles of Confederation
collegeVersion.body: The United States did not begin under the Constitution. Its first national framework was the Articles of Confederation, drafted during the Revolution and in force from 1781. The Articles created a loose league of largely sovereign states with a single-chamber Congress and no independent executive or national judiciary. This was deliberate: it kept power close to the states as a reaction against the centralized authority of the British Crown. In practice the design proved too weak to govern. Congress could request money from the states but could not tax them; it could not regulate commerce among the states or bargain forcefully over trade abroad. With an empty treasury, heavy war debt, and inflation, the government could pay neither its soldiers nor its creditors. Worse, amending the Articles required the unanimous agreement of all thirteen states, which made reform nearly impossible. Shays' Rebellion, an armed uprising of indebted farmers in western Massachusetts in 1786 and early 1787, convinced many leaders that the confederation could not maintain order or protect property. In February 1787 Congress authorized a convention in Philadelphia to revise the Articles. The delegates who gathered would instead discard them and design a new government.

collegeVersion.heading: The Convention and the Great Compromise
collegeVersion.body: Fifty-five delegates met at the Pennsylvania State House in Philadelphia beginning in May 1787. They chose George Washington to preside and agreed to debate in secret. Although Congress had authorized only revisions, the delegates quickly decided to write an entirely new constitution. The central conflict was representation. The Virginia Plan, largely James Madison's work, proposed a bicameral (two-chamber) legislature in which both houses were apportioned by population, an arrangement that favored populous states like Virginia. Smaller states countered with the New Jersey Plan, which kept a single chamber giving every state an equal vote. The deadlock threatened to end the convention. The resolution, credited to Roger Sherman of Connecticut and known as the Great Compromise (or Connecticut Compromise), split the difference: Congress would have two chambers. In the House of Representatives, seats would be apportioned by population, satisfying the large states; in the Senate, each state, large or small, would have two senators and thus an equal vote. This bicameral structure remains the basic shape of Congress today. The compromise made agreement possible, but it settled the arithmetic of representation only by raising a harder question the delegates could not avoid: how enslaved people would be counted.

collegeVersion.heading: The compromises over slavery
collegeVersion.body: Slavery shaped the Constitution even though the document never uses the word 'slave.' Southern delegates wanted enslaved people counted toward a state's population so that slaveholding states would gain more seats in the House and more votes in the Electoral College. Northern delegates objected that people held as property should not inflate their enslavers' political power. The Three-Fifths Compromise settled the dispute by counting each enslaved person as three-fifths of a free person for both representation and direct taxation. The formula was not a statement about human worth; it was a bargain that increased the political power of slaveholding states for decades while granting enslaved people no rights at all. A second bargain concerned the Atlantic slave trade. To keep the Deep South in the union, the delegates agreed that Congress could not prohibit the importation of enslaved people before the year 1808 (Article I, Section 9). Congress did ban the trade as soon as the clause allowed, effective in 1808, though slavery itself continued and expanded until the Civil War. These compromises are best understood plainly: the framers protected slavery in order to secure agreement, embedding it in the nation's founding structure and leaving a contradiction that later generations would have to confront.

collegeVersion.heading: Federalism, separation of powers, and checks and balances
collegeVersion.body: The Constitution's lasting design rests on three principles. Federalism divides authority between the national government and the states, giving each its own powers while making national law supreme within its sphere, a middle path between the failed confederation and a single centralized state. Separation of powers assigns the three basic functions of government to three branches: Congress (Article I) makes law, the president and executive branch (Article II) carry it out, and the federal courts (Article III) interpret it. Checks and balances then give each branch tools to limit the others so that no single branch dominates. The president can veto legislation, but Congress can override a veto; Congress can impeach and remove officials, including the president; the Senate confirms major appointments and approves treaties; and the courts can measure laws and actions against the Constitution. These ideas drew on Enlightenment political thought, especially Montesquieu's argument for separating powers and John Locke's claim that a government's authority derives from the consent of the governed, adapted to American conditions. The point was structural: liberty would be protected less by the personal virtue of officials than by an arrangement in which ambition was made to check ambition.

collegeVersion.heading: Ratification, the Bill of Rights, and an amendable Constitution
collegeVersion.body: The Constitution took effect only after ratification. Under Article VII, nine of the thirteen states had to approve it in special conventions. A fierce public debate followed between Federalists, who supported the Constitution and argued its case in The Federalist Papers (essays by Alexander Hamilton, James Madison, and John Jay), and Anti-Federalists, who feared a distant central government would swallow the states and endanger individual liberty. Their strongest objection was the absence of a bill of rights. New Hampshire became the ninth state to ratify on June 21, 1788, meeting the threshold, and the new government began operating in 1789. To answer the Anti-Federalists, the first Congress proposed amendments, and on December 15, 1791, ten of them were ratified as the Bill of Rights, guaranteeing freedoms such as speech, religion, the press, and fair legal procedure. Crucially, the framers built in a way to change the document. Article V allows amendments proposed by a two-thirds vote of both houses of Congress (or a convention) and ratified by three-fourths of the states. That process is why the Constitution could later abolish slavery (Thirteenth Amendment, 1865), bar the denial of voting rights on account of race (Fifteenth, 1870), and extend the vote to women (Nineteenth, 1920). The framework endures in part because it can be revised.

vocabulary.definition: The first national framework of the United States, in force from 1781, which created a weak central government that could not tax or regulate interstate trade and had no independent executive.
A lawmaking body with two separate chambers; under the Constitution, the House of Representatives and the Senate.
The 1787 agreement that gave states representation by population in the House and equal representation (two senators each) in the Senate.
The agreement to count each enslaved person as three-fifths of a free person when apportioning representation and direct taxes, which increased slaveholding states' political power.
The division of governing authority between a national government and the state governments, each with its own powers.
The assignment of lawmaking, enforcement, and interpretation to three distinct branches of government.
The powers each branch of government holds to limit the actions of the others, preventing any one branch from dominating.
The formal approval of the Constitution by state conventions; Article VII required nine of the thirteen states.
The first ten amendments to the Constitution, ratified in 1791, guaranteeing specific individual freedoms and legal protections.
A formal change to the Constitution, proposed by a two-thirds vote of Congress or a convention and ratified by three-fourths of the states.

eli10.simplifiedExplanation: The country's first rulebook, the Articles of Confederation, was too weak. The national government could not collect taxes or manage trade, so it kept running out of money and authority. In 1787 leaders met in Philadelphia and wrote a stronger rulebook, the Constitution. To get everyone to agree, they made deals. Big and small states split power by giving the House seats based on population and the Senate two seats per state. Other deals protected slavery, counting enslaved people as three-fifths of a person to boost slaveholding states' power. The new government spread authority across three branches that watch one another, and it left a built-in way to make changes later.
eli10.analogy: The Constitution works like the bylaws a group writes after a first, flimsy set of rules keeps causing fights. Nobody gets everything they want, so they negotiate: some rules favor the big members, some the small, and the group builds in a formal procedure for editing the bylaws when they no longer fit.
eli10.analogyLimits: Bylaws for a club can be rewritten easily and rarely involve grave injustice. The Constitution is far harder to amend, governs millions of people, and its founding bargains protected slavery, a moral catastrophe no ordinary set of bylaws carries. The analogy captures the negotiation and the editing process, not the stakes.

workedExample: Consider how the Three-Fifths Compromise changed political power. Suppose a Southern state has 100,000 free residents and 50,000 enslaved people. Under the compromise, its population for apportioning House seats counts the free residents plus three-fifths of the enslaved: 100,000 + (0.6 x 50,000) = 130,000. A Northern state with 130,000 free residents and no slavery would receive the same number of House seats and electoral votes, even though 50,000 people in the Southern state were counted while being denied every political right. Multiplied across the South, this arithmetic gave slaveholding states a durable bonus in Congress and in presidential elections for decades.

commonMistakes.mistake: Believing the Constitution was the first framework of U.S. government.
commonMistakes.correction: The Articles of Confederation came first (in force 1781). The Constitution replaced them because they were too weak to tax, regulate trade, or provide an executive.

commonMistakes.mistake: Reading the Three-Fifths Compromise as a limit on slavery or a comment on human worth.
commonMistakes.correction: It was a political bargain that inflated slaveholding states' representation and electoral power while giving enslaved people no rights; it strengthened slavery's hold on national politics.

commonMistakes.mistake: Treating separation of powers and checks and balances as the same thing.
commonMistakes.correction: Separation of powers divides government into three branches; checks and balances are the specific tools each branch uses to limit the others.

commonMistakes.mistake: Assuming the Bill of Rights was part of the original 1787 document.
commonMistakes.correction: The Constitution was signed in 1787 without a bill of rights; the first ten amendments were added later and ratified in 1791.

compareContrast.distinction: The Articles kept power in the states with no taxing authority and no executive; the Constitution created a stronger national government able to tax and regulate commerce, with three branches.
Federalists backed ratification and a strong national government; Anti-Federalists feared centralized power and demanded a bill of rights to protect individual liberty.

Separation of powers is the structural division into three branches; checks and balances are the mutual controls (veto, override, impeachment, confirmation, judicial review) that keep the branches in tension.

keyTakeaway: The Constitution replaced the failed Articles of Confederation with a stronger government built on federalism, separation of powers, and checks and balances, made possible by compromises that also protected slavery; its Article V amendment process is what later allowed the nation to abolish slavery and expand the vote.

questionBank.prompt: Why was the Articles of Confederation considered too weak to govern the new nation?
options: The national government could not tax or regulate interstate trade and had no independent executive.
It gave the president unchecked power over the state governments.
It abolished the state governments and centralized all power in Congress.
It allowed any single state to pass national laws on its own.
questionBank.explanation: Under the Articles, Congress could request but not levy taxes, could not regulate commerce among the states, and had no executive branch, leaving the government unable to pay debts or enforce policy. The other options invert or misstate the framework: it kept power in the states, had no strong executive, and left the states intact.
questionBank.skill: Recalling the weaknesses of the Articles of Confederation

questionBank.prompt: The Great (Connecticut) Compromise of 1787 resolved a dispute over which issue?
options: Whether the Constitution should include a bill of rights.
Whether the Atlantic slave trade should be permitted after 1808.
How the states would be represented in Congress.
Whether the president should have the power to veto laws.
questionBank.explanation: The compromise broke the deadlock between large states (who wanted representation by population) and small states (who wanted an equal vote) by creating a House apportioned by population and a Senate with two seats per state. The bill of rights, the slave trade, and the veto were separate matters.
questionBank.skill: Identifying what the Great Compromise settled

questionBank.prompt: A delegate from a small state wants his state to hold influence equal to that of large states in at least one chamber of Congress. Which feature of the final Constitution meets that goal?
options: The three-fifths counting of enslaved people.
Equal representation of every state in the Senate, with two senators each.
Representation apportioned by population in the House.
The clause protecting the slave trade until 1808.
questionBank.explanation: The Senate gives every state two senators regardless of size, so a small state has the same Senate vote as a large one. House representation is by population (favoring large states), while the three-fifths and slave-trade clauses concern slavery, not small-state parity.
questionBank.skill: Applying the structure of Congress to a state's interest

questionBank.prompt: How did the Three-Fifths Compromise affect political power in the decades before the Civil War?
options: It reduced the number of House seats held by slaveholding states.
It counted enslaved people fully and gave them representation in Congress.
It affected only taxation and had no effect on representation.
It increased slaveholding states' House seats and electoral votes by counting enslaved people who could not vote.
questionBank.explanation: By adding three-fifths of the enslaved population to a state's count for apportionment, the clause inflated slaveholding states' representation in the House and their votes in the Electoral College, even though those counted had no rights. It did not reduce their seats, did not grant enslaved people representation, and affected both taxation and representation.
questionBank.skill: Analyzing the political consequences of the Three-Fifths Compromise

questionBank.prompt: What do the Bill of Rights and later amendments demonstrate about the Constitution?
options: That it cannot be changed once it has been ratified.
That it was complete and final when signed in 1787.
That it can be amended, as when the Thirteenth Amendment (1865) abolished slavery.
That it can be changed only by a nationwide popular referendum.
questionBank.explanation: Article V provides an amendment process, and it has been used: the Bill of Rights (1791) and later amendments such as the Thirteenth (1865) show the document is revisable. It is not unchangeable, was not final in 1787 (the Bill of Rights came later), and is amended through Congress and the states, not a national referendum.
questionBank.skill: Recognizing that the Constitution is amendable and how

title: The Early Republic
in30Seconds: The Early Republic is the first generation of the United States under the Constitution, roughly 1789 to the 1820s. A brand-new government had to invent how to actually govern. Washington set lasting precedents, Hamilton built a financial system, and the leaders who had hoped to avoid parties split into two anyway. The country doubled in size, the Supreme Court claimed the power to judge laws, and a fight over slavery was postponed but never solved.
whyItMatters: Almost nothing about the American government was guaranteed to work. The Constitution was a plan on paper; the Early Republic is where people turned it into a working state and decided which choices would become traditions. The cabinet, the two-term presidency, judicial review, and a national financial system all date from these years. So does the party competition the founders dreaded and the sectional conflict over slavery that a series of compromises only delayed. Understanding this period explains why later American politics runs the way it does, and it is a case study in how fragile new institutions are made durable, or are not.
learningObjectives: Identify the key precedents George Washington set as the first president
Explain Hamilton's financial program and why it provoked opposition
Distinguish the Federalists from the Democratic-Republicans
Describe the significance of the Louisiana Purchase and Marbury v. Madison in 1803
Analyze how the Missouri Compromise managed, but did not resolve, sectional tension over slavery

collegeVersion.heading: A government invents itself
collegeVersion.body: When George Washington was first inaugurated in 1789, the Constitution described a government that did not yet exist in practice. Almost every early decision became a precedent. Washington assembled the first cabinet, appointing Alexander Hamilton as secretary of the treasury, Thomas Jefferson as secretary of state, Henry Knox as secretary of war, and Edmund Randolph as attorney general, establishing the practice of a president advised by the heads of executive departments. When he declined to run for a third term in his Farewell Address of 1796, he set the two-term tradition that held until the 1940s and was later written into the Twenty-second Amendment. In foreign policy, facing war between Britain and revolutionary France, he declared the United States neutral in 1793 and used the Farewell Address to advise the country to 'steer clear of permanent alliances.' These were not inevitable outcomes; they were choices by a leader aware that whatever he did would be copied.

collegeVersion.heading: Hamilton's financial system
collegeVersion.body: The new nation carried heavy Revolutionary War debt and had shaky credit. As treasury secretary, Hamilton produced a plan to fix both. His Report on Public Credit (January 1790) urged the federal government to honor its debts at face value and to assume the war debts the states still owed, tying creditors' interests to the success of the national government. His Report on a National Bank (December 1790) proposed a Bank of the United States, modeled on the Bank of England, to hold federal funds and stabilize the currency; Washington signed its charter in 1791. Hamilton also favored tariffs to encourage American manufacturing. The program worked financially, but it concentrated power in the federal government and favored merchants and creditors, which is exactly why it drew fierce opposition.

collegeVersion.heading: The parties nobody wanted
collegeVersion.body: The founders had hoped the republic could run without organized parties, which they associated with faction and corruption. It did not. Opposition to Hamilton's program, led by Jefferson and James Madison, hardened into the first party system. Hamilton's Federalists favored a strong central government, commerce and manufacturing, close ties with Britain, and a loose reading of the Constitution that permitted things like a national bank. Jefferson and Madison's Democratic-Republicans favored an agrarian republic of farmers, states' rights, sympathy with France, and a strict reading of the Constitution that limited federal power to its enumerated grants. The disputes were constitutional and economic, but also about competing visions of what kind of society the United States should be. The Whiskey Rebellion of 1794, when western Pennsylvania farmers resisted a federal excise tax and Washington personally led troops to suppress it, showed both the government's new strength and the depth of the disagreement over federal authority.

collegeVersion.heading: 1803: a bigger country and a stronger court
collegeVersion.body: Two events in 1803 reshaped the republic. In the Louisiana Purchase, the United States bought the vast Louisiana territory from France for $15 million, roughly doubling the size of the country and opening the trans-Mississippi West. The deal put Jefferson in an awkward spot: normally a strict constructionist, he doubted the government had explicit authority to acquire territory, but he set those doubts aside rather than lose the opportunity, a telling example of principle bending to circumstance. The same year, in Marbury v. Madison, Chief Justice John Marshall's Supreme Court declared part of a federal law unconstitutional for the first time and established judicial review, the courts' power to measure the acts of Congress and the president against the Constitution. Expansion and judicial review are both defining features of the American system, and both trace to this single year.

collegeVersion.heading: War, and a fight postponed
collegeVersion.body: Between 1812 and 1815 the United States fought Britain again in the War of 1812, driven by British impressment of American sailors, interference with neutral shipping, and tensions on the western frontier. Militarily it was a draw; the Treaty of Ghent, signed on December 24, 1814, simply restored the prewar boundaries. But the war fed a surge of national feeling. The harder problem was internal. As new states organized, the balance between slave and free states in the Senate became explosive. The Missouri Compromise of 1820 admitted Missouri as a slave state and Maine as a free state at the same time to keep that balance, and banned slavery in the remaining Louisiana territory north of the latitude line 36 degrees 30 minutes. It worked, for a while. But it managed the conflict over slavery rather than resolving it; the line was repealed in 1854 and struck down in 1857, and the underlying dispute would eventually reach the Civil War.

vocabulary.definition: An action taken for the first time that later serves as an example or rule for how a similar situation should be handled.
The group of heads of executive departments who advise the president; first assembled under Washington.
Hamilton's plan for the federal government to take over and pay the debts the individual states had run up during the Revolutionary War.
Interpreting the Constitution to permit powers reasonably implied by it, not only those explicitly listed; used to justify the national bank.
Interpreting the Constitution to allow only powers it explicitly grants, limiting federal authority; associated with Jefferson and Madison.
The power of courts to decide whether laws or executive actions conflict with the Constitution and to strike them down if they do.
A policy of not taking sides in a war between other nations; declared by Washington in 1793.
Loyalty to the interests of one region of a country over the nation as a whole; here, the growing divide between North and South over slavery.
Latin for 'the state existing before the war'; the basis of the Treaty of Ghent, which restored prewar boundaries.

eli10.simplifiedExplanation: Imagine a group finally finishes writing the rulebook for a brand-new club, and now they have to actually run it for the first time. Every first choice, who advises the leader, how long the leader stays, whether to pick sides in other people's fights, quietly becomes 'the way we do things.' The first American leaders had to make all those first choices. They also disagreed hard about how strong the central group should be, so they split into two teams even though they had promised themselves they wouldn't. Along the way the country bought a giant piece of land, the judges claimed the right to say when a rule breaks the rulebook, and everyone quietly avoided the biggest, ugliest argument, slavery, by making deals instead of settling it.
eli10.analogy: The Early Republic is like the first season of a company after the founders write the employee handbook: the handbook exists, but people are still figuring out what actually happens on day one, and the habits they fall into become permanent policy.
eli10.analogyLimits: A company can rewrite its handbook whenever managers want, and its disagreements rarely threaten to split the whole firm in two. A nation changing its constitution is far harder, and the argument over slavery was a moral catastrophe, not an office policy dispute, so the stakes were incomparably higher.

workedExample: Consider how one 1803 decision reveals the whole period's tension. Jefferson led the Democratic-Republicans, who insisted on strict construction: the federal government may do only what the Constitution explicitly authorizes. The Constitution says nothing about buying foreign territory. So when France offered the Louisiana territory for $15 million, Jefferson's own principles told him he might lack the authority. He considered seeking a constitutional amendment, but France might withdraw the offer first. He chose the purchase, doubling the country and setting aside his strict-construction doubts. Trace the logic: a leader's stated constitutional theory (strict construction) collided with a concrete opportunity (cheap, enormous land), and the opportunity won. That is exactly the kind of gap between principle and practice that defines how the Early Republic actually worked.

commonMistakes.mistake: Thinking the founders intended and welcomed political parties.
commonMistakes.correction: They feared parties as sources of faction. The two-party split emerged despite their hopes, out of the fight over Hamilton's program.

commonMistakes.mistake: Believing judicial review is written into the Constitution.
commonMistakes.correction: The Constitution does not explicitly grant it. The Supreme Court asserted it in Marbury v. Madison (1803), and it became established practice.

commonMistakes.mistake: Assuming the Missouri Compromise solved the slavery conflict.
commonMistakes.correction: It only postponed it, keeping a Senate balance and drawing a line. The line was repealed in 1854 and struck down in 1857, and the conflict led toward civil war.

commonMistakes.mistake: Confusing the Louisiana Purchase with later westward conquest or with statehood.
commonMistakes.correction: The 1803 purchase was a land transaction with France that doubled U.S. territory; settling, organizing, and admitting that land as states came later and belongs to the fuller expansion story.

commonMistakes.mistake: Thinking the United States clearly won the War of 1812.
commonMistakes.correction: The Treaty of Ghent (1814) restored the prewar status quo with no clear victor; the war's main effect was a surge of national feeling, not territorial gain.

compareContrast.distinction: Federalists (Hamilton) wanted a strong central government, commerce and manufacturing, and loose construction; Democratic-Republicans (Jefferson, Madison) wanted an agrarian republic, states' rights, and strict construction.
Loose construction reads the Constitution to permit implied powers (justifying the national bank); strict construction limits government to explicitly granted powers.
Both fell in the same year, but one expanded the nation's territory through a treaty with France, while the other expanded the judiciary's power by establishing judicial review.

keyTakeaway: In its first decades the United States turned a written constitution into a working government, setting lasting precedents, splitting into the parties its founders had hoped to avoid, doubling in size, and postponing rather than resolving the conflict over slavery.

questionBank.prompt: In the Louisiana Purchase of 1803, from which country did the United States buy the Louisiana territory?
options: France
Spain
Great Britain
Mexico
questionBank.explanation: The United States purchased the Louisiana territory from France for $15 million in 1803, roughly doubling the country's size. Spain had earlier controlled the territory but had ceded it back to France; Britain and Mexico were not the sellers.
questionBank.skill: Recalling the parties and terms of the Louisiana Purchase

questionBank.prompt: What constitutional principle did the Supreme Court establish in Marbury v. Madison (1803)?
options: Federal supremacy over state courts
The president's power to remove judges
Congress's power to charter a national bank
Judicial review of the constitutionality of laws
questionBank.explanation: Chief Justice John Marshall's opinion established judicial review, the courts' power to determine whether acts of the other branches are constitutional, and struck down part of a federal law for the first time. The other options describe different doctrines not established by this case.
questionBank.skill: Identifying the holding of Marbury v. Madison

questionBank.prompt: How did the Missouri Compromise of 1820 try to keep the balance between slave and free states?
options: It abolished slavery in Missouri while allowing it in Maine
It admitted Missouri as a slave state and Maine as a free state at the same time
It ended the importation of enslaved people into all new territories
It gave each territory a popular vote on slavery before statehood
questionBank.explanation: The compromise admitted Missouri as a slave state and Maine as a free state simultaneously to preserve the Senate balance, and banned slavery in Louisiana territory north of 36 degrees 30 minutes. It did not abolish slavery in Missouri, end importation (already banned in 1808), or introduce popular sovereignty, which came later.
questionBank.skill: Explaining the mechanism of the Missouri Compromise

questionBank.prompt: A modern commentator argues that the United States should avoid binding itself to a permanent military alliance. Which precedent from the Early Republic most directly supports appealing to this idea?
options: Hamilton's creation of the Bank of the United States
The Whiskey Rebellion of 1794
Washington's Farewell Address advising against permanent alliances
The Missouri Compromise line at 36 degrees 30 minutes
questionBank.explanation: In his 1796 Farewell Address, Washington counseled the nation to 'steer clear of permanent alliances,' the founding precedent for that argument. The national bank concerned finance, the Whiskey Rebellion concerned federal tax enforcement, and the Missouri Compromise concerned slavery, not foreign alliances.
questionBank.skill: Applying Washington's foreign-policy precedent to a new argument

questionBank.prompt: Jefferson generally insisted the federal government could exercise only powers the Constitution explicitly grants, yet he completed the Louisiana Purchase despite doubting it was authorized. What does this decision best illustrate about the Early Republic?
options: That the Federalists controlled the presidency in 1803
That the Constitution explicitly authorized buying foreign territory
That parties had disappeared by Jefferson's presidency
That leaders' constitutional principles could bend to concrete opportunities
questionBank.explanation: Jefferson's strict-construction principles collided with the chance to double the country cheaply, and the opportunity won, illustrating the gap between stated principle and practice. The Federalists did not hold the presidency (Jefferson, a Democratic-Republican, did); the Constitution did not explicitly authorize the purchase, which is why he hesitated; and parties were very much active.
questionBank.skill: Analyzing the tension between constitutional principle and political opportunity
